d: The Foundational Principles of Governed Knowledge Systems
x: Why a Canon? Engineering disciplines are organised around enduring principles that remain valid even as methods, technologies and implementations change. Mechanical engineering outlived the steam engine. Software engineering outlived the languages it was first written in. The principles endure because they describe obligations, not instruments. Knowledge engineering adopts the same structure. Its tools — expert systems, ontologies, knowledge graphs, foundation models — have already turned over several times, and will again. What does not turn over is the set of obligations a system incurs the moment it holds knowledge on behalf of people who will act on it. This document states those obligations. It is a Canon, not a manual. The Literature Landscape is where the discipline weighs evidence and persuades; the Canon is where it legislates. Everything that follows is written to be inherited unchanged by the methods, architectures and implementations built beneath it, and to remain true long after any of them is replaced. The Purpose of the Discipline Every mature discipline has a single sentence that explains why it exists — medicine’s first, do no harm , accounting’s true and fair view . Knowledge engineering has one too: The purpose of knowledge engineering is to preserve, improve and govern the evolution of justified knowledge so that it remains trustworthy across time, institutions and computational modalities. Every principle in this Canon serves that sentence. A statement that does not serve it does not belong here. Purpose These principles define the intellectual foundations of governed knowledge systems . Knowledge Foundry is one methodology that adopts them; it is not their source, and they do not depend on it. The Canon derives the principles that any governed knowledge system must satisfy — regardless of implementation technology, organisational setting, or computational modality. Subsequent methodology, architecture and implementation documents inherit them rather than redefining them. A principle earns its place here only if it is true of the discipline, not merely of one methodology. The test is stated in The Discipline and Its Four Levels and applied to every principle that follows. Relationship to the Literature Landscape KF-L001 answered one question: What does the literature establish? The Canon answers a different one: What design principles necessarily follow from that evidence? The Literature Landscape is the evidential authority; the Canon converts settled evidence into obligation. No new literature is introduced. Where a principle is grounded in the Landscape, its derivation is cited by chapter and by Landscape Proposition (L-P1–L-P6), Proposition B01, Proposition C01, the six Governance Primitives, or the requirements register (R1–R10). The Canon adds no evidence of its own. The Discipline and Its Four Levels A mature engineering discipline separates what is always true from what is one way of acting on that truth . Knowledge Foundry adopts four levels. Each inherits from the one above; none may masquerade as another. Level Answers Stability Home document Principle What is always true of a governed knowledge system? Enduring KF-1000 (this Canon) Method How do we act on that truth? Revisable KF-2000 (Methodology) Architecture With what structures and components? Substitutable KF-3000 (Reference Architecture) Implementation In what specific deployment? Disposable KF-4000 (Knowledge Operating System), and its domain instantiations The worked example that fixes the boundaries: Level Statement about provenance Principle A knowledge state is legitimate only if the transition that produced it is inspectable. Method Track each operational knowledge object with a provenance graph of its transitions. Architecture Represent that graph in a property-graph store with signed, append-only edges. Implementation A domain deployment — such as a university course domain or a professional-body knowledge domain — records provenance in its Knowledge Operating System. The Canon Admission Test Every candidate principle is admitted only if it survives two questions: 1. Would this still be true if Knowledge Foundry ceased to exist? 2. Would this still be true fifty years from now, even if today’s AI models were obsolete? If either answer is no — if the statement presupposes a particular method, structure, product, deployment or generation of technology — it belongs below the line, in the Methodology, the Reference Architecture, or an Implementation. The two questions guard the two ways a statement fails to be constitutional: by belonging to one project, or by belonging to one era. This test is what separates a discipline from a framework. It is applied to each of the ten principles, every one of which closes with a Below the line note recording what it excludes. Each principle is derived primarily from a chapter of the Landscape, but no principle is a summary of a chapter . A summary restates evidence; a principle states an obligation the evidence makes unavoidable. Several principles draw on the whole Landscape, and the later ones arise only when the chapters are read together. How to Read This Canon Part I defines the object and the system. Part II states the invariants that make principles necessary. Part III states the ten principles. Part IV draws their design consequences without descending into method. Part V is the bridge to KF-2000. Read in order, the Canon moves from what a governed knowledge system is to what its existence obliges — and stops where method begins. Part I · Foundations KF-1001 · The Nature of Governed Knowledge Systems Purpose. Establish the central object of the discipline and define what a governed knowledge system is. The central object Knowledge systems never reach past their representations to touch knowledge itself (Proposition B01; L-P1). What they hold and change is the Operational Knowledge Object : a versioned representation together with its attached evidence, justification and acceptance-state. It is the concrete instance of the abstract Conceptual Object — representation → claim → evidence → justification → acceptance — that B01 defines. The discipline takes the Operational Knowledge Object, not “knowledge,” as its unit of design. This is precision, not modesty. A system cannot engineer truth, because truth is not inspectable. It engineers the object that stands in for knowledge and carries the warrant a community attaches to it. Formal definition A governed knowledge system is a socio-technical system that holds operational knowledge objects and governs their transition from one justified state to another — across human, symbolic, parametric and hybrid modalities — so that warranted claims remain available, revisable and trustworthy over time. Four terms in this definition are canonical and are used throughout the programme: Governed evolution — the controlled transition of a knowledge system from one justified state to another; the discipline’s characteristic operation, and the persistent challenge the Landscape identifies (L-P6). Human–machine system — the system boundary includes the people and institutions that create, authorise and depend on its knowledge. They are inside the system, not external to it. Knowledge infrastructure — knowledge treated as durable, shared, continuously maintained substrate rather than as a bounded artefact or a project deliverable. Computational modality — the cross-cutting axis (Human · Symbolic · Parametric · Hybrid) along which the system’s operations are redistributed but never removed (L-P5). Deliverable. The definition above is the discipline’s fixed point. Every principle in Part III is a property of the system so defined; every method in KF-2000 is a way of realising one of those properties. Part II · Constitutional Invariants KF-1050 · What Never Changes Technology changes. Methods change. Architectures change. Products change. Institutions change. Yet some obligations remain invariant across all of them, and it is these invariants that make principles necessary. The ten principles of Part III are not free postulates; each one operationalises an invariant named here. This chapter is the Canon’s preamble: it states the properties that any governed knowledge system must exhibit in every era, before any principle prescribes how. Five invariants hold. Inspectability. Whatever a knowledge system holds must be capable of being examined. A system whose contents cannot be inspected cannot be justified, explained, audited or corrected. Inspectability is prior to all of these; it is the condition that makes governance possible at all. Justification. A claim held as knowledge must carry the grounds on which it is held. Warrant, not mere assertion, is what distinguishes knowledge from information. A system may hold much that is unjustified, but it may not call that knowledge. Provenance. The history of a claim — where it came from, how it changed, on whose authority — must be recoverable. A present state that cannot be traced to the transitions that produced it cannot be trusted, however plausible it appears. Governed evolution. Knowledge changes, and the change must be controlled rather than incidental. A system in which states can shift without proposal, evidence, authority and release does not hold knowledge; it accumulates content. Human accountability. Some identifiable person or body must answer for what a system accepts as knowledge. Operations may be distributed across people and machines, but accountability may not be discharged into a substrate. There is always someone who is answerable. These five are not yet the principles. They are the properties whose loss would make a system cease to be a governed knowledge system. The principles that follow give them force: they state, for each invariant, the obligation it imposes on anyone who would build such a system. An invariant answers what must always hold ; a principle answers what that obligates us to do . Part III · The Canonical Principles The ten principles are the constitutional core of the discipline. Each is stated as an obligation, derived from the Landscape, shown to survive both questions of the Admission Test, and closed with the line it must not cross. They are numbered I–X and carried under document IDs KF-1101–KF-1110 so that later documents can cite a principle in two characters. KF-1101 · Principle I — Knowledge systems govern operational knowledge objects, never knowledge itself Derived primarily from B01 (Proposition B01; L-P1; the Inspectable Objects Principle). Invariant: inspectability. A knowledge system does not contain knowledge. It contains representations, the evidence and justification attached to them, and their acceptance-state under some authority. “Knowledge” is the name a community gives to an operational knowledge object that has cleared those tests. Truth and the tacit remainder lie permanently outside the system’s reach. This principle fixes the object every other principle acts upon. It dissolves a standing confusion: whether a system “really contains knowledge” is mis-posed. No system does, and none needs to. What a system holds, warrants, governs and revises is the operational knowledge object. Admission Test. True of every knowledge system ever built, from a 1970s rule base to a foundation model, and true of any yet to be built. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): how an operational knowledge object is represented is method ; the store that holds it is architecture ; a particular deployment is implementation . The Canon fixes only that the object — not knowledge — is what is governed. KF-1102 · Principle II — A knowledge system is engineered as a lifecycle, not as an artefact Derived primarily from B02 (L-P2; the expanding object of engineering). Invariant: governed evolution. The object of knowledge engineering has widened, across five decades, from expert reasoning to whole hybrid systems. With that widening, the engineering task moved from constructing an artefact once to governing its continuous change. To engineer a knowledge system is to engineer its lifecycle: the unit of engineering is the transition , not the finished representation. Continuous evolution is not a feature added to a built artefact. It is the thing being built. A method designed for one-off, up-front construction contradicts this principle. Admission Test. Any system that holds knowledge over time faces change whether or not it is designed for it; the obligation to engineer that change is independent of any technology or project. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): which lifecycle stages to define, and how to move between them, is method ; the pipelines and stores that realise them are architecture . KF-1103 · Principle III — Knowledge becomes enduring capability only through collective authorisation Derived primarily from B03 (L-P3). Invariant: human accountability. Knowledge that endures is not a possession of an individual or a property of a machine. It is a capability of a collective, held in place by authorisation, legitimation and stewardship. Acceptance — the act by which a community with authority certifies a claim as settled — is what turns a well-justified representation into “what we know.” A governed knowledge system is socio-technical by necessity, not by preference. Its boundary includes the people and institutions that warrant its claims. A system that treats authorisation as external to itself has mislocated the source of the durability it depends on. Admission Test. The collective and authorised character of enduring knowledge holds across organisations, disciplines and centuries. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): which roles hold which decision rights, and through what workflow authorisation flows, is method and architecture ; who staffs those roles is implementation . KF-1104 · Principle IV — Governance is constitutive of knowledge, not supervisory over it Derived primarily from B04 (L-P4; the six Governance Primitives). Invariant: justification. Governance is not a control layer placed on top of finished knowledge. It is what makes a representation count as knowledge at all. Strip away evidence, authority, provenance, validation, versioning and reversibility — the six Governance Primitives — and what remains is information, not knowledge. The primitives are the operations by which warrant is conferred; warrant is what distinguishes the two. This inverts the intuition that governance constrains an otherwise-complete asset. Governance is the asset’s condition of existence. Stated at full strength: a knowledge state is only as legitimate as the governance that produced it. Admission Test. The dependence of knowledge-status on warrant, and of warrant on governance, is a claim about knowledge, not about any methodology or era. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): how each primitive is instantiated — the shape of a validation gate, the format of a provenance record — is method and architecture . The primitives themselves are constitutional. KF-1105 · Principle V — Computational modality redistributes epistemic labour but never discharges epistemic obligation Derived primarily from B05 (L-P5; “the substrate changes; the epistemic obligations do not”). Invariant: justification. A new computational substrate — parametric, agentic, hybrid — changes where knowledge resides and who or what performs each operation. It does not change the obligations to justify, authorise, preserve and govern the resulting claims. Foundation models introduced a new representation, not a new epistemology; they relocated capability across the symbolic–parametric boundary rather than abolishing it. This principle forbids the recurring error of granting a modality an epistemic discount — of treating a fluent generated answer as if it carried warrant it has not earned. Opacity of substrate is not a licence for opacity of obligation. Admission Test. The principle is written about any substrate, not today’s. It survives the obsolescence of current models precisely because it refuses to attach obligation to a technology. Passes both questions — and Question 2 is its point. Below the line (not Canon): how to honour an obligation in a difficult modality — grounding generation in retrieved evidence, reconstructing provenance for a model weight — is method ; the model and index that do so are architecture . KF-1106 · Principle VI — A knowledge system is irreducibly engineered, collective and governed at once Derived primarily from C01 (Proposition C01; the integrated reference model). Invariant: governed evolution. Engineering, capability and governance are not three kinds of knowledge system. They are three operations that every knowledge system undergoes simultaneously on a single object. No system is only engineered, only collective, or only governed. To hold any one of these steady while working only on another — the division of labour the Landscape found across the literature — is to describe part of a system, never the whole. The deficiency the Landscape identified was therefore one of coordination : the literature explains each operation in isolation and does not explain their coordination over the lifecycle of one governed object (Proposition C01). This principle makes coordination a first-class obligation. Admission Test. The irreducibility of the three operations is a structural fact about knowledge systems, independent of who coordinates them or when. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): the coordination mechanism — how a single change propagates across engineering, capability and governance — is the central method of KF-2000. The Canon fixes only that the three are inseparable. KF-1107 · Principle VII — Trust in a knowledge system is a property of its transitions over time, not of its state Derived from B04 and C01 (L-P6; the records-continuum and provenance traditions). Invariant: provenance. A knowledge system is not trustworthy because of what it holds at an instant. It is trustworthy because the history of how it came to hold it can itself be trusted. Trust is carried by transitions — by the appraisal, provenance, authenticity and controlled release that survive each change — not by any snapshot. Change is constitutive of a knowledge system; the question is whether trust survives it. This is the temporal principle. It obliges a system to treat its own past as evidence: to retain, reconstruct and authenticate prior states, so that a present claim can be traced to the transitions that produced it. Admission Test. That trustworthiness-over-time is a property of change rather than of state holds for any records system or knowledge system, in any era. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): retention windows, versioning schemes and authenticity mechanisms are method and architecture ; how long an institution keeps a given state is implementation . KF-1108 · Principle VIII — No knowledge state is legitimate without an inspectable justification for how it was reached Derived from B01 and B04 (Proposition B01; Evidence/Justification and Provenance primitives; R2, R4, R6). Invariants: justification, inspectability. Every transition of an operational knowledge object carries its justification: the evidence, reasoning and authority under which the new state was accepted. Acceptance without recorded, inspectable justification is assertion, not knowledge. A system can engineer justification even though it cannot engineer truth — justification is the richest thing it can govern — and so justification, not truth, is the standard to which every transition is held. Principle VIII is the per-transition consequence of Principle IV: if governance is constitutive, each individual change must bear the warrant that governance confers. A knowledge state whose justification cannot be inspected has no standing, however plausible it appears. Admission Test. The requirement that legitimate knowledge carry inspectable justification is epistemic, not methodological, and not tied to any generation of tools. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): the structure of a justification record and the interface that exposes it are method and architecture . KF-1109 · Principle IX — A knowledge system must remain explainable irrespective of the modality in which its knowledge resides Derived from B02, B05 and C01 (the explanation imperative; the parametric opacity findings). Invariants: inspectability, human accountability. The demand that a system explain its conclusions is one of the discipline’s oldest commitments, and it does not lapse when knowledge moves into an opaque substrate. Where the substrate cannot be read directly — as with parametric knowledge — explainability becomes an obligation the system meets by design around the substrate, not an excuse the substrate provides. Explainability is owed by the system, not by the component. The principle sets a standard the hardest modality must still meet. A system may hold knowledge it cannot introspect; it may not therefore hold knowledge it cannot account for. Admission Test. Explainability as an obligation of knowledge systems predates today’s models and will outlast them; the techniques will change, the obligation will not. Passes both questions — and Question 2 is its point. Below the line (not Canon): the techniques that deliver explanation — retrieval grounding, citation, surrogate inspection, neuro-symbolic structure — are method and architecture , and will change; the obligation will not. KF-1110 · Principle X — A knowledge system is designed for governed evolution, not for preservation Derived from the entire Landscape (L-P2, L-P6; Proposition C01). Invariant: governed evolution. The default condition of knowledge is change. A governed knowledge system is designed, from the first, for governed evolution. Preservation is a special, bounded case of evolution — the decision to hold a state trustworthy across time — not the system’s natural resting point. A design that treats stability as the norm and change as the exception has the discipline backwards. This principle gathers the other nine into a posture. The object is governed (I, IV); its engineering is a lifecycle (II); its durability is collective (III); its obligations survive any substrate (V, IX); its coordination is inseparable (VI); its trust and its legitimacy live in its transitions (VII, VIII). What persists through every iteration is not knowledge itself, but the governed transition from one accepted state to the next. Admission Test. That knowledge systems face continuous change, and are best designed for it, is true of the domain irrespective of any methodology or era. Passes both questions. Below the line (not Canon): the mechanics of a knowledge release — quality gates, rollback, promotion between states — are the core method of KF-2000; their components are architecture ; a running release cadence is implementation . Part IV · Design Consequences The principles are not methods, but they are not inert: they constrain the space of admissible methods, architectures and implementations. This part records those constraints without crossing into method. Each consequence is a boundary on KF-2000 and below. KF-1201 · Engineering Consequences The unit of engineering is the transition (II) and the object is the operational knowledge object (I). Governance cannot be bolted on after construction: versioning, provenance and justification are first-class from the first design increment (IV, VII, VIII). Representations must be inspectable, because a representation that cannot be inspected cannot be justified or explained (VIII, IX). Because the three operations are inseparable (VI), an engineering method that optimises one in isolation — a pipeline that builds without governing, or governs without accounting for modality — is inadmissible. KF-1202 · Governance Consequences All six Governance Primitives are present, or the system governs incompletely (IV). Authority is explicit and remains human, because legitimation is a collective act (III) and redistribution of labour across modalities does not redistribute accountability (V). Appraisal — deciding what to promote, retain and retire — is part of governance, not separate from it, because trust is a property of transitions over time (VII). Governance that only records change, without adjudicating whether a change should be promoted into an accepted state, satisfies none of these principles. KF-1203 · AI Consequences Parametric and agentic knowledge is subject to exactly the same obligations as symbolic knowledge (V). The substrate makes some obligations harder to honour — provenance and reversibility above all — but does not lift them. A generative core is engineered into a governed system, grounded in inspectable evidence, and made explainable by design around its opacity (VIII, IX). Autonomous agents may perform operations, but the authority to accept a claim into the knowledge state remains human (III, V). Any AI-native method that treats fluency as warrant, or model turnover as acceptable knowledge loss, violates the Canon. KF-1204 · Institutional Consequences Knowledge is infrastructure (KF-1001): an institution’s knowledge is a shared, maintained, evolving asset, not a collection of documents or a set of model weights. The organisation and its decision rights are inside the system (III). Continuity of collective memory survives personnel change and model change alike (VII, X). Institutions hold identifiable authority for knowledge transitions, and do not allow knowledge that lives only in a substitutable substrate to become knowledge they cannot guarantee they still possess. Part V · Transition to Methodology KF-1301 · From Principles to Methods The Canon ends where method begins. Its final task is to hand a clean set of obligations to KF-2000 and to fix, once, the rule that governs the handoff. Each principle becomes a demand on method without dictating the method: Principle Obligation handed to KF-2000 I Operate on operational knowledge objects as the unit of work II Engineer the lifecycle, not the artefact III Route authorisation through identified collective authority IV Instantiate all six Governance Primitives V Preserve every obligation across every modality VI Coordinate engineering, capability and governance on one object VII Preserve trust across transitions over time VIII Attach inspectable justification to every transition IX Deliver explanation irrespective of substrate X Default to governed evolution; treat preservation as its special case KF-2000 proposes methods that discharge these obligations; KF-3000 specifies architectures that realise those methods; KF-4000 demonstrates them in a reference implementation. The direction of inheritance is strict and one-way: a lower level may choose how to satisfy a higher one, but may never revise it. A method that cannot be reconciled with a principle yields to the principle — or the principle is challenged openly, here in the Canon, on the evidence of the Landscape, and not quietly overridden in practice. Relationship to Subsequent Documents KF-L001 — Literature Landscape establishes the evidence. KF-1000 — Canon establishes the principles. KF-2000 — Methodology defines the methods. KF-3000 — Reference Architecture specifies design patterns and system components. KF-4000 — Knowledge Operating System provides a reference implementation. Domain deployments — such as a university course domain, a professional-body knowledge domain, or an institutional decision system — are domain-specific instantiations of the Knowledge Operating System. Each document inherits, rather than revises, the Canon. A change to a principle is a constitutional amendment, made against the Landscape’s evidence and propagated downward; a change to a method, architecture or implementation is ordinary work that leaves the Canon untouched. Closing Statement The Literature Landscape demonstrated that the constituent elements of governed knowledge systems already exist across multiple mature traditions. The Canon states the enduring principles that integrate those elements into a coherent discipline. It is the constitutional foundation from which methodology, architecture and implementation derive. Its authority rests on a single discipline: every statement it contains would remain true if Knowledge Foundry itself were to disappear, and would remain true fifty years from now with today’s technologies long replaced. That is what makes it a Canon rather than a framework — and what the work built upon it must never be allowed to erode.

d: The canonical engineering lifecycle of a governed knowledge object, from capture to retirement
x: Purpose This document defines the canonical engineering lifecycle through which an Operational Knowledge Object evolves from initial capture to eventual retirement. It is the common engineering model beneath all Knowledge Foundry methods; the methods that follow in KF-2000 act on the stages defined here. The lifecycle models the evolution of justified knowledge , not the storage of information . A document-management system versions files and advances a record whenever it is saved; this lifecycle advances an object only when the obligations of its current stage are discharged. The difference is the gate. In a storage system a transition is a save event; here a transition is an act of warrant, and an object that has not earned the warrant of its stage does not advance, however complete it looks. How This Document Sits in the Programme KF-2001 is a Method-level document. It says how the discipline acts on the principles fixed by the Canon ( KF-1000 ); it does not restate or revise them. Consistent with the four-level separation, this document names no technologies, stores or products — those are architecture ( KF-3000 ) — and no deployments — those are implementation (KF-4000). Where a stage discharges a Canonical Principle, the principle is cited in a single Canon basis line; the authoritative stage-to-principle mapping is KF-2002 , and is not duplicated here. Method, Not Workflow This lifecycle specifies the engineering obligations associated with each stage — what must be true for an object to advance — not the workflow by which any particular organisation satisfies them. Method fixes the obligation; workflow fixes the order of work, the tools, the hand-offs and the cadence by which a given deployment meets it. Workflow therefore belongs to implementation (KF-4000), not here. Conformance is not a matter of following a prescribed sequence of steps. It is whether, for every object, every obligation and every lifecycle invariant is met. Two organisations may run very different workflows — one manual and deliberative, another largely automated — and both conform to this lifecycle, provided no gate is passed unearned and no invariant is broken. The Object and Its States The object under management is an Operational Knowledge Object throughout its life. What the lifecycle changes is its state , not its identity. The stage outputs below name successive states of one object — Candidate, Structured, Evaluated, Justified, Accepted, Operational, and so on — not distinct objects. An object becomes an Operational Knowledge Object in the full Canon sense once it carries representation, evidence, justification and an acceptance-state; the early stages assemble those attachments onto an object that already holds a stable identity. Terminology note (flagged design decision). “Operationalise” (Stage 5) makes an object’s knowledge actionable ; it is not the same word as “Operational Knowledge Object,” which names the artefact across its whole life. Where the two could be confused, this document calls the Stage-5 result the object’s actionable form and reserves “Operational Knowledge Object” for the artefact. The stage names from the source model are preserved unchanged. Lifecycle Overview Worked example. KF-5001 walks a single Operational Knowledge Object — a four-day-week Knowledge Brief — through every stage below, from Capture to Supersession. Each stage is a distinct engineering responsibility with a defined entry condition and an exit gate . An object progresses only when the exit gate of its current stage is satisfied; until then it remains in place or returns to an earlier stage. The stages are not all of one kind: Capture through Justify construct the object; Accept is a decision by authority, not engineering work, and is modelled as a transition; Operationalise realises it; Govern holds it in custody ; Apply uses it; Evolve changes it; Retire closes it. Application is the one step that does not transform the object — it is an operational context in which the object is used and from which evidence returns. The sequence above is the principal path , not the only path. As evidence changes, an object may return to an earlier stage, and from several steps it may pass directly to Retire. The lifecycle is a loop, not a ladder — a property inherited from the Landscape’s account of the knowledge object and made operational here through the return paths defined below. # Stage Engineering responsibility Output state Exit gate (in one line) 1 Capture Admit candidate information Candidate Origin recorded 2 Structure Give the object identity and form Structured Object is inspectable 3 Evaluate Assess quality before acceptance Evaluated Quality verdict recorded 4 Justify Establish epistemic legitimacy Justified Justification is inspectable — Accept (transition) Certify the object by authority Accepted Acceptance recorded by an authority 5 Operationalise Make knowledge actionable Operational (actionable) Actionable form linked to justification 6 Govern Maintain legitimacy over time Governed Ownership and review in force 7 Apply Use the object in practice (in use) → Outcomes Outcomes captured as feedback 8 Evolve Allow controlled improvement Next Version Change justified and versioned 9 Retire Conclude operational life Historical Reason recorded, history preserved The Three Dimensions of Every Transition A workflow advances one property: a status. This lifecycle advances three at once. Every transition changes not only the state of the object, but the evidence attached to it and the governance posture it has achieved. These three dimensions are independent — they answer different questions — and reading the lifecycle as only a sequence of states hides two-thirds of what each transition does. State — what the object is : the label that says how far it has progressed. Evidence — what is attached to the object: the accumulating record that travels with it. Governance posture — what is assured about the object: the governance property each step secures. Lifecycle step State (what it is) Evidence (what is attached) Governance posture (what is assured) Capture Candidate Origin Identity Structure Structured + metadata, relationships Inspectability Evaluate Evaluated + quality assessment Quality Justify Justified + justification Warrant Accept Accepted + acceptance record Authority Operationalise Operational + actionable form Operability Govern Governed + review history Ownership Apply (remains Governed) + operational outcomes Accountability in use Evolve Next Version + change record Reversibility Retire Historical + retirement record History Two features of this table matter. First, the three columns advance at different times: Apply adds evidence and governance assurance without changing the object’s state , which is precisely why application is a different kind of thing from the construction stages. Second, each column can be read on its own as a coherent progression — a reviewer auditing evidence need not trace state , and a reviewer auditing governance need not trace either. The lifecycle is richer than a pipeline because it is really three pipelines advancing on one object. The Nine Stages Stage 1 — Capture Purpose. Admit candidate information into the system. Capture is deliberately permissive: the aim is to bring material in, not yet to judge it. Nothing captured is trusted, and nothing captured is knowledge; everything enters as a candidate whose status must be earned downstream. The one obligation that cannot be deferred at capture is origin . Provenance can be recorded now but rarely reconstructed later: the moment a source is detached from its content, the object’s history is compromised for the rest of its life. Capture therefore records where the material came from as a condition of entry, even while deferring every question of quality and warrant. Typical inputs. Documents; research papers; interviews; AI outputs; meeting notes; regulations; datasets; observations. Entry condition. Material is presented to the system. Activities. Intake; source identification; provenance seeding; assignment of a candidate identifier. Exit gate. The candidate is recorded together with its origin. Output state. Candidate. Accountable role. Contributor. Key question. What has entered the system? Canon basis. Provenance invariant; Principle I (the object, not knowledge, is what enters). Stage 2 — Structure Purpose. Transform raw, opaque input into a structured object that can be reasoned about. Structuring is what makes everything downstream possible: an object that cannot be inspected cannot be evaluated, justified, explained or governed. The stage confers a stable identity and an inspectable form. Entry condition. A Candidate with recorded origin. Activities. Decomposition; metadata assignment; semantic typing; relationship identification; provenance recording. Exit gate. The object has a stable identity, a semantic type, its relationships, and a provenance record — that is, it is inspectable. Output state. Structured. Accountable role. Knowledge Engineer. Key question. What exactly is this object? Canon basis. Inspectability invariant; Principle I. Stage 3 — Evaluate Purpose. Assess quality before any question of belief is raised. Evaluation asks whether the object is good enough to be worth justifying — a different and prior question to why it should be believed . It is the first gate that can stop progression: an object may pass, be returned for restructuring, or be rejected outright. Entry condition. A Structured object. Activities. Source assessment; evidence-quality assessment; confidence estimation; consistency and completeness checks. Exit gate. A quality verdict — pass, return, or reject — is recorded with its reasons. Output state. Evaluated. Accountable role. Evaluator. Key question. Should this object be trusted? Canon basis. Principle IV (the Validation/Quality primitive). Stage 4 — Justify Purpose. Establish epistemic legitimacy. This is the epistemic core of the lifecycle: the stage at which an object earns the standing to be called knowledge. Justification attaches the reasons for belief to the object and makes them inspectable. Counter-evidence is recorded as a matter of obligation, not option — an object justified only by the evidence that supports it has not been justified, it has been advocated. A system can engineer justification even though it cannot engineer truth; justification, not truth, is the standard every transition is held to. Entry condition. An Evaluated object that passed. Activities. Assembly of supporting evidence; assembly of counter-evidence; statement of rationale; statement of assumptions; end-to-end traceability. Exit gate. The object carries an inspectable justification: supporting and counter-evidence, rationale, assumptions, and traceability to source. Output state. Justified. Accountable role. Evaluator (with domain authority as required). Key question. Why should this be believed? Canon basis. Principle VIII; Principle IV; justification invariant. ══ The Acceptance Transition ══ (Justify → Operationalise) Acceptance is the act by which an identified authority certifies a justified object as fit to be relied upon. It is the single most consequential moment in the lifecycle, and it is deliberately not a stage: nothing is transformed, no work is performed on the object. It is a decision about the object — the point at which human authority admits a justified representation into operational use. For that reason it is modelled as a named transition, a gate, rather than an engineering stage. This mirrors the treatment of Application below: both are things that happen to a governed object without being engineering transformations of it, and naming them honestly keeps the nine stages purely about work performed on the object. Acceptance is where the object acquires the acceptance-state that the Canon requires of a full Operational Knowledge Object (KF-1001). Until it is accepted, an object may be perfectly justified and still have no standing to be relied upon; justification establishes why it may be believed , acceptance establishes that we will act on it . The two are distinct, and conflating them is the failure this transition exists to prevent. Who acts. An Authority — an identified person or body with the right to certify knowledge for the community that will use it. Requires. A Justified object with inspectable justification. Produces. An acceptance-state recorded against the object — accepted, provisionally accepted, or refused — attributed to the authority and dated. On acceptance the object proceeds to Operationalise; on refusal it returns to Justify or Evaluate with reasons. Key question. On whose authority will we rely on this? Canon basis. Principle III (knowledge becomes capability through collective authorisation); Principle IV (the Authority primitive); human-accountability invariant. Stage 5 — Operationalise Purpose. Make accepted knowledge usable. Operationalisation converts an accepted object into an actionable form — the shape in which it can be applied in decisions, reasoning or automation. The binding constraint is that the actionable form must remain linked to its justification. A playbook, rule or prompt that has been severed from the evidence and reasoning that warrant it is ungoverned knowledge in use, and is the failure mode this stage exists to prevent. Entry condition. An Accepted object (see The Acceptance Transition above). Activities. Derivation of decision rules, playbooks, patterns, prompts, procedures or models; linkage of each to the underlying justification. Exit gate. An actionable form exists and is traceably linked to its justification. Output state. Operational (actionable). Accountable role. Knowledge Engineer. Key question. How can this knowledge be used? Canon basis. Principle II (lifecycle); Principle I. Stage 6 — Govern Purpose. Maintain legitimacy through time. Acceptance is not permanent, and Govern is the standing machinery that keeps an operational object legitimate as its context changes: ownership, review cycles, approvals, versioning, provenance upkeep and policy compliance. Govern is a stage, but governance is not confined to it. The Governance Primitives operate throughout the lifecycle — provenance from Capture, validation at Evaluate, justification at Justify, authority at Accept. Stage 6 does not introduce governance; it makes it continuous , and it names the person or body answerable for the object from this point forward. Entry condition. An Operational object. Activities. Assignment of ownership; scheduling of review cycles; approval workflows; version control; provenance maintenance; policy-compliance checks. Exit gate. Ownership is assigned and a review cycle is in force. (This gate is standing, not one-off: it must remain satisfied for the object to stay operational.) Output state. Governed. Accountable role. Steward (owner). Key question. Who is accountable? Canon basis. Principle IV; Principle VII; human-accountability invariant. Stage 7 — Apply Purpose. Use the governed object in the practice it was built to serve. Application is different in kind from every stage before it: it does not transform the object, it uses it. Its engineering value is that it is the lifecycle’s principal source of new evidence — the outcomes of use are the truest test of whether the knowledge is fit — and it is therefore the principal trigger for evolution. The lifecycle’s working rhythm is use, observe, improve , and Apply is the “use” and “observe” of that rhythm. Because application does not change the object’s state, an applied object remains Governed; what changes is the evidence attached to it (operational outcomes) and what is assured about it (its accountability in use). Outcomes feed forward into Evolve, or, where use shows the object is no longer needed, into Retire. Entry condition. A Governed object. Activities. Use in human decisions, AI reasoning, automation and organisational workflows; use in teaching and advisory work; capture of outcomes. Exit gate. Outcomes are captured and attached to the object as feedback. Output state. Operational Outcomes (feedback into Evolve or Retire); the object remains Governed. Accountable role. User. Key question. Did the knowledge produce value? Canon basis. Principle IX (knowledge must remain explainable in use); Principle III. Stage 8 — Evolve Purpose. Allow controlled improvement. Change is the default condition of knowledge, and Evolve is where change is performed as a first-class, justified operation rather than an untracked edit. Every change produces a new version; the prior version is preserved, never overwritten. A change is itself a transition, and so carries its own justification and provenance. Evolution is triggered principally by the outcomes of Application, and also by new external evidence, competing claims or a scheduled review — so an object may enter Evolve from Apply or directly from Govern. It takes several forms: amendment in the light of new evidence; adjudication of competing claims; supersession of one object by another; branching for divergent contexts; and consolidation of several objects into one. Each returns the object to the appropriate earlier stage for re-evaluation, re-justification and re-acceptance before its new version can be relied upon. Entry condition. A Governed object with a change trigger (application outcomes, new evidence, a competing claim, or a scheduled review). Activities. Amendment; incorporation of new evidence; adjudication of competing claims; supersession; branching; consolidation. Exit gate. A new version is produced under recorded justification and provenance, with the prior version retained. Output state. Next Version (which re-enters the lifecycle at Evaluate or Justify, and is re-accepted before returning to operational use). Accountable role. Steward, with the Evaluator and Authority as required. Key question. What has changed? Canon basis. Principle X; Principle II; governed-evolution invariant. Stage 9 — Retire Purpose. Conclude the operational life of the object. Retirement is a change of state, not a deletion: the object leaves active use but its record — content, justification, provenance and history — is preserved. An object is retired because it is obsolete, superseded, merged, archived or withdrawn; the reason is recorded, because the fact of retirement is itself part of the knowledge history a later reader may need. Retirement is reversible in principle. If evidence changes such that a retired object regains relevance — for example, a superseding object is itself withdrawn — the historical object can be reactivated through Evolve, with its provenance intact. Entry condition. A retirement reason holds for a Governed or applied object. Reasons. Obsolete; superseded; merged; archived; withdrawn. Exit gate. The object is moved to the historical state, its retirement reason recorded and its history preserved. Output state. Historical. Accountable role. Steward. Key question. Why is this object no longer active? Canon basis. Principle VII (trust across time); Principle X. Transitions and Return Paths The principal path runs Capture → Retire, but the lifecycle is governed as a loop. Three kinds of non-forward transition are canonical. Returns send an object back to an earlier stage when a gate cannot be met. Evaluate may return an object to Structure or Capture when it is ill-formed or its origin is inadequate. Justify may return an object to Evaluate when its justification fails. Acceptance may be refused , returning a justified object to Justify or Evaluate with the authority’s reasons — a refusal is as much a governed transition as an acceptance, and is recorded as one. Evolution re-entry. Evolve re-enters the lifecycle at Evaluate or Justify, and its new version passes through the Acceptance transition again before returning to operational use. A new version re-earns its warrant and its authority; it does not inherit them. Retirements may be reached from Govern, Apply or Evolve. An object that becomes obsolete, superseded or withdrawn passes directly to Retire without completing the forward path. Every transition — forward, return, acceptance, refusal or retirement — is itself a governed act: it is recorded, attributed and justified. There are no silent transitions. This is what distinguishes the lifecycle from a workflow in which status simply advances: here, movement between states is the very thing being governed. Engineering Events States and transitions describe what the lifecycle does. Events describe what causes it to act . The lifecycle is, formally, a state machine with three distinct kinds of element: States — what an object is at a given moment (Candidate, Structured, Justified, Accepted, Governed, Historical …). Transitions — the governed moves between states (Accept, Return, Evolve, Retire …). Events — the occurrences that trigger a transition (new evidence, a scheduled review, a challenge …). Events cause transitions; transitions produce new states: Separating events from transitions matters for two reasons. First, it makes the model a clean state machine — the form over which later automated validation and orchestration operate. Second, it locates where automation is safe: an event may be raised by a human or by an agent , but the transition it triggers remains governed — attributable, justified, and, where authority is required, certified by a human. An AI recommendation is an event, not an acceptance; automation may propose, but the invariants still hold on whatever transition follows. The canonical event types, and the transitions they typically trigger: Engineering event Typically triggers New evidence Evolve (or a Return to Justify) Scheduled review A governance review, then Evolve or Retire Policy or regulatory change Re-validation, then Evolve or Retire Challenge to a claim Return to Justify or Evaluate AI recommendation Capture of a new candidate, or an Evolve proposal User feedback / application outcome Evolve or Retire Authority decision The Acceptance transition (accept or refuse) An event does not itself change an object; it obliges the system to perform — and govern — a transition. No event bypasses a gate. Roles and Accountability The lifecycle defines role responsibilities , not posts or systems; how they are staffed is an implementation concern (KF-4000). One person may hold several roles; a role may be held by several people. What the method fixes is that every stage has an accountable role, and that acceptance and stewardship are always held by an identifiable human authority — labour may be distributed across people and machines, but accountability may not be discharged into a substrate. Role Principal stages Accountable for Contributor Capture What enters the system, and its recorded origin Knowledge Engineer Structure, Operationalise The object’s form and its actionable expression Evaluator Evaluate, Justify The quality verdict and the inspectable justification Authority the Acceptance transition Certifying an object as fit to be relied upon Steward (owner) Govern, Evolve, Retire The object’s standing legitimacy over time User Apply Using the object as governed, and returning outcomes Lifecycle Invariants The lifecycle principles below describe how the lifecycle behaves . The invariants here describe what must be true of an object at every instant, regardless of stage . An invariant is a continuously checkable property: an object that violates any invariant is non-conformant, whatever state it is in and however it reached it. These are the properties automated validation will assert, and the ground on which the Reference Architecture ( KF-3000 ) is designed. Six invariants hold across the whole lifecycle. Single identity. Every Operational Knowledge Object has exactly one immutable identity for its entire life. Identity is assigned at Capture and is never reassigned, reused or mutated. Editing produces new versions under the same identity; branching, consolidation and supersession create successor objects with their own identities, linked to their predecessors. They do not split, merge or overwrite an existing identity. (Identity, version and lineage are distinct concerns, and KF-3000 realises them separately.) Attributable transitions. Every state transition is attributable to an identified actor — a person, or an agent acting under a named human authority. No transition is anonymous. Justified transitions. Every state transition carries a recorded justification. A transition without a recorded reason is not permitted, even when it is automatic. Inspectable transitions. Every state transition is inspectable after the fact: what changed, why, by whom, and from which prior state can always be recovered. Provenance always present. No operational state exists without a complete provenance chain back to origin. Provenance is a precondition of operational use, not an annotation added afterward. Lineage preserved. Retirement, supersession and consolidation never destroy lineage. History is append-only; states are superseded, never erased. Where an invariant appears to echo a principle — justification, for instance — the two do different work. The principle is the behavioural rule that a transition must earn its justification in order to proceed; the invariant is the checkable property that, once made, the transition carries that justification for all time. Principles govern progression; invariants govern conformance. Invariants are ungraded. These six hold identically for every object, whatever its consequence or intended reliance. What does vary with reliance is the depth to which a gate’s obligations must be discharged — the strength of evaluation, the independence of review, the sufficiency of evidence. That depth is set by the object’s assurance class , defined in KF-2003 and attaching to the object’s scope of reliance at acceptance and release. An Exploratory object and a Consequential one cross the same gates and satisfy the same six invariants; the Consequential object must satisfy each gate to a greater depth. No assurance class ever lowers the invariant floor. Lifecycle Principles Beyond the invariants above, the lifecycle is governed by six behavioural rules, each a direct consequence of the Canon. Knowledge always begins as a candidate. Nothing is trusted on entry; status is earned stage by stage. (Principle I.) Every transition requires justification. A gate is a justification checkpoint; an object advances only when it has earned the warrant of its stage. (Principle VIII.) Acceptance is an act of authority, distinct from justification. Justification establishes why an object may be believed; acceptance establishes that an identified authority will rely on it. No object reaches operational use without both. (Principle III.) Governance accompanies every stage. Govern is where legitimacy is maintained , but the Governance Primitives operate from Capture onward. Governance is a property of the whole lifecycle, not a single step within it. (Principles IV and VI.) Knowledge may return to earlier stages as evidence changes. The lifecycle is a loop; returns, refusals and re-justification are normal operations, not exceptions. (Principle X.) Retirement preserves history rather than erasing it. An object leaves active use with its record intact, because trust is a property of transitions over time. (Principle VII.) Relationship to the Canon Each lifecycle stage operationalises one or more Canonical Principles: the per-stage Canon basis lines above indicate the principal derivation. The lifecycle as a whole is the method by which the Canon’s central operation — the controlled transition of a knowledge object from one justified state to another — is carried out in practice. The authoritative, complete stage-to-principle mapping is defined in KF-2002 and is not reproduced here, so that a change to the mapping has a single home. Relationship to the Reference Architecture Each lifecycle stage is realised through one or more architectural services — for capture, structuring, evaluation, justification, acceptance, governance, versioning and retirement. This document fixes what each stage must achieve and when it may advance ; it does not specify the services, stores or technologies that achieve it. That mapping is defined in KF-3000 , which a given deployment (KF-4000, and domain instantiations such as a university course domain or a professional-body knowledge domain) then implements. KF-3000 must also enforce the lifecycle invariants as continuous conformance checks, and handle the engineering events as the triggers its services respond to.

d: Operationalising the Canon through Engineering Practice
x: Purpose KF-2001 defines the lifecycle through which an Operational Knowledge Object evolves. KF-2002 defines the engineering practices that enable that lifecycle. A lifecycle answers what happens . An engineering practice answers how that responsibility is discharged . Each practice operationalises one or more Canonical Principles while supporting one or more lifecycle stages, and each is specified as a set of obligations rather than a prescribed procedure. Consistent with KF-2001 , this is method, not workflow: a practice fixes what must be true and what must be produced, not the order, tools or cadence by which a given organisation achieves it. Those belong to implementation (KF-4000), and the services that realise these practices belong to architecture ( KF-3000 ). No technology choices are made here. Relationship to KF-2001 The lifecycle defines engineering states ; engineering practices define engineering behaviour . The relationship is many-to-many. Multiple practices may operate within a single lifecycle stage, and a single practice may span several stages. The lifecycle therefore specifies when engineering responsibilities arise; the practices specify how they are fulfilled. The two documents share one spine. A lifecycle gate is satisfied by executing the practice that supports it; a lifecycle invariant is upheld by the obligations the practices carry; a lifecycle event is what calls a practice into action. Where KF-2001 states that a transition must be attributable, justified and inspectable, it is the practices below that produce the attribution, the justification and the inspectable record. The practices are, in effect, how the lifecycle keeps its promises. The Engineering Practice Specification Every practice is specified against the same nine fields, so that practices can be compared, audited and — later — validated uniformly. Immediately below each practice’s title, a single line names the accountable role — the KF-2001 role answerable for the practice’s discharge. Accountability cannot be discharged into a computational substrate, so the answerable role is made visible on every practice rather than left to be inferred. Canon principle — the Canonical Principle(s) the practice operationalises. Objective — the purpose of the practice. Engineering obligation — what must always be true wherever the practice applies (an obligation is invariant-like: it holds at every instant, not only at a gate). Supported lifecycle stages — the KF-2001 stages or transitions that depend on the practice, distinguishing the practice’s principal home from the stages it additionally supports. Typical activities — the engineering work normally performed. Artefacts produced — the mandatory outputs the practice must leave behind. Governance checkpoints — how compliance is verified, expressed as checks against gates, invariants and Governance Primitives. Success criteria — how success is recognised. Failure modes — the characteristic failures when the practice is absent or poorly executed. On artefacts. Engineering artefact means an inspectable record produced or maintained by a practice as evidence that an obligation has been discharged. An artefact may be represented in several forms, but its required semantic content is fixed by the practice, not by any file, form or database row that carries it. This keeps KF-3000 free to choose representations while remaining bound to the content each artefact must hold. On success criteria. Success criteria state the required condition. Quantitative thresholds, sampling rules and conformance measures are graded by the object’s assurance class ( KF-2003 · Materiality and Assurance ) and may be further specified by a domain governance profile or implementation, not here — so the criteria below are written to be observable (a reviewer can confirm them) without prematurely fixing metrics or the depth at which each is required. Practice Domains at a Glance Domain Focus Practices A Identity Representation A1, A2 B Evidence Justification B1, B2 C Operational Governance C1, C2, C3 D Operational Use D1, D2, D3 The four domains follow the arc of the lifecycle: A gives the object identity and form; B earns it justified trust; C governs its acceptance, custody and change; D puts it to use and concludes its life. Together the ten practices provide one principal practice for each of the nine lifecycle stages and the Acceptance transition; several also support neighbouring stages, as the crosswalk records. Part I · Domain A — Identity Representation Purpose: ensure every Operational Knowledge Object possesses a stable identity, explicit structure and inspectable representation. A1 · Operational Knowledge Object Identification Accountable role. Contributor. Canon principle. Principle I. Objective. Assign and maintain the identity through which an object is known for its entire life, and bind its origin to it from the first moment. Engineering obligation. Every Operational Knowledge Object has one immutable identity. Editing produces new versions under the same identity; branching, consolidation and supersession create successor relationships — they do not erase, reuse or mutate the identities of the objects involved. Concretely: edits create versions under the same object identity; branching creates new object identities linked to a common predecessor; consolidation creates a new successor identity linked to all source objects; supersession changes status and lineage, not identity. No object exists without a recorded origin. (Lifecycle invariants: single identity; provenance always present. Identity, version and lineage are distinct concerns, separated in KF-3000 .) Supported lifecycle stages. Capture (principal home); Structure (support). Typical activities. Intake registration; assignment of a durable identifier; recording of source and origin; disambiguation of a new object from existing ones (is this novel, a new version, a branch, or a consolidation of things already held?); carrying identity forward into structuring. Artefacts produced. An identity record (durable identifier bound to origin, distinct from version and lineage records); a provenance seed that later stages extend. Governance checkpoints. Uniqueness check — the identity resolves to exactly one object and no other object claims it; immutability check — no operation reassigns, reuses or mutates an existing identity; origin-recorded check — the Capture exit gate is met before the object advances. Exercises the Provenance/Traceability primitive. Success criteria. Every object resolves to exactly one identity with a recorded origin; a reviewer can retrieve any object by its identifier and trace it to its source; no two objects share an identifier, and no identifier has been reassigned across the object’s life. Failure modes. Two identities for one object, or one identifier reused for two; identity reassigned or mutated on edit rather than versioned, silently breaking lineage; branching or consolidation that overwrites a predecessor’s identity instead of creating a linked successor; origin unrecorded and later unreconstructable; a candidate admitted with no identifier at all. A2 · Knowledge Structuring Accountable role. Knowledge Engineer. Canon principle. Principles I and II. Objective. Transform raw captured material into an inspectable, structured object that downstream stages can reason about. Engineering obligation. The object is inspectable: its structure, semantic type and relationships are explicit and examinable, not implicit in unstructured content — and this holds identically whatever the computational modality of the underlying representation, symbolic or parametric (thereby also discharging Principle V within this practice). (Lifecycle invariant: inspectability, as the Structure exit gate.) Supported lifecycle stages. Structure (principal home). Typical activities. Decomposition into constituent claims; semantic typing; metadata assignment; identification of relationships to other objects; recording of provenance. Artefacts produced. A structured representation; a metadata record; a relationship map; an extended provenance record. Governance checkpoints. Inspectability check — the object can be examined, typed and related; structure-complete check — the Structure exit gate (identity, type, relationships, provenance) is met. Exercises the Provenance/Traceability primitive. Success criteria. A reviewer can identify the object’s type, constituent claims, relationships and provenance without reconstructing them from unstructured source material. Failure modes. Opaque objects that cannot be evaluated or justified downstream; structure left implicit in prose or weights; missing relationships that hide dependency; representations that resist inspection and therefore resist governance. Part II · Domain B — Evidence Justification Purpose: ensure every knowledge object earns justified trust through explicit evaluation and inspectable reasoning. B1 · Evidence Evaluation Accountable role. Evaluator. Canon principle. Principle IV. Objective. Assess the quality of a structured object before any question of belief is raised — decide whether it is good enough to be worth justifying. Engineering obligation. No object advances toward justification without a recorded quality verdict and its reasons; evaluation is kept distinct from justification. (Evaluate exit gate; the distinction B1↔︎B2 is load-bearing.) Supported lifecycle stages. Evaluate (principal home). Typical activities. Source assessment; grading of evidence quality; confidence estimation; consistency and completeness checks; recording of a pass, return or reject verdict with reasons. Artefacts produced. A quality-assessment record: the verdict, the criteria applied, and the reasons. Governance checkpoints. Quality-verdict check — the Evaluate exit gate is met and the verdict is recorded and inspectable. Exercises the Validation/Quality primitive. Success criteria. For any object that advanced, a reviewer can retrieve the recorded verdict, the criteria applied and the reasons; objects that were returned or rejected carry the same record and did not proceed. Failure modes. Evaluation conflated with justification (asking why believe it before asking is it worth the effort ); low-quality objects passed through; verdicts reached but not recorded; evaluation that advocates for an object rather than assessing it. B2 · Knowledge Justification Accountable role. Evaluator, with domain authority where required. Canon principle. Principles IV and VIII. Objective. Establish epistemic legitimacy by attaching an inspectable justification — supporting evidence, counter-evidence, rationale, assumptions and traceability — to the object. Engineering obligation. Every object that will enter operational use carries an inspectable justification, and counter-evidence is recorded as an obligation, not an option. Justification, not truth, is the standard, and it is required even where knowledge resides in parametric form, whose warrant must be reconstructed rather than read off an inference (again holding the obligation across modality, per Principle V). (Justify exit gate; lifecycle invariant: justified transitions; Principle VIII.) Supported lifecycle stages. Justify (principal home). Typical activities. Assembly of supporting and counter-evidence; statement of rationale; explicit statement of assumptions; construction of end-to-end traceability from claim to source. Artefacts produced. A justification record: supporting and counter-evidence, rationale, assumptions, and a traceability chain. Governance checkpoints. Justification-inspectable check — any reviewer can recover why the object may be believed; the Justify exit gate is met. Exercises the Evidence/Justification primitive. Success criteria. An independent reviewer can trace each material claim to its supporting and defeating evidence, recover the stated assumptions, and reproduce the recorded rationale. Failure modes. Advocacy — only confirming evidence recorded; justification that cannot be inspected; truth conflated with justification; assumptions left hidden, so the object’s warrant cannot be tested. Part III · Domain C — Operational Governance Purpose: maintain legitimacy, accountability and controlled evolution throughout the operational life of knowledge. C1 · Knowledge Acceptance Accountable role. Authority. Canon principle. Principle III. Objective. Have an identified authority certify a justified object as fit to be relied upon, producing the acceptance-state that admits it into operational use. Engineering obligation. No object reaches operational use without acceptance by an identified human authority, and every acceptance is attributable and recorded. Acceptance is distinct from justification: justification establishes why an object may be believed ; acceptance establishes that an authority will rely on it . (Acceptance transition; lifecycle invariant: attributable transitions; the human-accountability invariant of the Canon. This practice also exercises the Authority primitive of Principle IV.) Supported lifecycle stages. The Acceptance transition, Justify → Operationalise (principal home). Typical activities. Review of the justification by the authority; decision to accept, provisionally accept or refuse; recording of the acceptance-state, attributed and dated, with the scope of reliance; on refusal, return to Justify or Evaluate with reasons. Artefacts produced. An acceptance record (decision, authority, date, scope); a refusal record with reasons where applicable. Governance checkpoints. Authority-certified check — the object bears an acceptance attributed to a named authority; attribution check — the transition is not anonymous. Exercises the Authority primitive. Success criteria. For any operational object, a reviewer can identify the accepting authority, the date, the scope of reliance and the acceptance-state; refusals carry the authority’s recorded reasons. Failure modes. Acceptance conflated with justification; anonymous or implicit acceptance; acceptance discharged to a machine so that no human is answerable; fluent or plausible output relied upon with no acceptance at all. C2 · Governance Stewardship Accountable role. Steward. Canon principle. Principles IV and VII. Objective. Keep an operational object legitimate as its context changes, through ownership, review, versioning, provenance upkeep and policy compliance. Engineering obligation. Every operational object has an identified steward and a review cycle in force, and its provenance is maintained for as long as it is operational. Governance is continuous, not a one-time step. (Govern standing gate; lifecycle invariant: provenance always present; Principle VII: trust across transitions over time.) Supported lifecycle stages. Govern (principal home); the whole operational life (standing support). Typical activities. Assignment of ownership; scheduling and running of review cycles; approval workflows; version control; provenance maintenance; policy-compliance checks; response to scheduled-review and policy-change events. Artefacts produced. A stewardship assignment; a review schedule and its record; a governance and version log; a policy-compliance record. Governance checkpoints. Ownership-assigned and review-in-force check — the standing Govern gate remains satisfied; provenance-maintained check. Exercises the Versioning/Release and Provenance/Traceability primitives. Success criteria. For any operational object, a reviewer can identify its current steward, its review schedule and last review, its version history and its compliance status; none of these is absent. Failure modes. Ownerless operational knowledge; objects that drift out of review and go stale; provenance decay over time; governance that is recorded at acceptance and then never exercised — legitimacy on paper only. C3 · Knowledge Evolution Accountable role. Steward. Canon principle. Principles II and X. Objective. Perform change as a first-class, justified, versioned operation that improves the object while preserving its history and without leaving dependent knowledge silently inconsistent. Engineering obligation. Every change produces a new version under recorded justification and provenance; the prior version is retained; the new version re-earns its warrant by returning through evaluation, justification and acceptance; and the objects that depend on the changed one are identified and dispositioned. (Evolve gate; lifecycle invariants: lineage preserved, justified transitions; the governed-evolution invariant.) Supported lifecycle stages. Evolve (principal home); Evaluate, Justify and the Acceptance transition (support, via re-routing of the new version). Typical activities. Amendment in the light of new evidence; adjudication of competing claims; supersession; branching for divergent contexts; consolidation; impact analysis across dependent objects and actionable forms; routing the new version back to Evaluate/Justify and through re-acceptance. Evolution is called by events — new evidence, a challenge, a scheduled review, an application outcome. Artefacts produced. A new version; a change record (trigger, justification, provenance); lineage links for supersession, branch and merge; a dependency-impact record identifying objects, practices or applications requiring re-evaluation. Governance checkpoints. Change-justified-and-versioned check — the Evolve gate is met; prior-version-retained check; re-acceptance check — the new version passes the Acceptance transition before returning to use; dependency-impact check — affected dependencies have been identified and either revalidated, suspended or routed into Evolution. Exercises the Versioning/Release and Reversibility/Audit primitives. Success criteria. For any change, a reviewer can identify the trigger, the justification, the resulting version, the retained prior version, the affected dependencies and their disposition, and the re-acceptance of the new version before its return to use. Failure modes. Untracked edits; prior versions overwritten; evolution without re-justification or re-acceptance; lineage lost when objects are superseded, branched or merged; a changed object correctly versioned while its dependants are left silently inconsistent. Part IV · Domain D — Operational Use Purpose: ensure knowledge creates value while preserving explainability, feedback and historical integrity. D1 · Operationalisation Accountable role. Knowledge Engineer. Canon principle. Principles II and III. Objective. Convert an accepted object into an actionable form — the shape in which it can be used in decisions, reasoning or automation. Engineering obligation. The actionable form is traceably linked to the justification and acceptance beneath it; use never detaches from warrant. Only accepted objects are operationalised. (Operationalise exit gate.) Supported lifecycle stages. Operationalise (principal home). Typical activities. Derivation of decision rules, playbooks, patterns, prompts, procedures or models from the accepted object; linkage of each actionable form to the underlying justification and acceptance. Artefacts produced. One or more actionable forms; a linkage record binding each to its justification and acceptance. Governance checkpoints. Form-linked-to-justification check — the Operationalise exit gate is met and every actionable form traces back to warrant. Exercises the Versioning/Release primitive. Success criteria. For any actionable form, a reviewer can trace it to the object version, justification and acceptance-state from which it derives. Failure modes. Actionable forms severed from their justification — ungoverned knowledge in use; operationalisation of objects that were never accepted; forms that cannot be traced back to a source object. D2 · Knowledge Application Accountable role. User, under Steward oversight. Canon principle. Principle IX. Objective. Use governed knowledge in practice while preserving explainability, and capture the outcomes of use as new evidence. Engineering obligation. Knowledge remains explainable in use whatever the modality in which it resides, and the outcomes of application are captured and attached to the object. Application uses the object without transforming it; the object remains Governed. (Apply exit gate; Principle IX; explainability is owed by the system, not the substrate — and is therefore preserved across modality, per Principle V.) Supported lifecycle stages. Apply (principal home); Evolve and Retire (support, which application’s outcome events call). Typical activities. Use in human decisions, AI reasoning, automation and organisational workflows; use in teaching and advisory work; capture of outcomes; raising of feedback events that call Evolution or Retirement. Artefacts produced. An outcome record attached to the object, feeding the Evidence dimension and the evolution/retirement decision. Governance checkpoints. Explainability-in-use check — an account of how the knowledge produced a given result can be given, regardless of substrate; outcome-captured check — the Apply exit gate is met. Exercises the Reversibility/Audit primitive. Success criteria. For every material application outcome, the system can identify the object version used, its actionable form, the governing acceptance-state and the recorded path from input to result. Failure modes. Black-box application that cannot be accounted for; outcomes not captured, breaking the feedback loop; application of ungoverned or unaccepted objects; use that has quietly detached from the justification it was meant to carry. D3 · Knowledge Retirement Accountable role. Steward or designated Authority. Canon principle. Principles VII and X. Objective. Conclude the operational life of an object without destroying its lineage, recording why it is no longer active. Engineering obligation. Retirement is a change of state, not a deletion; lineage is preserved; the reason is recorded; and retirement is reversible in principle. History is append-only.
