(Retire gate; lifecycle invariant: lineage preserved; Principle VII.) Supported lifecycle stages. Retire (principal home). Typical activities. Determination of the retirement reason (obsolete, superseded, merged, archived, withdrawn); transition of the object to the historical state; recording of the reason; preservation of the full record; provision for reactivation through Evolution should evidence change. Artefacts produced. A retirement record (reason, date, authority); the preserved historical object with its lineage intact. Governance checkpoints. Reason-recorded and history-preserved check — the Retire gate is met; lineage-intact check — no history is erased and superseding links remain traceable. Exercises the Reversibility/Audit primitive. Success criteria. For any retired object, a reviewer can identify the retirement reason, date and authority, retrieve its full historical record and lineage, and determine the successor object where one exists. Failure modes. Deletion that destroys lineage; retirement with no recorded reason; silent removal; a superseding object that breaks the link back to the object it replaced. Crosswalk Each practice maps to the Canonical Principle(s) it operationalises, the role accountable for it, its principal lifecycle home, and the stages it additionally supports. Practice Canon Accountable role Principal home Additional support A1 · OKO Identification Principle I Contributor Capture Structure A2 · Knowledge Structuring Principles I, II Knowledge Engineer Structure — B1 · Evidence Evaluation Principle IV Evaluator Evaluate — B2 · Knowledge Justification Principles IV, VIII Evaluator (+ domain authority) Justify — C1 · Knowledge Acceptance Principle III Authority Acceptance transition — C2 · Governance Stewardship Principles IV, VII Steward Govern Operational life C3 · Knowledge Evolution Principles II, X Steward Evolve Evaluate, Justify, Acceptance D1 · Operationalisation Principles II, III Knowledge Engineer Operationalise — D2 · Knowledge Application Principle IX User (under Steward) Apply Evolve, Retire D3 · Knowledge Retirement Principles VII, X Steward / Authority Retire — Constitutional coverage. The crosswalk’s Canon column records each practice’s principal principle. Because two principles are cross-cutting rather than stage-bound, coverage of all ten is stated explicitly here: Principle I — A1, A2 (the object, and its inspectable representation) Principle II — A2, C3, D1 (engineering as a lifecycle) Principle III — C1, D1, D2 (collective authorisation and accountable use) Principle IV — B1, B2, C1, C2 (governance as constitutive; the six primitives) Principle V — A2, B2, D2 (the obligation preserved across every computational modality) Principle VI — the methodology as a whole: the lifecycle ( KF-2001 ) and these practices coordinate engineering, capability and governance on a single object; no one practice owns it, and the crosswalk itself is its evidence Principle VII — C2, D3 (trust preserved across transitions over time) Principle VIII — B2 (inspectable justification for every transition) Principle IX — D2 (explainability in use, across modalities) Principle X — C3, D3 (designed for governed evolution) The crosswalk records each practice’s principal Canon basis and principal lifecycle home. Additional stages, principles and Governance Primitives exercised by the practice are stated in its specification. Read down the principal-home column, the ten practices provide one primary practice for each of the nine lifecycle stages and the Acceptance transition. Read across the Canon column, every Canonical Principle must be discharged either through a principal mapping or an explicitly identified secondary obligation. Together, these two tests establish lifecycle coverage and constitutional coverage without assuming a permanent one-to-one correspondence between principles, stages and practices. Relationship to KF-3000 The practices defined here specify engineering responsibilities — what must be done, what must be produced, and how compliance is verified. KF-3000 defines the architectural services that realise those responsibilities, and must in particular provide the services that produce each practice’s mandatory artefacts and that enforce its governance checkpoints as continuous conformance checks. Because this document keeps identity, version and lineage distinct, and states each artefact by its required semantic content rather than its form, KF-3000 can justify each service by the practice obligation it fulfils, the artefact it maintains and the checkpoint it enforces — rather than inventing components one by one. No technology choices are made in this document; the practices are stated so that many architectures could satisfy them, and so that any that claims to must be measurable against the success criteria and failure modes recorded above.

d: How reliance and consequence determine the depth to which a governed knowledge object must be assured
x: Purpose This document defines materiality in Knowledge Foundry and the assurance classes through which materiality is operationalised. It fixes, in one place, the depth to which a governed knowledge object’s obligations must be discharged as a function of the reliance placed on it and the consequences of its being wrong. It exists because the lifecycle ( KF-2001 ), the practices ( KF-2002 ) and the architecture ( KF-3000 series) each state obligations without stating how much rigour each obligation demands for a given object. Uniform rigour is the wrong answer in both directions: it over-governs exploratory notes and under-governs consequential advice. Materiality supplies the missing dimension, and it supplies it once, so that gates, controls, reviews, evidence and traceability do not each invent their own interpretation. A single rule governs everything below: materiality grades the depth of assurance; it never grades the invariants. The six lifecycle invariants of KF-2001 hold identically for every object at every class. What scales is the evidence, review, authority and reconstruction depth layered above that floor. How This Document Sits in the Programme KF-2003 is a Method-level document. It defines an obligation shape — proportionality — that the architecture then realises. Its architectural realisation is fixed by KF-3001 IC-23 (Proportionate Discharge) , KF-3005 (gates and controls read the class), and the Scope-of-Reliance Record (SVC-06) to which class attaches. Its conformance consequences are carried by KF-3007 . This document names no technologies and no deployments. Assurance classes are one operational expression of materiality — the principal one — but they are not the whole of it. Materiality also informs which activities are recorded ( KF-3004 §5.1), which decisions require independent review, and how deep a reconstruction must go ( KF-3007 ). The classes make materiality actionable at the gate; the concept remains broader than the scale. Part I · Materiality 1. Definition Materiality is the degree to which an Operational Knowledge Object, claim, decision or transition may affect consequential action, institutional reliance, legal or professional obligation, financial exposure, public representation, or the preservation of important knowledge. Reliance is central to materiality but does not exhaust it. An object may carry high materiality because it will be relied upon, because being wrong would be costly, or because it stands for the institution publicly — often several at once. Materiality is therefore assessed across dimensions, not read off a single axis. 2. Dimensions of Materiality A material assessment weighs, at minimum: Reliance — will identified actors or systems act on this object, and how directly? Consequence — what is the severity of a wrong, stale or misused conclusion? Audience and representation — is the object internal, client-facing, or public; does it speak for the institution? Obligation — does any legal, regulatory, contractual or professional duty attach to it? Exposure — what financial, safety, reputational or operational loss could follow? Preservation value — is this a claim the institution must be able to reconstruct and defend later? No dimension alone fixes the class. The assessment takes the class that the highest-weighing dimensions justify. 3. Materiality Is Contextual and Version-Specific Materiality attaches primarily to an object’s intended use and reliance context , not permanently to the object itself. The same content may begin exploratory and become consequential when it enters a board paper, a policy submission or a client recommendation. Accordingly, assurance class attaches to the release / scope of reliance , not to the immutable object identity ( KF-3000 §2; SVC-06). A new intended use is a new reliance context and may carry a different class. This preserves the single-identity invariant: the object does not change identity when its class changes; a differently-classed reliance is a property of the release, recorded against it. Part II · Assurance Classes 4. The Scale Five classes grade the minimum rigour expected. They are ordinal: each inherits the expectations of those below it and adds to them. Class Name Meaning A0 Exploratory Early inquiry, incomplete evidence, no authorised reliance A1 Working Active development and internal collaboration A2 Routine (provisional name — see note) Approved for defined routine use A3 Consequential Capable of materially influencing significant decisions or actions A4 Critical Failure, error or loss could create severe institutional, legal, financial, safety or public consequences Naming note (A2). “Operational” was rejected for A2 because the term is already load-bearing three ways in the programme — in “Operational Knowledge Object”, as the Stage-5 lifecycle state, and as the KF-3000 §20 maturity profile. A2 is provisionally named Routine (alternatively Standard ); the name may be settled at first review without affecting the scale. 5. Governance Overlays Certain conditions are not degrees of reliance and must not be modelled as higher classes. Regulation, confidentiality, public exposure, client-facing status and legal privilege are overlays : orthogonal attributes that add specific obligations without moving the object up the scale. A low-consequence administrative record may be regulated; a high-consequence internal strategy may not be. The class determines depth; the overlays add duties. An object may be Routine and regulated , Consequential and confidential , Critical and public , or Working and legally-privileged . 6. Minimum Obligations by Class These are floors, not ceilings. A domain governance profile may add obligations; it may never remove the invariant floor (§9) or fall below the class minimum. Class Typical minimum governance expectation A0 Exploratory provenance captured; uncertainty visible; no acceptance required A1 Working named owner; versioning; basic evaluation; collaborative traceability A2 Routine defined scope of use; acceptance by an authorised role; monitored currency A3 Consequential independent review; explicit justification; counter-evidence recorded; stronger traceability; defined scope of reliance A4 Critical formal authority; segregation of duties where appropriate; comprehensive evidence; heightened monitoring, recovery and reconstruction depth The obligations are stated as outcomes a reviewer can confirm , not as fixed metrics. Thresholds and cadences are set by the applicable domain profile (KF-4000), consistent with KF-2002 ’s treatment of success criteria. Part III · Assigning and Changing Class 7. Who Assigns the Class The object owner (Steward) proposes the assurance class. For A3 and A4 , the designated governance authority confirms it. Automated classification may recommend a class but is never the final authority for consequential or critical objects. Any downstream user whose intended reliance exceeds the assigned class may request escalation ; unresolved escalation blocks that reliance until the class is confirmed. Assignment is itself a governed, attributable transition: it records who proposed, who confirmed, when, and on what basis. There is no silent classification. 8. Raising and Lowering Class Raising class is expected whenever reliance or consequence increases — a new audience, a new decision context, a new obligation. It is recorded as an attributable transition and re-tests the gates to the new depth. Lowering class is permitted only through an attributable decision that records the changed scope of reliance — for example, when a Consequential object becomes a historical reference no longer relied upon operationally. Historical evidence obligations are not retrospectively removed: a lowered class governs only future reliance; the evidence already required at the higher class remains preserved (lineage invariant, KF-2001 ). Part IV · Universality of Invariants 9. What Class Never Touches The six lifecycle invariants — single identity, attributable transitions, justified transitions, inspectable transitions, provenance always present, lineage preserved — hold identically at every class , including A0. An Exploratory object still has one identity, still records origin, still transitions attributably and justifiably. The class governs the depth of evidence and review , never the existence of the invariant properties. This is the boundary that keeps proportionality from becoming a loophole. Materiality answers “how deep”; it may never answer “whether at all” for any invariant. Part V · Exceptions and Escalation 10. Exceptions A time-limited, attributable governance exception may permit an object to operate one step below the class its use would otherwise require, provided: the gap is recorded; a named authority accepts the residual risk; the exception is visible until closed ( KF-3001 IC-19); and no invariant is waived . An exception may reduce required depth for a bounded period; it may never convert an invariant violation into conformance. 11. Escalation Where evidence of a mis-classification arises — an object relied upon beyond its class, or a class assigned below its dimensions — any actor may raise an escalation event ( KF-2001 event model). Escalation obliges the authority to re-confirm or re-assign the class before the contested reliance proceeds. Part VI · Relationship to Other Documents KF-2001 — the invariants that class never grades, and the gates whose depth it sets. KF-2002 — success criteria whose required depth is fixed here. KF-3001 · IC-23 — the architectural constraint that discharges obligations to class depth; IC-24 — event-native evidence, whose volume this document keeps proportionate. KF-3004 · §5.1 — the material-activity definition this document governs. KF-3005 · §28, §32 — gates and controls read the class. KF-3008 — the authority model that confirms A3/A4 classes. KF-3007 — the conformance model whose Integrity and Reconstructability tests are graded by class. Status and Next Step This document is Draft for Experiment . Its scale, minimum-obligation table and assignment rules are hypotheses to be tested by the first vertical slice (a MacroLab Singapore Business Impact Assessment, provisionally A3 Consequential). The slice is expected to show whether the class minimums are workable, whether the dimensions are sufficient, and whether A2’s name should be settled. The document moves to Validated with Exceptions , then Approved , only after that evidence is in.

d: The logical architecture of a governed knowledge system
x: Service-catalogue alignment (v0.3). The service catalogue (§12) and every service reference in this document have been renumbered to the definitive nineteen-service catalogue fixed by KF-3003 . The earlier provisional sixteen-service numbering — in which, for example, SVC-05 was Evaluation and SVC-15 was Conformance — has been superseded. KF-3003 is authoritative for the service catalogue; KF-3004 is authoritative for record ownership. KF-3000 ’s capability enumeration (§6–§10) remains the provisional umbrella model and is refined definitively by KF-3002 ; a note at §12 and §23 identifies the three services (Release, Operating Condition and Exception, Temporal Continuity) whose capability grounding is established there rather than in this document’s provisional capability list. Purpose This document defines the Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture: the technology-neutral arrangement of capabilities, services, records and control relationships required to realise the Canon, lifecycle and engineering practices of a governed knowledge system. KF-3000 does not prescribe a product, platform, vendor, storage model or deployment topology. It defines the logical responsibilities that any conforming architecture must discharge. The Reference Architecture answers: What must a governed knowledge system be architecturally capable of doing? KF-4000 answers: How are those capabilities instantiated in a particular implementation? Architectural Derivation Every architectural element must be traceable to an upstream obligation. An architectural component is admitted only when it can be justified by this chain. The Reference Architecture therefore does not begin with technologies. It begins with the obligations the system must preserve. Architectural Admission Test A proposed architectural capability or service belongs in KF-3000 only if all of the following are true: It discharges one or more obligations defined in KF-2001 or KF-2002 . Its responsibility can be stated without naming a specific technology or product. Its inputs, outputs and governed records can be identified. Its relationship to accountability and authority is explicit. Its conformance can be inspected or tested. Removing it would leave at least one lifecycle gate, invariant, practice obligation or Governance Primitive unsupported. If a proposed element fails these tests, it belongs either in KF-4000 or outside the Knowledge Foundry architecture. Part I · Architectural Foundations 1. Scope of the Reference Architecture The Reference Architecture governs the operational life of Operational Knowledge Objects and the engineering artefacts attached to them. Its scope includes: object identity and representation; evidence and justification; acceptance and authority; operationalisation and application; provenance and traceability; governance and stewardship; versioning, branching and lineage; change-impact analysis; outcome capture; retirement and historical preservation; identity and access governance; confidentiality and disclosure constraints; integrity protection; role- and authority-based permissions; retention and lawful disposition requirements; conformance and audit. Its scope does not include: specific software products; physical infrastructure; deployment geography; organisational workflow design; user-interface design; model or database selection; implementation-specific security technologies and controls; performance thresholds. Those concerns are defined in KF-4000 or in implementation-specific profiles. The Reference Architecture states the logical obligation to control access, disclosure and integrity; it does not name the encryption, identity-management or network technologies that realise it. 2. Architectural Unit The primary architectural unit is the Operational Knowledge Object . The architecture must treat the following as distinct but related concerns: A conforming architecture must preserve these distinctions even when an implementation stores them together. The three that are most often confused are fixed here precisely. An object is the enduring governed identity. A version is an immutable state of that object’s represented content and attached warrant at a point in its history. A release is a version authorised for a defined scope of operational reliance. A new version does not automatically become a release, and a release does not create a new object identity. Branching and consolidation create successor objects with new identities and explicit lineage links. They do not divide, merge or reuse the immutable identities of existing objects. 3. Architectural Invariants The following properties must hold across the architecture: Stable identity — each object has one immutable identity. Persistent provenance — origin and subsequent lineage remain attached throughout the object’s life. Inspectable state — the current lifecycle state and the basis for entering it are recoverable. Attributable transition — every state transition is assigned to an identifiable actor or authority. Justified transition — every transition carries its recorded warrant. Version preservation — prior versions are retained and recoverable. Separation of concerns — identity, state, version, lineage, acceptance and representation remain logically distinct. Human accountability — computational execution never removes identifiable human accountability. Traceable use — every material application can be traced to the object version, actionable form and acceptance-state used. Historical continuity — retirement preserves the object’s record and lineage. Modality independence — the obligations hold whether knowledge is represented symbolically, parametrically or through a combination of modalities. Continuous conformance — governance conditions are maintained over time, not verified only once. ( KF-3001 separates these into three categories gathered here: architectural principles, system invariants, and service-interaction constraints.) 4. Architectural Perspectives The same governed knowledge system must be inspectable through five complementary perspectives. 4.1 Object Perspective What objects exist, how are they identified, structured, related and versioned? 4.2 Evidence Perspective What evidence, counter-evidence, assumptions and justification warrant each object? 4.3 Lifecycle Perspective What state is the object in, what event triggered its movement, and what gate authorised the transition? 4.4 Governance Perspective Who owns, evaluates, accepts, reviews and retires the object? 4.5 Operational Perspective How is the object made actionable, where is it used, and what outcomes arise from that use? No one perspective is sufficient by itself. The architecture must preserve their relationships. Part II · Capability Architecture 5. Capability Domains The Reference Architecture is organised into four capability domains derived from KF-2002 . Domain Architectural purpose Principal upstream practices A. Identity Representation Establish what the object is and make it inspectable A1, A2 B. Evidence Justification Establish why the object may be trusted B1, B2 C. Operational Governance Control acceptance, custody and change C1, C2, C3 D. Operational Use Make knowledge actionable, observe its use and preserve its history D1, D2, D3 These four domains are supported by a fifth, cross-cutting domain: Domain Architectural purpose Upstream basis E. Cross-Cutting: Provenance, Assurance Access Preserve traceability, verify continuing conformance, and govern access and integrity across every domain Architectural invariants (§3); Governance Primitives; lifecycle gates; practice checkpoints and artefacts The first four domains mirror the practice structure of KF-2002 . The fifth gathers the three concerns that serve every domain rather than belonging to one: provenance and traceability , derived from practices A1, A2, B2, C2, C3 and D1; assurance and conformance , derived from the architectural invariants and the gates and checkpoints it exists to keep honest; and access and integrity , derived from the human-accountability and attributable-transition invariants and the Authority and Provenance Governance Primitives. Each capability below is specified against the same compact form: Purpose, Upstream basis, Required capabilities, Principal artefacts maintained, and a Conformance condition — a single high-level, testable statement of what an independent reviewer must be able to confirm. The detailed tests are deferred to KF-3002 and KF-3007 ; the conformance condition makes each capability testable in principle. 6. Domain A — Identity Representation Capabilities A-CAP-01 · Object Registration Purpose. Admit a candidate object and assign its durable identity. Upstream basis. KF-2002 A1. Required capabilities. assign an immutable object identifier; distinguish a new object from a version, branch, consolidation or duplicate; record the object’s origin; prevent identifier reuse; resolve an identifier to exactly one object. Principal artefacts maintained. Identity Record Provenance Seed Intake Record Conformance condition. For any object, an independent reviewer can resolve its identifier to exactly one object, retrieve its recorded origin, and confirm the identifier was never reused or reassigned. A-CAP-02 · Structured Representation Purpose. Represent an object in an inspectable form. Upstream basis. KF-2002 A2. Required capabilities. assign semantic type; represent constituent claims or elements; attach metadata; represent relationships to other objects; preserve the relationship between source material and structured form; accommodate multiple computational modalities while retaining inspectability. Principal artefacts maintained. Structured Representation Metadata Record Relationship Map Extended Provenance Record Conformance condition. For any object, a reviewer can retrieve its semantic type, constituent claims, metadata, relationships and provenance without reconstructing them from unstructured source material. A-CAP-03 · Object Resolution and Discovery Purpose. Enable authorised actors and services to locate and inspect objects and their related records. Upstream basis. KF-2002 A1, A2 (the read side of identity and representation). Required capabilities. resolve objects by identity; retrieve the current and historical states; traverse relationships and lineage; distinguish current, superseded, branched, consolidated, suspended and retired objects; expose sufficient context for downstream evaluation and governance. Principal artefacts maintained. Resolution Index (a derived, rebuildable index over existing records; A-CAP-03 reads and indexes rather than originating primary records) Conformance condition. For any identifier or relationship, a reviewer can resolve the object, retrieve its current and historical states, and traverse its lineage, distinguishing current, superseded, branched, consolidated, suspended and retired objects. 7. Domain B — Evidence Justification Capabilities B-CAP-01 · Evidence Registration Purpose. Register supporting and defeating evidence as first-class governed records. Upstream basis. KF-2002 B1 and B2. Required capabilities. identify evidence independently of the claims it supports; classify evidence type and origin; attach evidence to one or more claims or objects; distinguish supporting, defeating and contextual evidence; preserve evidence provenance. Principal artefacts maintained. Evidence Record Evidence-to-Claim Link Counter-evidence Record Conformance condition. For any claim, a reviewer can retrieve the supporting, defeating and contextual evidence attached to it, each with its own provenance. B-CAP-02 · Quality Evaluation Purpose. Assess whether an object is suitable to proceed toward justification. Upstream basis. KF-2002 B1. Required capabilities. apply stated evaluation criteria; record pass, return or reject verdicts; record confidence, completeness and consistency assessments; retain rejected and returned evaluations; prevent progression where the quality gate is unmet. Principal artefacts maintained. Quality Assessment Evaluation Verdict Evaluation Criteria Record Conformance condition. For any object that advanced, a reviewer can retrieve the recorded verdict, the criteria applied and the reasons; returned and rejected objects carry the same record and did not proceed. B-CAP-03 · Justification Construction Purpose. Assemble and preserve the warrant for belief. Upstream basis. KF-2002 B2. Required capabilities. connect claims to supporting and counter-evidence; record assumptions and rationale; preserve traceability from claim to source; expose the justification to independent inspection; preserve an inspectable evidence, evaluation and rationale record sufficient to explain how parametrically represented knowledge or capability was admitted, bounded and relied upon. Principal artefacts maintained. Justification Record Assumption Record Rationale Record Traceability Chain Conformance condition. For any operational object, a reviewer can trace each material claim to its supporting and defeating evidence, recover the stated assumptions and reproduce the recorded rationale. B-CAP-04 · Epistemic Status Management Purpose. Represent the current epistemic standing of the object without conflating it with acceptance or lifecycle state. Upstream basis. KF-2002 B2 (Principle VIII); the Landscape’s separation of justification from acceptance. Required capabilities. distinguish unassessed, quality-assessed, warrant-established, contested, warrant-weakened and insufficiently-supported conditions; represent confidence and unresolved challenge; preserve disagreement and competing claims; prevent epistemic status from being overwritten by operational acceptance. Principal artefacts maintained. Epistemic Status Record Challenge Record Conformance condition. For any object, a reviewer can determine its current epistemic status and any unresolved challenge, and confirm that acceptance has not overwritten it. 8. Domain C — Operational Governance Capabilities C-CAP-01 · Authority and Acceptance Purpose. Manage the governed transition from justified object to accepted operational object. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C1. Required capabilities. identify the accepting authority; record acceptance, provisional acceptance or refusal; define the scope and conditions of reliance; attribute and date the decision; return refused objects to the appropriate stage; prevent operational use without valid acceptance. Principal artefacts maintained. Acceptance Record Refusal Record Scope-of-Reliance Record Conformance condition. For any operational object, a reviewer can identify the accepting authority, the decision, the date and the scope of reliance; refusals carry the authority’s recorded reasons. C-CAP-02 · Stewardship and Ownership Purpose. Maintain identifiable accountability throughout the operational life of the object. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C2. Required capabilities. assign and transfer stewardship; identify responsible roles; ensure no operational object is ownerless; preserve historical accountability; distinguish execution by machines from accountability held by people. Principal artefacts maintained. Stewardship Assignment Responsibility Record Ownership History Conformance condition. For any operational object, a reviewer can identify its current steward and its ownership history, and confirm that no operational object is ownerless. C-CAP-03 · Review and Compliance Purpose. Preserve legitimacy as time, context and policy change. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C2. Required capabilities. schedule and record reviews; detect overdue reviews; assess policy or governance compliance; suspend or flag objects whose standing gate is no longer met; preserve review and compliance history. Principal artefacts maintained. Review Schedule Review Record Compliance Record Exception Record Conformance condition. For any operational object, a reviewer can retrieve its review schedule, last review, compliance status and any exception, and the system can detect overdue reviews. C-CAP-04 · Version and Release Management Purpose. Preserve controlled change without loss of history. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C2 and C3. Required capabilities. create immutable versions; designate current, superseded and historical versions; preserve prior versions; distinguish draft, accepted and released forms; associate each version with its justification and acceptance-state. Principal artefacts maintained. Version Record Release Record Supersession Link Conformance condition. For any object, a reviewer can enumerate its versions, identify the current, superseded and historical versions and any releases, and confirm no prior version was overwritten. C-CAP-05 · Lineage and Evolution Purpose. Govern amendment, branching, consolidation, supersession and reactivation. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C3. Required capabilities. represent predecessor and successor relationships; preserve branch and merge lineage; record change triggers and rationales; return changed objects through evaluation, justification and acceptance; prevent silent mutation. Principal artefacts maintained. Change Record Lineage Record Branch Record Consolidation Record Conformance condition. For any change, a reviewer can recover the predecessor and successor relationships, the change trigger and rationale, and confirm the changed object returned through evaluation, justification and acceptance. C-CAP-06 · Dependency Impact Management Purpose. Identify and disposition objects and actionable forms affected by change. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C3. Required capabilities. identify downstream dependencies; determine which dependants require revalidation; recommend suspension, re-evaluation or evolution of affected objects; record their disposition; prevent changed knowledge from leaving dependants silently inconsistent. Principal artefacts maintained. Dependency Impact Record Revalidation Record Suspension Recommendation Conformance condition. For any change, a reviewer can identify the affected dependants and their disposition, and confirm none was left silently inconsistent. C-CAP-07 · Event and Transition Management Purpose. Govern movement between lifecycle states. Upstream basis. KF-2001 (states, transitions, events, gates). Required capabilities. register lifecycle events; evaluate transition eligibility; enforce exit gates; record forward, return, suspension, reactivation and retirement transitions; attribute each transition; preserve transition history. Principal artefacts maintained. Event Record Transition Record Gate Decision Record Suspension Record Reactivation Record Conformance condition. For any lifecycle transition, an independent reviewer can recover the triggering event, the prior and resulting states, the applicable gate, the gate decision, the accountable actor and the recorded warrant. 9. Domain D — Operational Use Capabilities D-CAP-01 · Actionable Form Derivation Purpose. Derive actionable forms from an accepted object — the forms usable in decisions, reasoning and automation. Upstream basis. KF-2002 D1. Required capabilities. derive decision rules, playbooks, prompts, procedures, models and other actionable forms; identify the object version from which each form derives; preserve links to justification and acceptance; distinguish the actionable form from the source knowledge object; withdraw or update actionable forms when the source object changes. Principal artefacts maintained. Actionable Form Derivation Record Warrant Linkage Record Conformance condition. For any actionable form, a reviewer can identify the object version, justification and acceptance-state from which it derives, and confirm it is withdrawn or updated when its source object changes. D-CAP-02 · Controlled Application Purpose. Enable governed use while preserving traceability and explainability. Upstream basis. KF-2002 D2. Required capabilities. identify the object version and actionable form used; verify that acceptance and governance remain valid; record material use — materiality criteria and assurance classes are defined by KF-2003 · Materiality and Assurance (a domain governance profile may set additional thresholds within it); preserve the path from input to result; provide an explanation appropriate to the modality, materiality and decision context of the application, without claiming forms of interpretability the underlying representation cannot support; prevent use of suspended, retired or unaccepted objects. Principal artefacts maintained. Application Record Use Context Record Explanation Record Conformance condition. For every material application, a reviewer can identify the object version and actionable form used, the governing acceptance-state and the recorded path from input to result, and confirm that suspended, retired or unaccepted objects were not used. D-CAP-03 · Outcome and Feedback Capture Purpose. Capture what happened when knowledge was applied and return it as lifecycle evidence. Upstream basis. KF-2002 D2. Required capabilities. attach outcomes to the relevant object version and application; distinguish observation from judgement; raise review, evolution or retirement events; aggregate outcomes without erasing individual provenance; preserve adverse and contradictory outcomes. Principal artefacts maintained. Outcome Record Feedback Record Trigger Record Conformance condition. For any application, a reviewer can retrieve the captured outcomes attached to the object version, distinguish observation from judgement, and trace any review, evolution or retirement event raised from them. D-CAP-04 · Retirement and Historical Preservation Purpose. Conclude operational use while preserving lineage and reversibility. Upstream basis. KF-2002 D3. Required capabilities. record retirement reason, date and authority; remove an object from active operational use; preserve the full historical record; maintain successor and supersession links; assemble the restoration package that permits governed reactivation through Evolution; prevent destructive deletion of governed history. Principal artefacts maintained. Retirement Record Historical Object Record Restoration Package Conformance condition. For any retired object, a reviewer can identify the retirement reason, date and authority, retrieve its full historical record and lineage, and confirm that reactivation remains possible and no history was destroyed. 10. Domain E — Cross-Cutting: Provenance, Assurance Access Domain E is cross-cutting. It gathers the three capabilities that serve every other domain rather than belonging to one. Its assurance members do not create or alter the substantive knowledge represented by an object, nor do they authorise lifecycle transitions; they evaluate the objects, records, controls and service actions through which the architecture demonstrates conformance. Its provenance and access members maintain records of their own, but likewise never authorise a transition or alter substantive content. E-CAP-01 · Provenance and Traceability Purpose. Preserve origin, derivation, custody and end-to-end traceability across every stage of the object lifecycle. Upstream basis. Architectural invariants 2, 3, 4, 9 and 10; KF-2002 A1, A2, B2, C2, C3 and D1. Required capabilities. preserve source origin; trace representations and claims to source material; trace versions to predecessor versions and change events; trace actionable forms to object versions, justification and acceptance; trace applications and outcomes to the forms and versions used; preserve custody and attribution across transitions; detect broken lineage or incomplete traceability. Principal artefacts maintained. Provenance Seed Extended Provenance Record Traceability Chain Derivation and Custody Links Conformance condition. For any object, version, actionable form, application or outcome, a reviewer can trace it to its origin and to every predecessor state, and any broken lineage or incomplete traceability is detectable. E-CAP-02 · Invariant Monitoring Purpose. Continuously verify that the architectural invariants of §3 hold across all objects. Upstream basis. Architectural invariants (§3); lifecycle invariants ( KF-2001 ). Required capabilities. evaluate each architectural invariant against live and historical objects; detect and record violations; raise conformance exceptions; verify continuously rather than once. Principal artefacts maintained. Invariant Test Register Conformance Exception Record Conformance condition. For any architectural invariant, the system can demonstrate across the object population that it holds, and any violation raises a recorded conformance exception. E-CAP-03 · Gate and Checkpoint Assurance Purpose. Verify that every lifecycle gate and practice governance checkpoint was enforced and satisfied. Upstream basis. Lifecycle gates ( KF-2001 ); practice governance checkpoints ( KF-2002 ). Required capabilities. confirm each transition passed its exit gate; detect gate bypass; verify that the checkpoint artefacts required by KF-2002 exist for each transition; record verification. Principal artefacts maintained. Gate Conformance Record Checkpoint Verification Record Conformance condition. For any transition, the system can demonstrate that its exit gate and the required KF-2002 checkpoints were enforced and satisfied, and detect any bypass. E-CAP-04 · Artefact Completeness Verification Purpose. Verify that every mandatory artefact required by a practice exists, is inspectable and is retrievable. Upstream basis. KF-2002 mandatory artefacts; the artefact definition of KF-2002 . Required capabilities. enumerate the required artefacts for each object and lifecycle state; detect missing or unretrievable artefacts; confirm semantic completeness — that an artefact holds its required content, not merely that a record exists. Principal artefacts maintained. Artefact Completeness Record Conformance condition. For any object and lifecycle state, the system can enumerate the required artefacts and demonstrate that each exists, is retrievable and holds its required content. E-CAP-05 · Audit and Reconstruction Purpose. Enable independent reconstruction of an object’s full history for audit. Upstream basis. Architectural invariants 3–5, 9–10; conformance evidence (§21). Required capabilities. reconstruct the end-to-end lifecycle of any object — states, transitions, warrant, authority and use; produce inspectable audit trails; support external inspection without privileged reinterpretation. Principal artefacts maintained. Audit Trail Reconstruction Record Conformance condition. For any object, the system can reconstruct its end-to-end lifecycle — states, transitions, warrant, authority and use — as an inspectable audit trail, without privileged reinterpretation. E-CAP-06 · Access and Integrity Assurance Purpose. Ensure that governed objects, artefacts and transitions are accessed and altered only by authorised actors operating within their assigned roles. Upstream basis. Human-accountability invariant; attributable-transition invariant; the Authority and Provenance Governance Primitives. Required capabilities. distinguish authority, accountability and access permission; control who may view, create, modify, accept, release, apply, suspend and retire an object; protect governed records against unauthorised alteration; record access and material administrative action; enforce disclosure or use restrictions attached to an object; preserve access-control history as roles and ownership change. Principal artefacts maintained. Access Policy Record Permission Assignment Disclosure Constraint Record Access and Administrative Action Log Conformance condition. For any governed object, artefact or transition, a reviewer can determine which roles may view or alter it, confirm that access and material administrative actions were logged, and confirm that governed records were protected against unauthorised alteration. A note on independence. Logical independence does not require a single implementation component. The assurance capabilities (E-CAP-02 to E-CAP-05) may be distributed across monitoring, policy-evaluation, audit and reporting components, provided assurance remains independent of the services whose conformance it evaluates. Part III · Logical Service Architecture 11. From Capabilities to Services An architectural service is a stable logical responsibility exposed to authorised actors or other services through defined inputs, outputs, records and controls. It may be realised by software, assigned human work, or a governed combination of both. Capabilities state what the architecture must be able to do; services state the responsibilities through which those capabilities are made available. A service may realise several capabilities, and a capability may require several services: the relationship is many-to-many. Services are logical, not technological. 12. Core Architectural Services This is the definitive nineteen-service catalogue , fixed here in alignment with KF-3003 . It is grouped by domain: A (identity and representation); B (evidence, evaluation and justification); C (governance, lifecycle, version, release and dependency); D (operationalisation, application and retirement); and E (five cross-cutting services — provenance, access, operating condition, conformance and time). Version, acceptance and release are three separate services, and the assurance concerns previously folded into one “Conformance and Audit” service are separated into provenance (SVC-15), operating condition (SVC-17), conformance and audit (SVC-18) and temporal continuity (SVC-19). SVC-01 · Object Registry Service Maintains durable identity, object resolution and basic status. SVC-02 · Representation Service Maintains structured representations, semantic types, metadata and object relationships. SVC-03 · Evidence Service Registers evidence, counter-evidence and evidence relationships. SVC-04 · Evaluation Service Supports quality assessment, verdicts and evaluation history. SVC-05 · Justification Service Maintains rationale, assumptions, warrant, epistemic status and claim-to-evidence traceability, holding epistemic status distinct from acceptance. SVC-06 · Authority and Acceptance Service Manages acceptance decisions, authority, scope and refusal. SVC-07 · Stewardship and Review Service Maintains ownership, review cycles and compliance status. SVC-08 · Lifecycle and Transition Service Manages object state, events, gates and governed transitions — including suspension and reactivation, which are lifecycle transitions. It holds the sole authority to write lifecycle state. SVC-09 · Version and Lineage Service Maintains immutable versions, branches, consolidations, supersession and historical lineage, kept strictly distinct from acceptance and release. SVC-10 · Release Service Designates an accepted version as eligible for a defined scope and period of operational reliance, and governs withdrawal, supersession and revalidation of that eligibility. Release is a distinct governed decision, separate from version creation (SVC-09) and acceptance (SVC-06). SVC-11 · Dependency Service Represents dependencies and performs change-impact analysis; recommends suspension where dependants are affected. SVC-12 · Operationalisation Service Creates and manages actionable forms and their warrant linkages. SVC-13 · Application and Outcome Service Records use, explanation, results and feedback. SVC-14 · Retirement and Preservation Service Manages retirement, historical state and restoration packages. SVC-15 · Provenance and Traceability Service Maintains origin, custody, derivation and end-to-end traceability. It is the principal service of the provenance capability (E-CAP-01) and maintains the provenance and traceability artefacts produced across Domains A, B, C and D. SVC-16 · Access and Integrity Service Governs who may view, create, modify, accept, release, apply, suspend and retire objects and artefacts; protects governed records against unauthorised alteration; enforces disclosure constraints; and logs access and material administrative action. It mediates access and permission; it does not itself authorise lifecycle transitions or hold substantive accountability, both of which remain with human roles. SVC-17 · Operating Condition and Exception Service Maintains service and transaction operating condition, determines the fail-posture when a required condition is unavailable or indeterminate, and holds operational exceptions until they are closed. (Its capability basis — Operating Condition assurance — is fixed definitively in KF-3002 ; KF-3000 ’s provisional capability model folded this concern into general assurance.) SVC-18 · Conformance and Audit Service Verifies invariants, gates, artefact completeness and architectural conformance, and reconstructs object history for audit. It realises the assurance capabilities of Domain E and reads the records of every other service without altering them. Logical independence does not require a single component: SVC-18 may be distributed across monitoring, policy-evaluation, audit and reporting components, provided assurance remains independent of the services it evaluates. SVC-19 · Temporal Continuity Service Owns the common temporal model, historical sequencing, reconstruction and the preservation of recorded, effective and event time across governed records. (Its capability basis — Temporal Continuity — is fixed definitively in KF-3002 ; it is not enumerated in KF-3000 ’s provisional capability list.) 13. Service Interaction Principles The services must interact according to the following rules: No service may alter object identity after assignment. No lifecycle transition may occur without a Transition Record. No accepted operational object may lack a Justification Record and Acceptance Record. No actionable form may exist without a traceable source object version. No application may use an object whose acceptance or governance state is invalid. No version change may overwrite a prior version. No retirement operation may destroy lineage. No automated service may become the final accountable authority. All material service actions must be attributable and auditable. Architectural services may automate work but may not silently bypass practice obligations. The Conformance and Audit Service may read the governed records and control evidence of every service. It must not alter the records under examination, authorise the transitions it verifies, or rely solely on assertions produced by the service being assessed. Access to governed records, and any change to permissions, is mediated by the Access and Integrity Service; no service grants itself access or alters its own permissions outside it. Suspension and reactivation are lifecycle transitions owned by the Lifecycle and Transition Service; other services may recommend or trigger them but may not record the transition themselves. Part IV · Architectural Records 14. Record Classes The architecture distinguishes seven principal record classes, and a set of common properties every record must carry. 14.1 Object Records Describe what the object is, and where it came from. Examples: Identity Record, Intake Record, Structured Representation, Metadata Record, Relationship Map, Provenance Seed, Extended Provenance Record. 14.2 Epistemic Records Describe why the object may be believed. Examples: Evidence Record, Counter-evidence Record, Quality Assessment, Justification Record, Assumption Record, Rationale Record, Traceability Chain, Epistemic Status Record. 14.3 Governance Records Describe who authorised, owns and reviews the object. Examples: Acceptance Record, Refusal Record, Scope-of-Reliance Record, Stewardship Assignment, Review Record, Compliance Record. 14.4 Evolution Records Describe how the object moved and changed through time. Examples: Event Record, Transition Record, Gate Decision Record, Version Record, Change Record, Lineage Record, Dependency Impact Record, Suspension Record, Reactivation Record, Retirement Record. 14.5 Operational Records Describe how the object was made usable and what happened when it was used. Examples: Actionable Form, Derivation Record, Application Record, Outcome Record, Explanation Record. 14.6 Assurance Records Describe whether the architecture is meeting its own obligations. Examples: Invariant Test Register, Gate Conformance Record, Checkpoint Verification Record, Artefact Completeness Record, Audit Trail, Conformance Exception Record. 14.7 Access Integrity Records Describe who may access or alter an object, and what access occurred. Examples: Access Policy Record, Permission Assignment, Disclosure Constraint Record, Access and Administrative Action Log. 14.8 Common Record Properties Every governed record, of whatever class, must carry at minimum: a stable record identity; the object and version to which it relates; record type; creation time, and effective time where different; creator or originating service; accountable role where applicable; status; provenance; version or revision information; integrity status; retention or disposition condition; links to superseding or correcting records. Where a record is corrected, the correction is appended or versioned; the prior record is not silently overwritten. The distinction between creation time and effective time is required: a policy change may be recorded on one date and take effect from another, and both must be recoverable. 15. Record Relationship Model At minimum, the architecture must support the following logical relationships: The logical model fixes these relationships. It does not prescribe whether they are implemented in documents, relational tables, graphs, event streams, model context, or another substrate. Part V · Control Architecture 16. Gate Enforcement Each lifecycle gate must be represented as an inspectable architectural control. Lifecycle point Required architectural check Capture exit Identity and origin exist Structure exit Representation, type, relationships and provenance are inspectable Evaluate exit Quality verdict and reasons exist Justify exit Supporting evidence, counter-evidence, assumptions, rationale and traceability exist Acceptance transition Identified authority has recorded the acceptance-state and scope Operationalise exit Actionable form is linked to object version, justification and acceptance Govern standing gate Stewardship and review remain in force Evolve exit Change, version, lineage and dependency impacts are recorded Apply exit Application outcome and traceability are captured Retire exit Retirement reason, authority and historical preservation are recorded Each check is enforced at execution by the Lifecycle and Transition Service (SVC-08) and verified after the fact by the Conformance and Audit Service (SVC-18): the first prevents an unearned transition, the second proves that none occurred. 17. Control Types The architecture must support five classes of control. 17.1 Preventive Controls Stop an invalid transition or use before it occurs. 17.2 Detective Controls Identify missing, stale or contradictory conditions. 17.3 Corrective Controls Return an object to an earlier stage, suspend it or trigger Evolution. 17.4 Evidentiary Controls Produce inspectable proof that an obligation was discharged. 17.5 Historical Controls Preserve prior states and enable reconstruction of what occurred. 18. Human Authority Boundaries The architecture must distinguish: computation; recommendation; evaluation support; transition execution; accountable authorisation. Automated systems may perform or assist the first four where permitted. They may not erase the requirement for an identifiable human authority where the Canon assigns acceptance, stewardship or accountability to a person or body. Part VI · Conformance Architecture 19. Architectural Conformance Conformance is assessed as coverage, not one-to-one correspondence , and to a depth proportionate to assurance class ( KF-2003 ). A capability may be realised by several mechanisms and a mechanism may serve several capabilities; what must hold is that every obligation is covered, not that each maps to exactly one element. The nine clauses below are the structural integrity checklist; the four proportionate tests through which they are applied — Constitutional, Operational, Integrity and Reconstructability coverage — are defined authoritatively in KF-3007 · Architectural Conformance Framework . The six lifecycle invariants are demonstrated at full strength for every object regardless of class; the depth of evidence and reconstruction required of graded obligations scales with the object’s assurance class. An implementation conforms to KF-3000 when it demonstrates that: every required capability is realised by at least one identified mechanism; every mandatory artefact can be produced and retrieved; every governance checkpoint can be enforced or inspected; every architectural invariant is maintained, at full strength, for every object; every lifecycle transition is attributable and reconstructable to the depth its assurance class requires; every practice in KF-2002 is supported; every Governance Primitive is instantiated; access and integrity controls protect governed records and are themselves inspectable; no implementation choice collapses distinctions the Reference Architecture requires to remain separate. 20. Progressive Implementation Profiles The profiles below describe progressive implementation maturity. They do not constitute full conformance with KF-3000 . An implementation is conformant only when it satisfies the complete requirements of §19, or an explicitly defined domain profile approved by the Knowledge Foundry governance authority. These implementation-maturity profiles are orthogonal to the per-object assurance classes of KF-2003 : a maturity profile describes how much of the architecture an implementation has stood up, while an assurance class describes how much rigour a particular object is governed to. A Foundational implementation and a Full-Conformance one may both hold Exploratory and Consequential objects; the class sets the depth, the profile sets the reach. The profiles are cumulative: Foundational Supports identity, provenance, structure, evaluation, justification and acceptance. Governed Adds stewardship, reviews, versioning, lineage and controlled evolution. Operational Adds actionable forms, governed application, outcome capture and retirement. Full Conformance Adds continuous assurance, dependency impact, access and integrity governance, modality independence and complete lifecycle traceability — satisfying §19 in full. 21. Conformance Evidence A conforming implementation must be able to produce: a capability-to-service mapping; a practice-to-capability mapping; an artefact implementation map; a lifecycle gate-control map; an authority, access and accountability map; an invariant test register; an access and integrity control register; a record-retention and lawful-disposition policy; evidence of representative end-to-end lifecycle execution. Wherever possible this evidence is event-native — emitted by the governed acts themselves rather than authored separately ( KF-3001 IC-24; KF-3004 §5.2) — and its required depth is graded by assurance class ( KF-2003 ). The Conformance and Audit Service (SVC-18) is the architectural means by which this evidence is produced and kept current; the model that determines what must be reconstructable, and to what depth, is KF-3007 · Architectural Conformance Framework .
