Part VIII · Relationship to KF-4000 KF-3000 fixes the logical architecture. KF-4000 defines how that architecture is instantiated in a particular Knowledge Operating System, organisational environment or domain implementation. An implementation may: combine several logical services into one component; distribute one service across several components; allocate responsibility across people and machines; use different storage and representation models; adopt different deployment and integration patterns. It may not: omit a required capability; bypass a lifecycle gate; remove mandatory human accountability; destroy provenance, versions or lineage; collapse justification into acceptance; detach actionable forms from their warrant; weaken access, disclosure or integrity controls below the logical obligation; substitute technological sophistication for architectural conformance. Subordinate Documents KF-3000 is the umbrella architecture: it establishes the whole logical model and is not the place for further detail. Subordinate documents deepen specific parts without revising this one: KF-3001 · Architectural Principles and Invariants — separating the architectural principles, system invariants and service-interaction constraints presently gathered in §3 and §13. KF-3002 · Capability Model KF-3003 · Logical Service Catalogue KF-3004 · Information and Record Model KF-3005 · Lifecycle and Control Architecture KF-3006 · Architectural Integration Model — how the architectural elements collaborate to produce, govern, evolve and retire an Operational Knowledge Object; the integrated systems view that precedes conformance. KF-3007 · Architectural Conformance Framework — the four proportionate tests (Constitutional, Operational, Integrity, Reconstructability) through which §19 is applied, graded by assurance class. KF-3008 · Architectural Authority Framework KF-3009 · Architectural Crosswalks and Traceability Two cross-programme documents are load-bearing for this architecture and are cited throughout: KF-2003 · Materiality and Assurance (the assurance-class scale and the depth to which graded obligations are discharged) and KF-0002 · Controlled Vocabulary and Architectural Distinctions (the authoritative terms and the user-facing projection of the architecture’s states). Closing Statement The Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture is not a diagram of software components. It is the logical arrangement of responsibilities required to preserve justified knowledge as it moves through identity, evaluation, acceptance, use, change and retirement. Its purpose is to ensure that every implementation remains answerable to the same constitutional and engineering obligations, regardless of the technologies through which those obligations are realised.

d: Governing the Design and Behaviour of the Knowledge Foundry Architecture
x: Purpose KF-3000 defines the logical architecture required to realise the Knowledge Foundry methodology. KF-3001 defines the rules that govern the design and behaviour of that architecture. It establishes: the principles that guide architectural decisions; the invariants that must remain true across every conforming implementation; the constraints that govern interactions among architectural services; the mechanisms — architectural decision and conformance — by which those rules are applied and demonstrated. KF-3001 does not prescribe technologies, products, deployment topologies or implementation procedures. Its purpose is to ensure that different implementations may vary in form without departing from the constitutional and engineering obligations of the Knowledge Foundry. It does not repeat the Canon, restate the lifecycle, or reproduce the capability catalogue. Its role is narrower and more technical: to translate constitutional commitment and system obligation into durable rules for architectural design. The Organising Grammar The document has three primary forms of architectural rule — principle, invariant and interaction constraint — and two mechanisms through which those rules are applied and demonstrated: architectural decision and conformance. A principle permits several conforming designs; an invariant permits none that violate it within its scope; a constraint keeps an invariant true while the system operates; a decision chooses among designs that all satisfy the rules; and conformance shows that all of it holds. Keeping the three rule forms distinct — and separating them from the two mechanisms that apply and demonstrate them — is what stops the architecture drifting into either component compliance (possessing all the named services while letting them bypass one another) or technology compliance (using sophisticated tooling while failing to preserve warrant, authority, provenance or history). Relationship to Upstream Documents KF-3001 is derived from the Canonical Principles of KF-1000 ; the lifecycle stages, gates and invariants of KF-2001 ; the engineering obligations and governance checkpoints of KF-2002 ; and the architectural capabilities, services and controls of KF-3000 . The derivation chain is: Admission test. A rule belongs in KF-3001 only where violating it could allow an implementation to reproduce the visible structure of KF-3000 while defeating its intended governance, epistemic or historical function. A rule that fails this test is a generic architecture slogan, a restated Canon principle, a data model, a security standard or an implementation guide — and belongs elsewhere. Part I · Foundations 1. Architectural Rule Types KF-3001 defines three forms of architectural rule. 1.1 Architectural Principle A durable design rule that guides architectural choices. A principle constrains design judgement, permits more than one conforming solution, applies across capabilities and services, and is evaluated through the decisions it shapes. 1.2 System Invariant A condition that must remain true whenever its stated scope and activation conditions apply. An invariant is not satisfied by a one-time check; it is independently testable; and it cannot be waived by implementation convenience. Some invariants are universally active; others apply only when a relevant condition exists (for example, counter-evidence, dependants, or a material application), which its Scope line states. 1.3 Service Interaction Constraint A rule governing how logical services, actors and records may interact. A constraint protects one or more invariants, assigns or limits architectural responsibility, prevents bypass, silent mutation or collapse of required distinctions, and is enforced through service contracts and controls. 2. Rule Application and Demonstration The three rule forms are applied to design and shown to hold through two mechanisms. These are not themselves rules. 2.1 Architectural Decision Rule A rule for selecting between alternative conforming designs. A decision rule makes trade-offs explicit, records the obligations affected, requires justification and approval, and preserves reversibility where practical. Decision rules are specified in Part V. 2.2 Conformance The demonstration that the principles, invariants and constraints are satisfied: through decisions, mappings and design evidence for principles; through preventive controls, detective checks and tests for invariants; and through service contracts and prohibited-path testing for constraints. Conformance is specified in Part VI. It applies the rules; it is not itself a rule. 3. Relationship Among the Rules Principles guide design. Invariants define the required condition. Interaction constraints preserve that condition during operation. Decision rules govern choices where several designs can satisfy the same obligations. Conformance demonstrates the result. 4. Rule Specification Each architectural principle is specified through a Statement, a Rationale, an Upstream basis and its Architectural consequences; where misreading is likely or audit requires it, Prohibited interpretations and Conformance evidence are added. AP-01 is given in full as the exemplar of the complete template. Each system invariant is specified through its Statement and a compact metadata line giving Scope, the obligation it Protects, its Violation condition, and the services that Uphold it. Required evidence is defined generically in Part VI. Each interaction constraint is specified through its Statement and a compact metadata line giving the invariant it Protects, the participating services, and the required record or control. Permitted and prohibited interactions are stated within the constraint. 5. Precedence Where architectural rules appear to conflict, the following precedence applies: Canonical Principles; human-accountability and formally assigned authority; system invariants; lifecycle gates and standing governance conditions; service interaction constraints; architectural principles; local architectural preferences; implementation convenience. A lower-order rule may not be used to defeat a higher-order obligation. Applicable law and binding regulation remain external constraints on the architecture and cannot be displaced by this precedence order. KF-3001 governs architectural precedence, not legal conformance. Part II · Architectural Principles Family A · Derivation and Sufficiency AP-01 · Obligation-Derived Architecture Statement. Every architectural element must be justified by an upstream Canonical, lifecycle, practice, artefact, checkpoint or conformance obligation. Rationale. The architecture exists to realise the methodology, not to reproduce familiar technology categories. Upstream basis. KF-1000 ; KF-2001 ; KF-2002 ; the KF-3000 Architectural Admission Test. Architectural consequences. every capability and service carries an upstream basis; technology-led components are admitted only after their logical responsibility is established; unsupported services are excluded from the reference architecture; crosswalks are maintained from principle to implementation. Prohibited interpretations. a technology belongs because it is commonly used; architectural completeness means including every enterprise platform category; a powerful component may replace an unfulfilled obligation. Conformance evidence. Principle-to-practice, practice-to-capability and capability-to-service mappings, together with recorded architectural admission decisions. AP-02 · Necessary and Proportionate Architecture Statement. The architecture includes every responsibility necessary to discharge its obligations reliably and excludes responsibilities that cannot be justified by an upstream obligation, dependency or assurance need. Rationale. Architectural economy means proportionate commitment, not minimum component count. A capability that makes several obligations reliable, scalable or independently verifiable is justified even where it maps to no single lifecycle step. Upstream basis. The method–architecture–implementation separation of KF-1000 and KF-3000 . Architectural consequences. capabilities are logical and non-duplicative; an enabling or assurance capability is admitted where a dependency or assurance need justifies it; implementation concerns remain in KF-4000; services may be combined in implementation where their logical responsibilities remain distinguishable. AP-03 · Conformance over Structural Resemblance Statement. Architectural conformance is established by discharged obligations and preserved invariants, not by reproducing a particular component diagram. Rationale. Different implementations may realise the same logical architecture through different arrangements of people, software and models. Upstream basis. KF-3000 Conformance Architecture. Architectural consequences. conformance is judged against §19 of KF-3000 and the invariants of this document, not against a reference topology; two structurally dissimilar implementations may both conform; resemblance to the service catalogue is neither necessary nor sufficient for conformance. Family B · Separation of Concerns AP-04 · Preserve Semantic Distinctions Statement. Concepts that carry different governance or epistemic meanings remain logically distinct even where they share a physical representation. At minimum, the architecture distinguishes: object from representation; object from version; version from release; lifecycle state from epistemic status; justification from acceptance; authority from access permission; application from evolution; retirement from deletion; and service responsibility from human accountability. Rationale. Collapsing these distinctions permits silent bypass of lifecycle and governance obligations. Upstream basis. KF-3000 §2 (Architectural Unit) and the separation-of-concerns invariant. Architectural consequences. a shared store may hold two concepts only if each remains independently addressable and changeable; no operation may alter one distinguished concept as an undocumented side effect of altering another; the information model of KF-3004 must preserve each distinction explicitly. Prohibited interpretations. physical co-location is treated as logical identity; a single record type is allowed to stand for both a version and a release, or both justification and acceptance. AP-05 · Separate Knowledge Content from Its Warrant Statement. The represented content of an object remains distinguishable from the evidence, rationale, assumptions, evaluation and acceptance that warrant its use. Rationale. Warrant and content change on different schedules and under different authority; fusing them lets a content edit inherit stale warrant, or a warrant change mutate content. Upstream basis. KF-2002 B1, B2, C1. Architectural consequences. a content change does not silently inherit prior warrant; a warrant change can be represented without mutating object identity; actionable forms retain traceable links to their warrant. AP-06 · Separate Execution from Authority Statement. The ability to perform an operation does not imply authority to approve it. Rationale. Execution capacity is a technical property; authority is an institutional one. Conflating them lets whatever can act also decide. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C1, C2; the human-accountability invariant. Architectural consequences. automated execution may support evaluation, transition or release; accountable acceptance, stewardship and designated authorisations remain attributable to an authorised person or body; access permission does not itself constitute acceptance authority. Prohibited interpretations. holding write permission to a record is read as holding authority to accept, release or retire it. Family C · Governance and Accountability AP-07 · Governance Is Continuous Statement. Governance conditions remain in force throughout operational life rather than being treated as one-time admission checks. Rationale. Legitimacy decays; a check passed once does not stay passed. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C2; the Govern standing gate; Canon Principle IV. Architectural consequences. stewardship, review, compliance and acceptance validity are monitored; objects may be suspended when standing conditions lapse; conformance checks operate continuously or at defined intervals. AP-08 · Accountability Remains Human Statement. Every material governance decision remains attributable to an identifiable human authority or accountable body. Rationale. Computational systems may act, recommend and record, but they cannot absorb institutional accountability. Definition. An accountable body is a formally constituted human decision-making body whose membership, mandate and decision record are recoverable. A system, an anonymous organisational function or an unminuted committee is not an accountable body. Upstream basis. KF-1000 Principle III and the human-accountability invariant; KF-2002 C1. Architectural consequences. acceptance, stewardship, release, suspension and retirement each resolve to a human authority or accountable body; automation may prepare and execute these decisions but is never their final locus of accountability. Prohibited interpretations. an automated approval step is treated as discharging accountability; “the system decided” is accepted as an answer to “who is answerable”. AP-09 · Control Must Produce Evidence Statement. Every material governance action and transition leaves an inspectable record sufficient to reconstruct what occurred, why it occurred and under whose authority. Rationale. A control that leaves no evidence cannot be audited and therefore cannot be trusted to have operated. Upstream basis. KF-2001 transition rules; KF-2002 artefact obligations. Architectural consequences. controls are evidentiary as well as preventive; transitions without records are invalid; administrative actions affecting governed state are auditable. Family D · Continuity, Change and History AP-10 · Identity Persists Through Change Statement. Changes to representation, state, warrant or operational form do not silently alter object identity. Rationale. Identity is the thread on which history is strung; if it moves, lineage breaks. Upstream basis. KF-2002 A1, C3. Architectural consequences. versions inherit object identity; branches and consolidations create new identities with explicit lineage; identifiers are never reused. AP-11 · Change Is Additive to History Statement. Governed change adds to the historical record rather than replacing it. Rationale. Trust in a knowledge system is a property of its transitions over time; overwriting the past destroys the evidence of trustworthiness. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C3, D3; Canon Principle VII. Architectural consequences. prior versions and decisions remain recoverable; corrections are appended or versioned; retirement preserves lineage; rollback does not erase the intervening history. AP-12 · Dependency-Aware Evolution Statement. Change to an object is assessed in relation to the objects, actionable forms and applications that depend upon it. Rationale. A correctly versioned object can still leave its dependants silently inconsistent; provenance is the connective tissue that makes changed states, decisions and lineages reconstructable, and dependency is the reason a local change is never only local. Upstream basis. KF-2002 C3; KF-L001 Literature Landscape (B04 · Governing Knowledge Change). Architectural consequences. dependencies are represented explicitly; impact analysis accompanies material change; affected dependants are revalidated, suspended or evolved; semantic rollback is not treated as a purely local operation. Family E · Modality, Implementation and Failure AP-13 · Modality-Independent Obligation Statement. Governance and epistemic obligations apply regardless of whether knowledge is represented, interpreted or applied through human judgement, symbolic structures, parametric models or hybrid systems. Rationale. The computational substrate may change while the epistemic obligations remain ( KF-1000 Principle V). Upstream basis. KF-1000 Principle V (modality independence); KF-L001 (B05 · Foundation Models and the Knowledge Sciences). Architectural consequences. the architecture does not assume all knowledge is explicitly inspectable in the same way; explanation and provenance requirements are adapted to modality without being discarded; opacity is treated as a constraint to be governed, not an exemption. Prohibited interpretations. a modality that resists inspection is granted an exemption from justification, provenance or explanation; interpretability is claimed of a representation that cannot support it. AP-14 · Logical before Physical Design Statement. Logical responsibility is defined before selecting physical components, technologies or deployment patterns. Rationale. Technology chosen ahead of responsibility tends to dictate — and quietly narrow — the responsibilities the architecture will admit. Upstream basis. The logical-architecture boundary of KF-3000 . Architectural consequences. services are specified through responsibilities, inputs, outputs, records and controls; one logical service may be distributed across several components; several logical services may be combined in one component; physical co-location does not erase logical separation. AP-15 · Humans and Machines Form One Governed System Statement. Human and computational work are architected as one governed system rather than as separate formal and informal layers. Rationale. An informal human layer outside the governed system is where provenance, attribution and accountability are lost. Upstream basis. KF-1000 Principle III; the human–AI governance obligations of the Canon. Architectural consequences. human decisions become governed records; machine actions remain attributable; hand-offs between people and services preserve provenance; informal human approval may not substitute for recorded acceptance. AP-16 · Explicit Failure and Degraded State Statement. The architecture represents failure, uncertainty and degraded governance explicitly rather than silently treating absence of evidence as evidence of conformance. Rationale. A governed system must distinguish “condition satisfied” from “condition not checked”, “evidence unavailable” and “control failed”. These are different states, and collapsing them into an implicit pass is how silent failure enters a system that otherwise looks conformant. Upstream basis. KF-2002 governance checkpoints; KF-3000 control architecture (detective and corrective controls); the continuous-conformance invariant. Architectural consequences. gate outcomes include pass, fail, pending and indeterminate where appropriate; service unavailability does not silently produce approval; missing evidence is represented as missing, not as satisfied; degraded operation is visible and bounded; fail-open and fail-closed behaviour is explicitly decided and recorded. Prohibited interpretations. an unreachable check is treated as a pass; absence of a violation record is treated as proof that no violation occurred. Part III · System Invariants 6. Identity and Representation Invariants INV-01 · Unique Object Identity Every Operational Knowledge Object has exactly one immutable identity. Scope: all objects, all lifecycle states. Protects: AP-04, AP-10; Canon Principle I. Violation: an identity resolves to more than one object, an object holds more than one active identity, or an identifier is reused. Upheld by: SVC-01 (with SVC-03). INV-02 · Representation Traceability Every governed representation is traceable to the object and version it represents. Scope: all structured representations. Protects: AP-04. Violation: a representation cannot be resolved to a single object and version. Upheld by: SVC-02, SVC-03. INV-03 · Logical Distinction Identity, representation, version, release, state, lineage, justification and acceptance remain logically distinguishable. Scope: the whole architecture. Protects: AP-04, AP-05. Violation: two of these collapse such that one cannot be changed or inspected without the other. Upheld by: SVC-01, SVC-02, SVC-06, SVC-07, SVC-09, SVC-10. 7. Evidence and Justification Invariants INV-04 · Provenance Persistence Every object retains recorded origin and subsequent provenance throughout its lifecycle. Scope: capture to historical state. Protects: AP-11, AP-12; the provenance invariant. Violation: origin or subsequent provenance is lost or unrecoverable. Upheld by: SVC-03. INV-05 · Justification before Operational Reliance No object enters operational reliance without an inspectable justification meeting the applicable gate. Scope: the Justify → Acceptance → Operationalise path. Protects: AP-05; Canon Principle VIII. Violation: an object is relied upon operationally without an inspectable justification meeting its gate. Upheld by: SVC-06, SVC-07, SVC-09. INV-06 · Counter-Evidence Visibility Material counter-evidence and unresolved challenge remain attached to the object’s epistemic record. Scope: objects for which material counter-evidence or unresolved challenge exists. Protects: AP-05. Violation: material counter-evidence or unresolved challenge is detached, hidden or overwritten. Upheld by: SVC-04, SVC-06. INV-07 · Acceptance Does Not Rewrite Epistemic Status Operational acceptance may define permitted reliance but may not erase uncertainty, disagreement or evidential weakness. Scope: the Acceptance transition and operational life. Protects: AP-05; IC-09. Violation: acceptance overwrites, hides or resets recorded epistemic status. Upheld by: SVC-06, SVC-07. 8. Governance and Accountability Invariants INV-08 · Attributable Transition Every lifecycle transition identifies both the service or actor that executed it and, where a governance decision is involved, the human authority or accountable body under whose authority it occurred. Scope: all transitions. Protects: AP-08, AP-09; Canon Principle III. Violation: a transition lacks an identified executor, or a governance-bearing transition lacks an identified human authority or accountable body. Upheld by: SVC-09. INV-09 · Human Accountability Every material acceptance, stewardship, release, suspension and retirement decision resolves to an identifiable human authority or a formally constituted accountable body. Scope: all material governance decisions. Protects: AP-08; Canon Principle III and the human-accountability invariant. Violation: such a decision lacks an identifiable human authority or accountable body. Upheld by: SVC-07, SVC-08, SVC-09, SVC-10 and SVC-14, with SVC-16 governing authority and permission assignments. INV-10 · Standing Governance Every operational object has valid stewardship, review status and applicable governance conditions in force. Scope: all operational objects. Protects: AP-07; Canon Principles IV and VII. Violation: an operational object is ownerless, unreviewed or out of compliance. Upheld by: SVC-08. INV-11 · Authorised Change No governed record or state is materially altered outside authorised service and role boundaries. Scope: all governed records and states. Protects: AP-06, AP-09. Violation: a governed record or state is altered outside its authorised service and role. Upheld by: SVC-16 (with every service). 9. Change and Historical Invariants INV-12 · Version Preservation Every prior governed version remains recoverable after change. Scope: all versioned objects. Protects: AP-11; the version-preservation invariant. Violation: a prior version becomes unrecoverable. Upheld by: SVC-10. INV-13 · Lineage Preservation Branching, consolidation, supersession, retirement and reactivation preserve explicit predecessor and successor relationships. Scope: all change and closure operations. Protects: AP-10, AP-11. Violation: a predecessor or successor link is lost or made ambiguous. Upheld by: SVC-10 (with SVC-14). INV-14 · No Silent Mutation Every material change produces a change, version or correction record. Scope: all governed records and states. Protects: AP-09, AP-11. Violation: a material change leaves no change, version or correction record. Upheld by: SVC-10 (with every service). INV-15 · Dependency Disposition No materially changed object returns to operational use until affected dependencies have been identified and dispositioned. Scope: evolution of objects that have dependants. Protects: AP-12. Violation: a materially changed object returns to use with dependants unidentified or undispositioned. Upheld by: SVC-11 (with SVC-09). INV-16 · Retirement Preserves History Retirement removes an object from active operational use without destroying its identity, records or lineage. Scope: all retirements. Protects: AP-11; Canon Principle VII. Violation: retirement destroys identity, records or lineage. Upheld by: SVC-14. 10. Operational Invariants INV-17 · Warranted Actionable Form Every actionable form traces to a specific object version, justification and valid acceptance-state. Scope: all actionable forms eligible for release or use. Protects: AP-05; IC-12. Violation: a releasable or usable actionable form has no traceable link to version, justification and acceptance. Upheld by: SVC-12. INV-18 · Governed Application No suspended, retired, unaccepted or governance-invalid object is used in a governed application. Scope: all governed applications. Protects: AP-07, AP-16. Violation: such an object is used in a governed application. Upheld by: SVC-13. The architecture distinguishes the ways this can fail — prevention failure, detection failure and deliberate override — so that a violation is diagnosable rather than merely flagged. INV-19 · Outcome Traceability Every material application outcome can be traced to the object version, actionable form and use context that produced it. Scope: all material applications. Protects: AP-09; the traceable-use invariant. Violation: a material outcome cannot be so traced. Upheld by: SVC-13. INV-20 · Modality-Appropriate Explainability Every material application supports an account appropriate to its modality, risk and decision context. Scope: all material applications. Protects: AP-13; Canon Principle IX. Violation: a material application supports no account appropriate to its modality, risk and context. Upheld by: SVC-13. 11. Assurance Invariants INV-21 · Inspectable Conformance The architecture can produce evidence showing whether each required capability, gate and invariant is satisfied. Scope: the whole architecture. Protects: AP-09. Violation: the architecture cannot show whether a required capability, gate or invariant holds. Upheld by: SVC-15. INV-22 · Assurance Independence A service may not be the sole judge of the validity of the records or controls it produces. Scope: all conformance judgements. Protects: IC-18. Violation: a service certifies its own records or controls with no independent check. Upheld by: SVC-15. INV-23 · Audit Non-Interference Assurance and audit operations do not alter the governed records under examination. Scope: all assurance and audit operations. Protects: IC-17. Violation: an assurance or audit operation alters a governed record under examination. Upheld by: SVC-15. INV-24 · No Silent Success An unmet, unevaluated or indeterminate required condition is never represented as satisfied. Scope: all required conditions, gates and checks. Protects: AP-16, AP-09. Violation: an unmet, unevaluated or indeterminate condition is represented as satisfied — for example, service unavailability yields approval, or missing evidence is read as a pass. Upheld by: SVC-15 (with SVC-09 for gate outcomes). Part IV · Service Interaction Constraints 12. State and Transition Constraints IC-01 · Lifecycle State Authority Only the Lifecycle and Transition Service may alter the recorded lifecycle state of an object. Other services may request, recommend or trigger a transition but may not change state directly. Protects: INV-08, INV-11. Participants: SVC-09; all requesting services. Required control: every state change carries a Transition Record attributable to SVC-09. IC-02 · Gate Enforcement A requested transition may execute only where the applicable gate has been evaluated and the gate decision is recorded as part of the same governed transition operation. Protects: INV-05, INV-08, INV-24. Participants: SVC-09 (with SVC-15 assurance). Required control: the Gate Decision Record and Transition Record are transactionally bound, share the same transition identifier, and cannot produce a completed transition independently of one another. IC-03 · Suspension Ownership The Lifecycle and Transition Service owns the suspension transition and record. Triggering services provide the reason and evidence. Protects: INV-08, INV-10. Participants: SVC-09; triggers from SVC-08, SVC-11, SVC-15. Required control: a Suspension Record (SVC-09) references its Suspension Recommendation or reason (originating service). IC-04 · Reactivation through Evolution A retired or suspended object may return to operational use only through the applicable Evolution, evaluation, justification and acceptance path. Protects: INV-05, INV-16. Participants: SVC-09, SVC-14; via SVC-10, SVC-05, SVC-06, SVC-07. Required control: reactivation produces a Transition Record and re-passes the Acceptance transition; SVC-14 supplies the Restoration Package. 13. Identity, Version and Lineage Constraints IC-05 · Identity Immutability No service may modify or reuse an assigned object identifier. Protects: INV-01. Participants: SVC-01; all services. Required control: identifier assignment is write-once and append-only. IC-06 · Version Immutability No service may overwrite a released or governed version. Corrections create a new version or an append-only correcting record. Protects: INV-12, INV-14. Participants: SVC-10; all services. Required control: version records are immutable; corrections are versioned or appended. IC-07 · Branch and Consolidation Identity Branching or consolidation creates successor object identities and explicit lineage links; it does not mutate predecessor identity. Protects: INV-01, INV-13. Participants: SVC-10 (with SVC-01). Required control: a Branch or Consolidation Record with predecessor and successor links. IC-08 · Release Separation Creating a version does not automatically release it. Release requires the applicable acceptance and governance conditions. Protects: INV-05, INV-17; AP-04. Participants: SVC-10, SVC-07. Required control: a Release Record distinct from the Version Record, linked to an Acceptance Record. 14. Evidence, Acceptance and Use Constraints IC-09 · Justification–Acceptance Separation The Justification Service establishes and records warrant. The Authority and Acceptance Service records authorised reliance. Neither may silently substitute for the other. Protects: INV-05, INV-07; AP-05. Participants: SVC-06 and SVC-07 (co-responsible); SVC-15 (assurance). Required control: Justification Record and Acceptance Record are distinct and separately attributable; the boundary is verified by assurance, not enforced by either peer against the other. IC-10 · Operationalisation Eligibility The Operationalisation Service may prepare a provisional actionable form from a non-operational object only where it is clearly marked non-releasable. It may release a form, or make it eligible for use, only when the form is linked to an accepted object version. Protects: INV-17. Participants: SVC-12 (checks SVC-07). Required control: a Warrant Linkage Record binds any releasable or usable form to an accepted version; provisional forms are marked non-releasable. IC-11 · Application Eligibility The Application and Outcome Service must verify acceptance, release and governance status before material use. Protects: INV-18. Participants: SVC-13 (checks SVC-07, SVC-08, SVC-09). Required control: an eligibility check recorded in the Application Record. IC-12 · Warrant Link Preservation No service may detach an actionable form or application record from the object version and warrant on which it depends. Protects: INV-17, INV-19; AP-05. Participants: SVC-12 and SVC-13 (co-responsible), with SVC-03 maintaining traceability and SVC-06 the warrant. Required control: warrant links are non-nullable and versioned with the form. 15. Governance and Access Constraints IC-13 · Authority Is Not Permission Possession of technical permission does not confer evaluation, acceptance, release, stewardship or retirement authority. Protects: INV-09, INV-11; AP-06. Participants: SVC-16, SVC-07. Required control: permission assignments and authority assignments are separate records. IC-14 · Least Necessary Alteration A service may alter only the records and states assigned to its logical responsibility. Protects: INV-11. Participants: all services. Required control: each record class names its authoritative maintainer ( KF-3000 §24); alteration outside it is rejected and logged. IC-15 · Material Administrative Action Changes to authority, permissions, stewardship, retention, release or governance state are recorded and attributable. Protects: INV-09, INV-11. Participants: SVC-16 (with SVC-08). Required control: an Access and Administrative Action Log entry per material change. IC-16 · Automated Authority Boundary Automated services may recommend and execute authorised operations but may not become the final accountable authority where human authority is required. Protects: INV-09; AP-08. Participants: SVC-07, SVC-08; all automated services. Required control: the accountable authority on a material decision resolves to a human role or accountable body. 16. Assurance Constraints IC-17 · Read-Only Assurance Boundary The Conformance and Audit Service may inspect governed records and control evidence but may not alter the records it evaluates or authorise the transitions it verifies. Protects: INV-23. Participants: SVC-15. Required control: assurance operates through read-only access to the records under examination. IC-18 · No Sole Self-Certification Conformance may not rely solely on assertions produced by the service or actor being assessed. Each material conformance judgement must include evidence generated independently of the assessed service’s own conformance assertion — such as record inspection, cross-service reconciliation, control testing or external review. Protects: INV-22. Participants: SVC-15; all assessed services. Required control: each conformance judgement cites at least one independently generated source of the kinds named above. IC-19 · Exception Visibility A failed control, waived requirement or unresolved exception remains visible until corrected, formally accepted as risk, or rendered irrelevant by retirement. Protects: INV-21, INV-24. Participants: SVC-15 (with SVC-08). Required control: an Exception Register entry persists until one of the three closure conditions is recorded. IC-23 · Proportionate Discharge The rigour to which a material obligation is discharged — gate exit depth, control strength, required evidence and reconstruction depth — is a function of the object’s assurance class ( KF-2003 ), applied at the release / scope-of-reliance to which the class attaches. Higher assurance classes require deeper discharge; lower classes require less. The lifecycle invariants are not graded: single identity, attributable transitions, justified transitions, inspectable transitions, provenance and preserved lineage hold identically at every class. Only the depth of evidence and review scales. Protects: AP-02 (Necessary and Proportionate Architecture); the six lifecycle invariants (ungraded). Participants: SVC-08, SVC-18, and every gate-executing service. Required control: each gate and control resolves the object’s assurance class and applies the minimum obligations KF-2003 fixes for that class, never less than the ungraded-invariant floor. 17. Provenance and Record Constraints IC-20 · Provenance Continuity Every material hand-off between actors or services preserves origin, derivation and attribution links. Protects: INV-04, INV-19. Participants: SVC-03; all services at hand-off. Required control: provenance links are carried through, not regenerated, at each hand-off. IC-21 · Append-Only Correction A material governed record may be corrected, but the original record and the correction relationship remain recoverable. Protects: INV-12, INV-14. Participants: all services maintaining records; SVC-10 for versioned corrections. Required control: corrections append; they do not overwrite. IC-22 · Time Semantics Preservation Every governed record carries recorded time and, where relevant, effective time; where the underlying event occurred at a third distinct time, event time is also preserved. ( Recorded time is when the system received the fact; effective time is when it is valid in the represented domain; event time is when the real-world event occurred.) Protects: INV-14; the Common Record Properties of KF-3000 §14.8; aligns with KF-3004 . Participants: all services. Required control: recorded time is mandatory on every governed record; effective and event time are recorded where they differ. IC-24 · Event-Native Evidence Conformance evidence is emitted by the governed act, not authored as a separate artefact. The record a governed act produces is its conformance evidence: an acceptance record evidences acceptance, a transition record is the audit event, a validation is the test result, a provenance link evidences derivation, a supersession link evidences lineage. A distinct evidence artefact is admitted only where the act’s own record cannot carry the required proof. This constraint bounds the cost of assurance and prevents the accumulation of evidence-about-evidence. Protects: INV-22; the conformance-evidence obligation (CTRL-CNF-01, KF-3005 ). Participants: all services producing governed records; SVC-18 reads without re-authoring. Required control: the governed act’s own record is registered as the conformance evidence for that act; a separate artefact is produced only against a recorded justification that the act’s record is insufficient. Aligns with KF-3004 §5.2. Part V · Architectural Decision Rules 18. Decision Record Requirement Every material architectural decision records: the question being decided; the upstream obligations affected; alternatives considered; the invariants and constraints involved; trade-offs accepted; the accountable decision-maker; the effective date; and the review or reversal condition. 19. Decision Tests A proposed architectural decision must pass the following tests. 19.1 Obligation test. Which upstream obligation does the decision support? 19.2 Invariant test. Could the decision cause any invariant to cease to hold within its scope? 19.3 Separation test. Does the decision collapse concepts that KF-3000 requires to remain distinct? 19.4 Accountability test. Does it obscure who is answerable? 19.5 Traceability test. Can the resulting actions and records be reconstructed? 19.6 Reversibility test. Can the decision be revised without destroying history or lineage? 19.7 Modality test. Does the design remain valid across the computational modalities it claims to support? 19.8 Failure test. Does the design represent failure, unavailability and indeterminacy explicitly rather than as silent success? 19.9 Sufficiency test. Does the design discharge the obligation without introducing unnecessary architectural commitment? 20. Variations, Exceptions and Non-Conformance Three cases are distinguished, and they are not interchangeable. 20.1 Architectural Variation A design that differs from the reference form but continues to satisfy all principles, invariants and constraints is a conforming variation. It requires an Architectural Decision Record, not an exception. 20.2 Principle Exception A time-bounded departure from an architectural principle may be permitted where: the affected principle is identified; no Canonical Principle or system invariant is violated; the rationale and risk are recorded; the exception is approved by an identified authority; its scope and duration are bounded; compensating controls are stated; and a review or expiry condition is defined. 20.3 Non-Conformance A design or operation that violates a Canonical Principle, a system invariant or a mandatory interaction constraint is non-conforming. It cannot be converted into conformity merely by recording an exception. A proposed exception that cannot preserve an invariant is non-conformance, not an architectural variation. Part VI · Conformance 21. Principle Conformance Principle conformance is demonstrated through architectural decisions, mappings and design evidence showing that the principle shaped the architecture. 22. Invariant Conformance Invariant conformance is demonstrated through preventive controls; detective checks; representative test cases; record inspection; exception and violation reporting; and evidence that the invariant remains true over time within its scope. This is the Required evidence referenced by each invariant in Part III. 23. Interaction Conformance Interaction conformance is demonstrated through service responsibility matrices; logical service contracts; transition and authorisation tests; audit records; prohibited-path testing; and evidence that services cannot silently bypass the required interaction constraints. 24. Required Conformance Artefacts A conforming architecture maintains: an Architectural Principle Register; an Invariant Register; a Service Interaction Constraint Register; an Assurance Class Register (recording each release’s assigned class and overlays, per KF-2003 ); an Architectural Decision Record Register; an Exception Register; an Invariant Test Register; a Principle-to-Capability crosswalk; an Invariant-to-Control crosswalk; and an Interaction Constraint-to-Service crosswalk. KF-3002 must derive capabilities consistent with these principles and sufficient to preserve all system invariants and enforce all interaction constraints. KF-3003 must define service responsibilities and contracts that enforce the interaction constraints, and complete the constraint-to-contract detail behind §27. KF-3004 must define records capable of proving invariant and transition conformance, and fix the recorded/effective/event time semantics of IC-22. KF-3005 must encode gates and lifecycle controls without permitting bypass, including the transactional binding of gate decision and transition (IC-02). KF-3008 must define authority and accountability, kept distinct from the technical permission assigned by SVC-16. KF-3007 must define tests and evidence for principle, invariant and interaction conformance. KF-3009 must preserve end-to-end traceability across all mappings. KF-4000 may choose technologies and physical designs freely within these boundaries. Closing Statement Architectural freedom exists within constitutional constraint. The Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture does not require every implementation to look the same. It requires every implementation to preserve the same essential distinctions, responsibilities, histories and lines of accountability. KF-3001 defines those non-negotiable conditions, and fixes the grammar — principle, invariant, constraint; applied by decision, shown by conformance — in which the remainder of the architecture series is written.

d: The Required Abilities of a Governed Knowledge Architecture
x: Purpose KF-3002 defines the architectural capabilities required to realise the Knowledge Foundry methodology and preserve the principles, invariants and interaction constraints established in KF-3001 . A capability is an enduring ability the architecture must possess, independent of organisational workflow, accountable role, logical service arrangement, information-storage model, technology, vendor, deployment topology or computational modality. KF-3002 answers: What must a conforming Knowledge Foundry architecture be able to do? KF-3003 answers: Through which logical services are those abilities exposed and coordinated? KF-3004 answers: Through which records and relationships are those abilities represented and evidenced? KF-3005 answers: Through which lifecycle controls are those abilities constrained? Capability Derivation Every capability must be traceable to an upstream obligation. A capability belongs in KF-3002 only when its absence would leave a Canonical Principle, a lifecycle stage/gate/invariant, an engineering-practice obligation, a mandatory engineering artefact, a KF-3001 invariant or interaction constraint, or a conformance requirement unsupported. Capability Admission Test A proposed capability is admitted only where it expresses an enduring architectural ability; is independent of any specific technology or organisational procedure; has an identifiable upstream basis; has observable required behaviours; has identifiable information objects and relationships; would create a defined architectural risk on failure; has demonstrable conformance; and is not already fully contained within another capability. Capability Boundaries A capability is not a lifecycle stage, an engineering practice, a logical service, a human role, an artefact, a control, an application feature or a technology component. The relationships are: Part I · Capability Model Foundations 1. Capability Domains The model contains five capability domains and twenty-four constituent capabilities. Domain Purpose Capabilities Principal upstream basis A · Identity Representation Establish and preserve what the object is and how it can be inspected 3 KF-2002 Domain A B · Evidence Justification Establish and preserve the warrant for belief 4 KF-2002 Domain B C · Operational Governance Govern authority, custody, versioning, release, change and transition 8 KF-2002 Domain C D · Operational Use Make knowledge actionable and learn from its use 4 KF-2002 Domain D E · Assurance, Protection Continuity Preserve provenance, integrity, conformance and explicit operating condition across all domains 5 KF-3000 and KF-3001 Domains A–D describe the abilities that act upon the Operational Knowledge Object and its operational life. Domain E is cross-cutting: it does not author, evaluate or alter the substantive content of an Operational Knowledge Object, nor does it independently authorise lifecycle transitions. It preserves and evaluates the provenance, integrity, temporal condition, protection and conformance evidence surrounding that content. 2. Capability Levels KF-3002 uses two levels. A domain capability is a broad architectural ability grouping related subordinate capabilities (for example, Operational Governance ). A constituent capability is a bounded, independently testable architectural ability (for example, Authority and Acceptance Management ). KF-3002 does not decompose below constituent capability level; detailed service operations belong in KF-3003 and implementation functions in KF-4000. 3. Capability Specification Each constituent capability is specified through eleven fields: Capability statement — the enduring ability; Purpose — why the ability is required; Upstream derivation — practices, principles, invariants and constraints; Scope — what falls inside and outside the capability; Required behaviours — what the architecture must be able to do; Principal information objects — the logical information structures acted upon or produced; Capability relationships — typed relationships to other capabilities; Protected invariants — KF-3001 invariants preserved; Operating criticality — the consequence of the capability’s inability or degradation; Failure conditions — what inability or misuse looks like; Conformance condition — observable proof that the capability exists. A principal information object is a logical information structure created, consumed or maintained by a capability. It may be an engineering artefact, governed record, representation, decision, status, linkage or result. It is not necessarily an Operational Knowledge Object; the OKO is the governed subject, while information objects are the structures through which capabilities act upon and evidence it. Operating criticality classifies the consequence of a capability being unavailable or degraded, using the categories: conformance-critical , governance-critical , operationally critical , recoverable with bounded manual control , and advisory . A capability may combine a category with a default failure posture (fail-open or fail-closed). This classification does not set implementation availability targets; it lets KF-3005 and KF-3007 determine the consequence of unavailability. 4. Capability Relationship Types Capabilities relate through five typed relationships, replacing any single undifferentiated notion of dependency: Prerequisite — an ability that must already exist or produce an input before this one can operate; Collaborating capability — an ability participating with this one in the same governed operation; Constraining capability — an ability that limits or validates this one’s execution; Triggered capability — an ability invoked as a consequence of this one; Evidence provider / consumer — an ability supplying, or receiving, conformance evidence. Typing these relationships removes false circularity: two capabilities that collaborate in one operation are not mutual prerequisites. Relationships do not create authority; authority is assigned through KF-3008 . 5. Common Capability Requirements Every capability must: preserve the relevant KF-3001 invariants; operate within the applicable interaction constraints; produce or maintain inspectable evidence of material actions; expose failure, pending and indeterminate conditions explicitly; preserve attribution between human and computational action; operate across supported computational modalities; preserve recorded time and effective time where relevant; preserve the authoritative-maintainer boundary assigned to each information object in KF-3003 and KF-3004 , altering such information only through a governed interaction; remain logically distinguishable even where combined physically; support conformance inspection. Part II · Domain A — Identity Representation Domain Statement The architecture must be able to establish what an Operational Knowledge Object is, preserve its identity and make its representation and context inspectable. A-CAP-01 · Object Registration Capability statement. The architecture can register a candidate Operational Knowledge Object and assign it one durable, immutable identity, and can determine how an intake relates to existing objects. Purpose. Establish the object as a governable entity from the moment of capture, and route the intake correctly without itself performing version or lineage operations. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 A1; KF-3001 AP-04, AP-10; INV-01; IC-05. Scope. Includes candidate registration; identity assignment; initial origin capture; duplicate and prior-object assessment; classification of intake as a new object, version candidate, branch candidate or consolidation candidate. Excludes detailed semantic structuring; acceptance; release; the creation of the resulting version, branch or consolidated successor. A-CAP-01 determines whether an intake should create a new object identity or be routed to an existing object’s version or lineage path; it does not itself create the resulting version, branch or consolidated successor (those are C-CAP-04 and C-CAP-06). This preserves the distinction: identity resolution ≠ version creation ≠ lineage operation. Required behaviours. assign an immutable object identifier; prevent identifier reuse; distinguish object identity from record identity; determine whether intake represents a new object or relates to an existing one; bind origin and intake context to the identity; route version, branch and consolidation candidates to the responsible capability; expose ambiguous or unresolved identity conditions; prevent progression where identity is absent or conflicting. Principal information objects. Object Identity Record; Intake Record; Provenance Seed; Identity Resolution Decision. Capability relationships. - Constrained by: E-CAP-03, E-CAP-04 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 - May trigger: C-CAP-04, C-CAP-06 Protected invariants. INV-01; INV-04; INV-11; INV-24. Operating criticality. Governance-critical; normally fail-closed — no progression without a resolved, unique identity. Failure conditions. Duplicate identity; reused identifier; unidentified object; origin absent; unresolved ambiguity represented as resolved; version or branch incorrectly registered as an unrelated object. Conformance condition. For any registered object, an independent reviewer can recover its identity, origin, intake decision and, where applicable, its relationship to predecessor or source objects. A-CAP-02 · Structured Representation Capability statement. The architecture can create and maintain an inspectable representation of an object’s semantic content, type, constituent elements and relationships. Purpose. Enable evaluation, justification, governance, discovery and explanation to operate on explicit representations. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 A2; KF-3001 AP-04, AP-05, AP-13; INV-02; INV-03. Scope. Includes semantic typing; constituent claim or element representation; metadata; object relationships; source-to-representation linkage; multiple representations of one object version. Excludes evidence evaluation; justification; operational acceptance; physical representation technology. Required behaviours. assign and maintain semantic type; represent constituent claims or elements; represent relationships among elements and objects; preserve the distinction between content and warrant; support human, symbolic, parametric and hybrid representations; indicate representation limitations and opacity; link every representation to the object and version represented. Principal information objects. Structured Representation; Semantic Type Record; Metadata Record; Object Relationship Record; Representation Limitation Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: A-CAP-01 - Constrained by: E-CAP-03 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 - May trigger: C-CAP-04 Protected invariants. INV-02; INV-03; INV-04; INV-20. Operating criticality. Governance-critical — inspectability is a precondition of evaluation, justification and governance. Failure conditions. Representation not linked to object or version; structure implicit and unrecoverable; type absent or contradictory; semantic relationship lost; modality limitations concealed; content and justification collapsed. Conformance condition. A reviewer can identify what the representation expresses, which object and version it represents, how its material elements relate and what limitations apply to its modality. A-CAP-03 · Object Resolution and Contextual Discovery Capability statement. The architecture can locate and retrieve an object together with the governed context required to interpret its identity, state, warrant, relationships and history. Purpose. Ensure that retrieval does not detach content from its governance and epistemic context. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 A1, A2; KF-3001 AP-05, AP-09; INV-02, INV-03, INV-04; IC-12. Scope. Includes discovery by object identity, version, semantic type, relationship, lifecycle state, epistemic status, steward, lineage, and acceptance or release condition. Excludes ranking algorithms; user-interface design; physical indexes; implementation-specific search technology. Required behaviours. resolve an identifier to exactly one object; retrieve current and historical versions; expose lifecycle and epistemic status separately; traverse object relationships and lineage; retrieve relevant warrant and governance context; distinguish current, superseded, branched, consolidated, suspended and retired objects; prevent context-free retrieval from being represented as governed knowledge. Principal information objects. Resolution Result; Governed Context Package; Relationship Path; Lineage Path; Retrieval Provenance Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: A-CAP-01, A-CAP-02 - Constrained by: E-CAP-03 - Evidence providers: B-CAP-04, C-CAP-08, E-CAP-01 Protected invariants. INV-01; INV-02; INV-03; INV-04; INV-17. Operating criticality. Recoverable with bounded manual control — discovery may degrade for a bounded period without blocking governed transitions, provided degradation is visible. Failure conditions. Ambiguous resolution; stale version presented as current; content retrieved without its relevant acceptance or warrant; retired or suspended status concealed; lineage or relationship path broken. Conformance condition. Given a valid retrieval request, the architecture can return the correct object and enough governed context to determine what it is, which version is being inspected, its present standing and the basis on which it may be relied upon. Part III · Domain B — Evidence Justification Domain Statement The architecture must be able to represent, evaluate and preserve the grounds on which an object may be believed without conflating evidential quality, justification and operational acceptance. B-CAP-01 · Evidence Registration and Relationship Capability statement. The architecture can register evidence and counter-evidence as governed records and relate them explicitly to claims, objects and assessments. Purpose. Make evidential support, challenge and origin independently inspectable. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 B1, B2; KF-3001 AP-05; INV-04; INV-06; IC-20. Scope. Includes evidence and counter-evidence registration; evidence-to-claim and evidence-to-object linkage; evidence classification (support, challenge, context); evidence provenance; evidence availability status. Excludes quality evaluation (B-CAP-02); justification assembly (B-CAP-03); acceptance; adjudication of the truth of the evidence. Required behaviours. assign evidence-record identity; capture evidence origin and type; distinguish support, challenge and context; relate evidence to specific claims or objects; preserve evidence independently from the conclusion drawn from it; retain conflicting evidence; identify missing or unavailable evidence explicitly. Principal information objects. Evidence Record; Counter-Evidence Record; Evidence-to-Claim Link; Evidence Classification; Evidence Availability Status. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: A-CAP-01, A-CAP-02 - Constrained by: E-CAP-03 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 Protected invariants. INV-04; INV-06; INV-24. Operating criticality. Governance-critical — warrant depends on inspectable evidence. Failure conditions. Evidence embedded but not identifiable; evidence detached from its source; counter-evidence hidden or deleted; support relationship stated without basis; unavailable evidence represented as favourable evidence. Conformance condition. For each material claim, the architecture can recover the evidence and counter-evidence related to it, their origins, roles and present availability. B-CAP-02 · Quality Evaluation Capability statement. The architecture can assess the quality and fitness of a structured object or evidence item against explicit criteria and record the resulting verdict. Purpose. Determine whether an object is suitable to proceed toward justification. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 B1; KF-3001 AP-09, AP-16; INV-21; INV-24. Scope. Includes application of evaluation criteria; assessment of quality, consistency, completeness and confidence; recording of pass, fail, return, pending and indeterminate verdicts; retention of verdicts and reasons. Excludes justification construction (B-CAP-03); acceptance (C-CAP-01); the definition of organisational thresholds, which belong to the applicable governance or implementation profile. Required behaviours. apply defined evaluation criteria; preserve criteria and applicable thresholds; evaluate quality, consistency, completeness and confidence; distinguish pass, fail, return, pending and indeterminate; retain all verdicts and reasons; route failed or incomplete assessments appropriately; prevent unevaluated conditions from appearing as passed. Principal information objects. Evaluation Criteria Record; Quality Assessment; Evaluation Verdict; Evaluation Exception; Confidence Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: A-CAP-02, B-CAP-01 - Constrained by: E-CAP-04 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-05 - Provides evidence to: E-CAP-02 Protected invariants. INV-05; INV-21; INV-24. Operating criticality. Governance-critical — the quality gate precedes justification. Failure conditions. Undocumented criteria; verdict without reasons; pending assessment treated as passed; low-quality object advanced; evaluation altered after the fact without history. Conformance condition. For any evaluation, a reviewer can recover the criteria, inputs, evaluator, result, confidence, reasons and disposition. B-CAP-03 · Justification Construction and Inspection Capability statement. The architecture can assemble, preserve and expose an inspectable warrant connecting claims to evidence, counter-evidence, rationale and assumptions. Purpose. Establish why an object may be believed without claiming that justification guarantees truth. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 B2; KF-3001 AP-05; INV-05; INV-06; IC-09. Scope. Includes claim-to-evidence linkage; assumptions and rationale; the end-to-end traceability chain; the admission and reliance rationale for parametrically represented capability; preservation of unresolved challenges. Excludes acceptance (C-CAP-01); evidence registration (B-CAP-01); quality evaluation (B-CAP-02); any claim that justification guarantees truth. Required behaviours. relate claims to supporting and defeating evidence; record assumptions and rationale; preserve unresolved challenges; create an end-to-end traceability chain; support independent inspection; preserve an inspectable admission and reliance rationale for parametric capability; prevent acceptance from substituting for justification. Principal information objects. Justification Record; Assumption Record; Rationale Record; Traceability Chain; Challenge Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: B-CAP-01, B-CAP-02 - Constrained by: E-CAP-03 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 - May trigger: C-CAP-01 Protected invariants. INV-04; INV-05; INV-06; INV-07. Operating criticality. Governance-critical — justification is the warrant on which reliance rests. Failure conditions. Rationale unsupported; assumptions hidden; counter-evidence omitted; traceability incomplete; accepted status treated as epistemic proof; modality opacity used as an exemption from warrant. Conformance condition. An independent reviewer can reconstruct the material reasons for and against belief, identify the assumptions and trace each material claim to its evidential basis. B-CAP-04 · Epistemic Status Management Capability statement. The architecture can represent and maintain the epistemic standing of an object independently from its lifecycle, release and acceptance states. Purpose. Preserve uncertainty, dispute and evidential weakness even where operational reliance is permitted. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 B1, B2, C1; KF-3001 AP-04, AP-05; INV-03; INV-07; IC-09. Scope. Includes representation of epistemic conditions from unassessed through insufficiently supported; confidence and uncertainty; contestation; attributable status-change events; prior epistemic states. Excludes lifecycle state (C-CAP-08); acceptance (C-CAP-01); release (C-CAP-05). Required behaviours. represent unassessed, quality-assessed, warrant-established, contested, warrant-weakened and insufficiently supported conditions; preserve confidence and uncertainty; record unresolved challenges; distinguish epistemic status from acceptance; update status only through attributable evidence or assessment events; preserve prior epistemic states. Principal information objects. Epistemic Status Record; Confidence Record; Contestation Record; Epistemic Status Change Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: B-CAP-01, B-CAP-02, B-CAP-03 - Collaborates with: C-CAP-01 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 Protected invariants. INV-03; INV-06; INV-07; INV-14. Operating criticality. Governance-critical — protects the separation of epistemic standing from acceptance. Failure conditions. Acceptance overwrites evidential weakness; uncertainty reduced without evidence; dispute removed without disposition; lifecycle state used as proxy for epistemic status. Conformance condition. The architecture can show an object’s present and historical epistemic standing separately from whether it is accepted, released or operationally active. Part IV · Domain C — Operational Governance Domain Statement The architecture must be able to control authority, stewardship, review, versioning, release, change, dependency and transition throughout the operational life of an object. Version, acceptance and release are kept as distinct capabilities because they occur at different points and are governed by different obligations. C-CAP-01 · Authority and Acceptance Management Capability statement. The architecture can record and govern the decision by which an identified authority permits reliance upon a justified object. Purpose. Separate epistemic warrant from institutional permission to rely. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 C1; KF-3001 AP-06, AP-08; INV-05, INV-08, INV-09, INV-17; IC-09, IC-13. Scope. Includes acceptance, provisional-acceptance and refusal decisions; authority identification and scope verification; the scope, conditions and duration of reliance; decision rationale. Excludes justification construction (B-CAP-03); permission assignment (E-CAP-03); version creation (C-CAP-04); release designation (C-CAP-05); stewardship (C-CAP-02). Required behaviours. identify the accepting authority or accountable body; verify that the authority’s mandate, scope and effective period apply to the decision; record acceptance, provisional acceptance or refusal; define scope, conditions and duration of reliance; preserve decision rationale; prevent acceptance where mandatory prerequisites are absent; route refusal or conditional acceptance appropriately. Principal information objects. Acceptance Record; Refusal Record; Scope-of-Reliance Record; Authority Assignment Reference; Acceptance Condition Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: B-CAP-03, B-CAP-04, E-CAP-03 - Collaborates with: C-CAP-08 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 - May trigger: C-CAP-05, C-CAP-08 Protected invariants. INV-05; INV-08; INV-09; INV-17; INV-24. Operating criticality. Governance-critical; normally fail-closed — no acceptance without an applicable authority. Failure conditions. Acceptance without an identified applicable authority; acceptance substituting for justification; technical permission mistaken for acceptance authority; acceptance where mandatory prerequisites are absent; refusal neither routed nor recorded. Conformance condition. Every accepted object carries a decision attributable to an authority or accountable body whose mandate, scope and effective period were applicable, together with the reliance scope, conditions, date and supporting justification. C-CAP-02 · Stewardship and Responsibility Management Capability statement. The architecture can assign, maintain and transfer stewardship and responsibility for an operational object. Purpose. Ensure sustained human accountability throughout operational life. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 C2; KF-3001 AP-08; INV-09; INV-10; INV-11. Scope. Includes steward assignment and transfer; identification of accountable roles; stewardship history; the mandate and membership of an accountable body where used. Excludes acceptance decisions (C-CAP-01); review scheduling (C-CAP-03); access-permission assignment (E-CAP-03). Required behaviours. assign a steward before operational release; identify accountable roles; transfer stewardship without loss of history; prevent ownerless operational state; distinguish service execution from human accountability; preserve mandate and membership where an accountable body is used. Principal information objects. Stewardship Assignment; Responsibility Record; Stewardship History; Accountable Body Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: A-CAP-01 - Collaborates with: C-CAP-08 - Constrained by: E-CAP-03 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 Protected invariants. INV-09; INV-10; INV-11. Operating criticality. Governance-critical — no operational object may be ownerless. Failure conditions. Ownerless operational object; stewardship transfer that loses history; service execution mistaken for accountability; accountable body without recoverable mandate or membership. Conformance condition. For every operational object and material governance decision, the architecture can identify the responsible steward and applicable human authority or accountable body. C-CAP-03 · Review and Compliance Management Capability statement. The architecture can schedule, execute and record reviews and determine whether standing governance conditions remain satisfied. Purpose. Preserve legitimacy as evidence, policy and context change. Review determines whether the object’s warrant, utility and governance standing remain adequate. Compliance determines whether applicable formal obligations are satisfied. A review may include compliance evaluation, but one does not substitute for the other. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 C2; KF-3001 AP-07, AP-16; INV-10, INV-18, INV-21, INV-24. Scope. Includes review scheduling; due and overdue detection; evaluation of applicable policy and governance requirements; recording of review outcomes, compliance findings and exceptions; triggering of suspension, evolution or retirement. Excludes the transition execution itself (C-CAP-08); acceptance (C-CAP-01); the definition of external policy. Required behaviours. establish review cycles; detect due and overdue reviews; evaluate applicable policy and governance requirements; record review outcomes, compliance assessments and exceptions; trigger suspension, evolution or retirement; prevent expired governance conditions from remaining silently valid. Principal information objects. Review Schedule; Review Record; Compliance Assessment; Compliance Finding; Governance Exception; Review Trigger. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: C-CAP-02 - Collaborates with: C-CAP-08 - Constrained by: E-CAP-04 - May trigger: C-CAP-06, C-CAP-08 - Provides evidence to: E-CAP-02 Protected invariants. INV-10; INV-18; INV-21; INV-24. Operating criticality. Governance-critical; recoverable within a defined period — a late review is bounded and must be visible as overdue. Failure conditions. Expired governance condition remaining silently valid; overdue review undetected; compliance breach unrecorded; review outcome without disposition. Conformance condition. The architecture can establish whether every operational object has a valid steward, review status and applicable governance conditions in force. C-CAP-04 · Version Management Capability statement. The architecture can create, preserve and resolve immutable versions of an Operational Knowledge Object without altering its enduring identity. Purpose. Preserve every state of represented content and warrant as an immutable, recoverable version, distinct from acceptance and release. A version must exist before an object can be evaluated, justified, accepted or released; version creation is therefore prior to, not consequent on, acceptance. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 C2, C3; KF-3001 AP-04, AP-11; INV-03, INV-12, INV-14; IC-06. Scope. Includes creation of candidate and governed versions; preservation of prior versions; the version-to-identity relation; predecessor and successor identification; correction and supersession relationships; the distinction of version state from acceptance and release state. Excludes the acceptance decision (C-CAP-01); release designation (C-CAP-05); lineage and evolution operations (C-CAP-06). Required behaviours. create candidate and governed versions; preserve prior versions; relate versions to their object identity; prevent overwrite; identify predecessor and successor versions; preserve correction and supersession relationships; distinguish version state from acceptance and release state. Principal information objects. Version Record; Version State; Predecessor–Successor Link; Correction Record. Capability relationships. - Prerequisites: A-CAP-01, A-CAP-02 - Collaborates with: E-CAP-05 - Constrained by: E-CAP-03 - Evidence providers: E-CAP-01 Protected invariants. INV-03; INV-12; INV-14; and constraint IC-06. Operating criticality. Governance-critical; fail-closed — a prior version is never overwritten. Failure conditions. Version overwritten; version detached from object identity; predecessor or successor relationship lost; version state conflated with release state. Conformance condition. For any object, a reviewer can enumerate its immutable versions, their order, and their correction and supersession relationships, distinct from whether any version is accepted or released. C-CAP-05 · Release Management Capability statement. The architecture can designate an accepted version as eligible for a defined scope and period of operational reliance. Purpose. Separate controlled operational release from both version creation and acceptance, so that creating a version does not release it and accepting a version does not automatically make every successor released. Upstream derivation. KF-2002 C2; KF-3001 AP-04, AP-06; INV-05, INV-17; IC-08. Scope. Includes verification of acceptance; binding of release to a specific immutable version; release scope and effective period; prevention of automatic release inheritance; withdrawal, suspension and supersession of releases; release history. Excludes version creation (C-CAP-04); the acceptance decision (C-CAP-01); actionable-form release (D-CAP-01). Required behaviours. verify acceptance; bind release to a specific immutable version; define release scope and effective period; prevent automatic inheritance of release by a new version; withdraw, suspend or supersede releases; preserve release history. Principal information objects. Release Record; Release Scope; Effective Period; Withdrawal Record; Supersession Record. INV-05; INV-17; and constraint IC-08. Operating criticality. Governance-critical; normally fail-closed — no release without a bound, accepted version. Failure conditions.
