KF-3008 defines the authority model behind AUT-01/02 and the delegation, stewardship, access and computational-participation assignments; KF-3004 defines the logical records that represent them. KF-3007 defines the tests and evidence for information, service and system conformance. KF-3009 preserves traceability from Canonical Principle through practice, invariant, capability, service, information object, control and implementation. KF-4000 may implement this logical architecture through relational, graph, document, event-stream, object-store, ledger, file or human-maintained structures, and may denormalise, replicate, index or distribute — provided it does not create conflicting authoritative records, collapse required semantic distinctions, overwrite immutable history, remove required provenance, substitute a projection for authoritative state, make historical reconstruction impossible, treat missing or indeterminate information as satisfied, or prevent independent conformance inspection. Closing Statement The Governed Information and Record Model defines the memory of the Knowledge Foundry architecture. It ensures that substantive knowledge, warrant, authority, operational use and assurance remain distinguishable yet connected; that every material decision and transition is evidenced; that history survives change; and that the architecture can reconstruct not merely what it currently holds, but how that state came to exist and why it was permitted to be relied upon. Each record family resolves to exactly one authoritative maintainer, each historical view is derived rather than duplicated, each status represents one conceptual dimension, and each crosswalk demonstrates the obligation it claims.

The State, Transition, Gate and Control Model of the Knowledge Foundry Document Class: Reference Architecture · Parent Document: KF-3000 · Governed By: KF-3001 · Derived From: KF-2001 , KF-2002 , KF-3002 , KF-3003 and KF-3004 · Status: Draft · Version: 0.2 Editorial Position KF-3005 is the behavioural architecture of the Knowledge Foundry. The documents before it are largely structural: KF-3001 states what must remain true, KF-3002 what the architecture must be able to do, KF-3003 where logical responsibility resides, and KF-3004 what information exists and how it is preserved. KF-3005 defines how governed change is permitted and executed . It is therefore neither a restatement of the nine-stage methodology lifecycle in KF-2001 nor a workflow specification for a particular implementation. KF-2001 defines the lifecycle method ; KF-3005 defines the architectural machinery that makes that lifecycle enforceable. Purpose KF-3005 defines the behavioural architecture through which governed entities move between valid states. It specifies lifecycle domains; state machines; permitted transitions; transition-request semantics; gate compositions; reusable controls; execution and persistence rules; exception and degraded-state behaviour; recovery and reconciliation; concurrency and conflict handling; and control and transition evidence. KF-3004 defines what governed information exists. KF-3005 defines how that information may change. KF-3005 introduces no new authoritative information classes; it uses the KF-3004 objects and governs their creation, update, correction, status change and historical preservation. The document is centred on the transition rather than on the state. A state is a governed condition; a transition is the operation through which the architecture changes that condition. Accordingly, KF-3005 answers a single, narrow question: Under what conditions may a governed entity move from one state to another; which authority may permit that movement; which controls must be satisfied; how is the transition executed; and what evidence must remain afterwards? Alignment and Reconciliation Note This document is reconciled against the nineteen-service catalogue shared by KF-3002 and the KF-3004 v0.2 record model (SVC-01 … SVC-19), in which the authoritative owners referenced here are: SVC-05 Justification (epistemic standing); SVC-06 Authority and Acceptance; SVC-08 Lifecycle and Transition; SVC-09 Version and Lineage; SVC-10 Release; SVC-12 Operationalisation; SVC-13 Application and Outcome; SVC-14 Retirement and Preservation; SVC-15 Provenance; SVC-16 Access and Integrity; SVC-17 Operating Condition and Exception; SVC-18 Conformance and Audit; SVC-19 Temporal Continuity. All service, record ( KF-3004 ), invariant ( KF-3001 , INV-* ) and interaction-constraint ( IC-* ) references in this document use that catalogue and the KF-3004 v0.2 record codes, including its §15.1 current-state / event-history rule and its §7.2 composite-decision rule. Upstream caution. Where the scaffold named services that do not exist under a single owner — an “Epistemic Status Service,” a standalone “Release Service,” an “Operating Condition and Exception Service” — this document binds them to the frozen catalogue owners above. Any copy of KF-3003 that still enumerates only sixteen services predates this catalogue and should be read as superseded by the KF-3002 / KF-3004 v0.2 service model; the mismatch is an upstream KF-3003 versioning item, not a KF-3005 divergence. Changes in v0.2 Relative to v0.1: the abnormal-condition vocabulary (failure, exception, violation, degradation, indeterminate, conflict) is consolidated into a single distinction table (§3); the “no single universal state machine” and “recovery is forward restoration, not historical erasure” principles are made explicit (§7, §44); “gates orchestrate reusable controls” is stated directly with a worked decomposition (§29); the three governed catalogues — Transition, Gate and Control — are named as an organising principle (§21); and the mis-labelled state-assertion clause is relocated to its proper place at the end of the state architecture (§20). Substantive content, identifiers and crosswalks from v0.1 are preserved. Part I · Behavioural Architecture Foundations 1. Scope KF-3005 governs changes involving Operational Knowledge Objects; object versions; representations; epistemic standing; acceptance; release; stewardship and governance standing; actionable forms; applications; retirement; service operating condition; and conformance standing. It excludes organisational workflow design; user-interface sequence; technology-specific transaction management; physical event-bus design; database locking; service deployment; detailed authority assignment ( KF-3008 ); and assurance methodology ( KF-3007 ). 2. Core Behavioural Concepts 2.1 Lifecycle — the permitted broad phases through which a governed entity may pass. 2.2 State — the effective governed condition of one entity within one state machine. 2.3 Transition — a governed operation attempting to move an entity from a valid source state to a permitted target state. 2.4 Gate — the authoritative decision composition determining whether a proposed transition may execute. 2.5 Control — a reusable mechanism that validates, prevents, detects, constrains, records or evidences one condition required by a gate or transition. 2.6 Trigger — an event, request, decision, elapsed period or condition initiating consideration of a transition. 2.7 Transition Request — the governed proposal to perform a specific transition on an identified entity. 2.8 Exception — a formally approved, bounded departure from normal control behaviour that does not violate an invariant. 2.9 Failure — an unsuccessful attempt to execute an otherwise valid operation. 2.10 Violation — a breach of a Canonical Principle, invariant or mandatory interaction constraint. 2.11 Recovery — the governed restoration of architectural consistency following interruption, failure, degradation or conflict. The five terms are canonical throughout KF-3005 and subsequent documents: 3. Abnormal Conditions The architecture distinguishes six conditions that must never be silently collapsed into one another. Each has different evidence, ownership and disposition. Condition Meaning Failure A valid operation did not complete successfully. Exception A formally authorised and bounded departure from normal control behaviour that does not violate an invariant. Violation A breach of a Canonical Principle, invariant or mandatory constraint. Degradation Reduced ability while operating within explicitly governed limits. Indeterminate condition The architecture cannot establish whether a required condition holds. Conflict Authoritative records or service states disagree. Two rules govern the boundary between them. First, an exception cannot convert an invariant violation into conformance — an authorised departure and a breach of an invariant are different in kind, not degree. Second, an indeterminate condition is never treated as satisfied : it is surfaced, not resolved by default (see §30, §43). 4. Behavioural Grammar The signature behavioural sequence of KF-3005 is centred on the transition — the transition, not the state, is the unit of governed change: 5. Behavioural Invariants Every transition must preserve: (1) the affected entity is uniquely identified; (2) the authoritative current state is resolved; (3) the transition is legally permitted by the applicable state machine; (4) required evidence is available or explicitly indeterminate; (5) applicable permission and authority are valid; (6) gate controls are executed; (7) Gate Decision and Transition Records are bound to one transition identifier; (8) no completed transition is partially recorded; (9) prior history remains recoverable; (10) affected services receive the resulting event; (11) failures and indeterminate outcomes remain visible; (12) conformance evidence is produced; (13) no transition bypasses a protected invariant; (14) semantic reversal does not erase the original transition. 6. Behavioural Specification Types KF-3005 defines four specification types: State-Machine Specification (permitted states and transitions for one entity class); Transition Specification (one governed state change); Gate Specification (the decision composition controlling one or more transitions); Control Specification (one reusable validation or enforcement mechanism). Part II · Lifecycle Domain Architecture 7. No Single Universal State Machine The architecture defines no single universal state machine . KF-3004 has already established that several state dimensions remain distinct, and KF-3005 preserves that separation: each governed condition belongs to its own state machine, and an entity may occupy states across several machines simultaneously. None of these states silently determines another. For one Operational Knowledge Object at one instant: Each of the six values above is owned by a different authoritative service and changes only through its own governed transition. 8. Lifecycle Domains KF-3005 defines several related but independent lifecycle domains, each with an authoritative state service drawn from the frozen KF-3003 catalogue. State-Assertion Rule (applying KF-3004 §15.1) A transition record preserves the historical act ; a state record represents the effective current condition ; both are established consistently through one governed transition operation. A discrepancy between transition history and current state must produce an integrity or indeterminate condition (a Conflict, per §3). Consistent with §7, none of the state dimensions silently determines another: an object may simultaneously be Operational, Released, Supported-but-Contested, Restricted (form), Degraded (condition) and Exception-Open (conformance). Part IV · Transition Architecture 21. Three Governed Catalogues KF-3005 defines its permitted behaviour through three distinct catalogues , deliberately kept separate rather than flattened into one control list: the Transition Catalogue (§27) — the permitted governed changes; the Gate Catalogue (§31) — the decision compositions controlling those changes; the Control Pattern Library (Part VI) — the reusable checks and enforcement mechanisms invoked by gates and transitions. Separation is what allows one control to be reused across many gates, and one gate across many transitions. 22. Transition Specification Every governed transition is specified through: transition identifier; name; purpose; governed entity; source state; target state; permitted trigger; preconditions; required evidence; required authority class; required permissions; applicable gate; required controls; authoritative executing service; collaborating services; records created or changed; execution atomicity; events published; cross-domain effects; failure behaviour; recovery behaviour; conformance evidence. 23. Transition Request Every request identifies: request identity; transition type; governed entity; source state claimed; target state requested; trigger; requesting actor or service; authority basis where applicable; supporting evidence; requested effective time; urgency; related exception; concurrency token or state reference. A request does not authorise or execute the transition. 24. Transition Eligibility A transition is eligible for gate evaluation only where: the entity exists; the source state is authoritative and current; the transition is permitted by the state machine; required evidence can be resolved; required authority and permissions are identifiable; no unresolved state conflict prevents assessment; and the applicable operating-condition policy permits evaluation. 25. Transition Atomicity A governed transition is architecturally atomic : it has one indivisible governed outcome — Completed or Not Completed . A completed transition establishes consistently: Gate Decision Record; Transition Record; resulting authoritative state; required status records; material provenance; event-publication record; conformance evidence. A transition must never leave the architecture in a state where a gate says pass but the state did not change; the state changed but no transition record exists; a release was created but its acceptance reference is missing; or one service believes an object suspended while another treats it as active. A transition that cannot establish all required effects must abort , remain pending , enter recovery , or complete under an explicitly defined bounded-degradation pattern. It must not appear completed while required records remain absent. Atomicity does not mandate a single database transaction. Where technical atomicity is impossible, the architecture must define provisional state, recovery obligations, reconciliation, bounded duration and compensating controls. 26. Idempotency and Replay A repeated request carrying the same transition identity must not produce duplicate transitions. Replay distinguishes continuation of an interrupted transition; retry after failure; deliberate repetition of a prior transition; and semantic re-execution under new evidence. 27. Gate Specification Each gate is specified through: identifier; name; purpose; applicable transitions; required entry state; required information objects; required authority; required controls; decision composition; permitted decision outcomes; blocking conditions; exception rules; records produced; events published; conformance evidence. Assurance-class parameterisation. A gate’s exit criteria, the depth of evidence it requires, and the review or authority it demands are applied to the depth the object’s assurance class requires ( KF-2003 ), resolved at the release / scope-of-reliance to which the class attaches and enforced by KF-3001 IC-23. A higher class raises required rigour; it does not add new gates. The gate’s protection of the six ungraded lifecycle invariants is identical at every class — only the depth above that floor scales. 29. Gates Orchestrate Controls A gate is not one large control. A gate orchestrates several reusable controls, each of which establishes whether one required condition holds. This is what permits the same control to be reused across several gates. The Release Gate illustrates the pattern: The gate composes the results of these controls into one decision; it does not re-implement them. The full gate-to-control mapping is given in §56. 30. Standard Gate Outcomes Every gate supports, where applicable: Pass, Fail, Return, Pending, Indeterminate, Pass with Approved Restriction. An outcome of Indeterminate is never silently treated as Pass. 31. Part VII · Transition Pattern Library 35. Standard Transition Pattern The final step, Record Conformance Evidence , is the emission of evidence the preceding steps already produced — the gate decision, the transition record, the published events — not the separate authoring of an evidence artefact. The governed act is its own evidence ( KF-3001 IC-24; KF-3004 §5.2). A distinct artefact is added only where the act’s own records cannot carry the required proof. 36. Specialised Patterns Creation (creates a governed entity where none existed); Promotion (moves an entity into a more operationally eligible state after satisfying additional obligations — candidate→evaluated, accepted→released, provisional form→eligible); Restriction (reduces permitted reliance without removing all eligibility); Suspension (temporarily removes eligibility pending review, recovery or correction); Withdrawal (ends a release, acceptance or form eligibility without retiring the object); Supersession (replaces a version, release, representation or form with a successor, preserving lineage); Correction (creates a governed correction without erasing the original); Retirement (ends active eligibility of the enduring object while preserving history); Reactivation (routes a retired or suspended entity through renewed evolution before eligibility is restored); Recovery (restores a failed, interrupted or degraded operation to a consistent governed condition). Part VIII · Composite Decision Architecture 37. Composite Decisions A gate decision may depend on several independently authoritative conditions. The gate records references to those authoritative records rather than reproducing them ( KF-3004 §7.2), so no gate becomes a competing source of truth. 38. Retirement Decision Composition (GATE-RET-01) Part IX · Exception and Degraded-State Architecture 41. Exception Classes Operational Exception (a bounded departure affecting execution without changing architectural obligations); Governance Exception (a formally authorised, time-limited departure from a governance practice where no invariant is violated); Architectural Variation (a conforming alternative design); Architectural Violation (a breach of a mandatory invariant or constraint); Indeterminate Condition (validity cannot currently be established). Consistent with §3, an exception cannot convert an invariant violation into conformance. 42. Exception Specification Each exception records: identity; affected transition / gate / control; scope; reason; authority; effective period; compensating controls; prohibited consequences; monitoring; expiry; review; closure; conformance effect. 43. Fail-Open and Fail-Closed Behaviour Every control and gate declares whether failure or indeterminate standing causes fail-closed, bounded degraded operation, manual review, temporary restriction, retry, suspension or abort. Fail-open behaviour requires explicit justification and bounded scope. The default for governance-critical operations is fail-closed. Part X · Recovery and Reconciliation Architecture 44. Recovery Is Forward Restoration, Not Historical Erasure Recovery restores permitted operation; it does not rewrite the past. In a governed architecture, “rollback” must not erase the attempted transition, the gate decision, the failed action, intermediate records or recovery activity. A semantic reversal adds to history — it is a new governed transition returning an entity to an earlier operational condition, not a deletion of the original act. Accordingly the architecture separates technical rollback (transactional consistency) from semantic reversal (a new restoring transition), and both from reinstatement (restoration of eligibility after revalidation), replay (re-execution of an interrupted or deferred operation) and reconciliation (detection and correction of inconsistency between services or records). 45. Recovery Modes Abort (terminate without changing governed state); Retry (repeat an idempotent operation); Replay (continue or re-execute from governed event history); Technical Rollback (restore transactional consistency without erasing evidence of the attempt); Semantic Reversal (a new transition restoring an earlier operational condition — it adds to history); Reconciliation (compare authoritative records and repair inconsistency); Revalidation (reassess whether prior eligibility remains valid); Reinstatement (restore eligibility after successful revalidation and gate approval). 46. Recovery Requirements Recovery must preserve the failed or interrupted attempt; identify the last consistent state; prevent duplicate execution; reconcile authoritative services; preserve temporal order; record compensating action; validate post-recovery invariants; publish recovery events; and produce conformance evidence. Part XI · Concurrency and Conflict Architecture 47. Concurrency Principles A transition evaluates authoritative state immediately before execution. (2) A stale source-state reference invalidates the request. (3) Conflicting transitions are serialised, rejected or explicitly reconciled. (4) A future-effective decision is reconsidered where a blocking event occurs before effect. (5) No service assumes a previously retrieved eligibility condition remains valid indefinitely. (6) Cross-service state changes are reconciled through authoritative events and transition identifiers. The architecture requires transition identifiers, state-version or concurrency tokens, effective-time checks, immediate pre-execution revalidation, conflict detection, explicit precedence and idempotent retry — without prescribing a locking technology. 48. Conflict Types Concurrent version changes; acceptance withdrawal during release; release withdrawal during application; retirement during pending evolution; conflicting authority decisions; stewardship transfer during approval; retrospective correction affecting a completed decision; dependency discovery after release; service-state disagreement; event-ordering ambiguity. 49. Conflict Disposition Reject the later request; prioritise mandatory suspension; queue for reassessment; merge non-conflicting changes; create a branch; suspend operational use; escalate to accountable authority; mark indeterminate; or reconcile after recovery. Transition Conformance Source and target states permitted; required controls executed; applicable gate produced a valid decision; authority and permission valid; records complete and consistent; atomicity preserved; events published; history recoverable; no invariant violated; conformance evidence independently inspectable. 51. Control Conformance Purpose and scope defined; required inputs available; evaluation logic inspectable; outcomes recorded; failure behaviour defined; protected invariants identifiable; evidence independently testable. 53. KF-4000 may implement this behavioural architecture through state machines, workflow engines, rules engines, transaction managers, event-driven architectures, human approval processes, AI-agent orchestration, manually maintained registers, or combinations. It may not bypass a required gate; collapse gate decision and transition execution; treat indeterminate evidence as satisfied; permit silent state mutation; erase failed transitions or recovery history; infer authority from permission; release or apply ineligible knowledge; create conflicting authoritative states; make transition history unreconstructable; or substitute automation for accountability. Closing Statement KF-3005 defines the governed behaviour of the Knowledge Foundry architecture. It establishes how state may change, how transitions are requested and executed, how gates compose authoritative decisions from independently owned records, how controls preserve invariants, how failures and exceptions remain visible, and how every material change leaves sufficient evidence for historical reconstruction and assurance. KF-3004 defines the architecture’s memory; KF-3005 defines the disciplined behaviour through which that memory is allowed to change.

d: How the architectural elements collaborate to produce, govern, evolve and retire an Operational Knowledge Object
x: The Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture is intentionally modular. Each document defines one architectural concern in isolation, so that responsibilities stay clear and the architecture can evolve without unnecessary coupling. Integration therefore cannot be inferred from any single document: it is itself an architectural concern, and must be described as one. KF-3006 provides that description. Purpose The documents before this one describe the architecture part by part : what must remain true ( KF-3001 ), what it must be able to do ( KF-3002 ), where responsibility sits ( KF-3003 ), what information exists ( KF-3004 ), and how governed change is permitted and executed ( KF-3005 ). Each is complete in its domain and silent on the others. KF-3006 describes the architecture as one working system . It answers a single question: How do all architectural elements collaborate to produce a governed Operational Knowledge Object? It is the point in the KF-3000 series where the reader should feel the machine come alive: capabilities are realised by services, services are invoked by transitions, transitions pass gates, gates orchestrate controls, controls protect obligations, obligations emit evidence, evidence accumulates as traceability, and traceability is what conformance later inspects. None of that collaboration is visible from any single domain document. This one makes it visible. KF-3006 summarises, never redefines. Where it names a service, a gate, a control, an invariant or a record, the authoritative definition remains in its home document; this model shows only how the element participates in the whole. Its value is integrative, not additive. Figure 1 · The Integration Spine One flow carries the whole architecture, from the obligations the Canon imposes to the conformance that inspects the result: Every element in the KF-3000 series occupies one band of this spine, and every chapter of this document explains one of its arrows. A reader who holds this figure in mind can place any architectural element by asking only where on the spine it acts. Scope and the Integration Admission Test KF-3006 is technology-neutral and deployment-neutral. It describes collaboration between architectural elements, not the components, products or topologies that realise them (those are KF-4000). A statement belongs in KF-3006 only if: it describes an interaction between two or more architectural elements defined elsewhere in the series; it can be stated without naming a specific technology, product or deployment; and it preserves — never relaxes — the lifecycle invariants and interaction constraints of KF-2001 and KF-3001 . A statement that redefines an element belongs in that element’s home document; a statement that names a technology belongs in KF-4000. 1 · Introduction 1.1 Purpose To demonstrate that the Knowledge Foundry architecture functions as a coherent system rather than a collection of independent components, by describing the relationships and behaviours through which its elements collaborate over the life of an Operational Knowledge Object (OKO). 1.2 Scope In scope: the relationship types between architectural elements; the behaviour of the architecture over time; the integrated journey of one OKO; the recurring integration patterns; the architectural event catalogue; and the way evidence, traceability and assurance are produced as by-products of ordinary architectural work. Out of scope: redefinition of any element; component design; technology selection; workflow, cadence and staffing (KF-4000); and the judgement of whether an operation conforms ( KF-3007 ). 1.3 Relationship to Other Documents KF-3006 depends on all five domain documents and on KF-2003 (assurance). It is depended upon by KF-3007 , which inspects the traceability this model shows the architecture producing. 2 · Principles of Architectural Integration These are the philosophy of integration, not its mechanics. Each is inherited from a higher level and constrains how the elements may be wired together. Integration follows the Canon. Elements may be combined only in ways consistent with the Canonical Principles. Integration is not free wiring; it is constrained composition. Every interaction preserves the lifecycle invariants. No collaboration between elements may break single identity, attributable transitions, justified transitions, inspectable transitions, provenance or preserved lineage. The invariants are the floor beneath every interaction ( KF-2001 ; KF-3001 ). Integration is event-driven, not document-driven. Elements collaborate by raising and responding to events that trigger governed transitions, not by passing documents hand to hand. What moves through the system is a governed state change, not a file ( KF-2001 event model). Evidence is a by-product of behaviour. Conformance evidence is emitted by the governed act, not authored by a separate administrative step ( KF-3001 IC-24; KF-3004 §5.2). Integration is designed so that doing the work is recording the work. Integration preserves traceability. Every interaction leaves the relationships, events and evidence needed to reconstruct what happened, to the depth the object’s assurance class requires ( KF-2003 ; KF-3007 Test 4). Responsibilities remain loosely coupled. Each capability has one accountable service and each record family one authoritative maintainer; services collaborate through governed interactions across named boundaries, never by reaching into one another’s records ( KF-3003 SP-2/SP-3; KF-3004 §7). Loose coupling is what lets an implementation substitute one service without disturbing the others. 3 · Participating Architectural Elements The elements that take part in integration, each summarised for use here; the citation is the authority. Element In one line Home Operational Knowledge Object (OKO) the governed unit: representation + evidence + justification + acceptance-state, under one identity KF-1101 Lifecycle the staged progression Capture → … → Retire through which an OKO evolves KF-2001 Capability an enduring ability the architecture must possess KF-3002 Service a logical mechanism that realises capabilities and maintains records KF-3003 Information / Record object a governed unit of information with one authoritative maintainer KF-3004 Actor a person or agent that raises events and performs work KF-2001 Role a bundle of responsibilities an actor holds KF-2001 Authority the human right to certify, accept, release, steward or retire KF-1103; KF-3006 §5.3 Gate a justification checkpoint that decides whether an OKO may advance KF-2001 ; KF-3005 Control a reusable test of one required condition KF-3005 Invariant a property that must hold at every instant KF-2001 ; KF-3001 Evidence the durable record that an obligation was discharged, emitted by the act KF-3004 §5.2 Traceability the reconstructable web of relationships, events and evidence KF-3006 §10 Assurance class the grade that sets how deep the above must go KF-2003 4 · Architectural Relationships This chapter replaces the hundreds of arrows scattered across the domain documents with a controlled vocabulary of relationship types . Every legitimate interaction in the architecture is an instance of one of these types. (These are element-level integration relationships; the record-level relationship types — VERSION_OF, RELEASES, SUPERSEDES and the rest — remain KF-3004 ’s.) 4.1 The Canonical Relationship Vocabulary Every legitimate interaction is an instance of one of the nine canonical relationships below. Each belongs to a category that fixes what kind of relationship it is — so that “Service X invokes Y” and “Service X consumes Y” are never read as the same claim. Relationship Category Reads as Governing rule constrains normative Principle / interaction constraint → element composition must remain consistent with the Canon and the interaction constraints ( KF-1000 ; KF-3001 ) realises implementation Capability → Service each capability has exactly one accountable service; supporting services may assist ( KF-3003 SP-2) invokes behavioural Transition → Service(s) each transition invokes one or more services; no transition is serviceless ( KF-2001 ) consumes information Service → Information object a service reads an authoritative record through a governed interaction, never by overwriting it ( KF-3004 §7) produces information Service / Transition → Information object the authoritative maintainer produces and maintains its records ( KF-3004 §7) evaluates governance Gate → Control(s) a gate orchestrates several reusable controls; it does not re-implement them ( KF-3005 §29) protects assurance Control → Obligation / Invariant a control protects at least one explicit obligation, risk, policy or invariant ( KF-3005 §32) generates evidential Transition / Obligation → Conformance Evidence evidence is emitted by the act — event-native and proportionate — not authored separately ( KF-3001 IC-24; KF-3007 Test 3) traces provenance derived state → source; successor → predecessor provenance and lineage links are carried through and preserved, never overwritten ( KF-2001 invariants 5–6) Three further structural relationships support composite decisions and grading and are used throughout the model: references — a composite decision cites the authoritative records it relied on without copying their content ( KF-3004 §7.2); attributed-to — every transition resolves to an identified actor or human authority ( KF-2001 invariant 2); and graded-by — the depth to which a graded obligation is discharged is set by the object’s assurance class ( KF-2003 ; KF-3001 IC-23). 4.2 The Core Relationship Chain Read end to end, twelve relationship types compose into one chain — the spine of the architecture: Every arrow is one of the controlled types in §4.1. The architecture is integrated precisely because these relationships form a closed chain from principle to conformance, with no orphan element and no unnamed arrow. 4.3 Cardinality and constraint, by relationship For the four relationships most often misread as one-to-one: realises (Capability→Service): one accountable service per capability; a service may be accountable for several capabilities; supporting services are many-to-many. Accountability is single; realisation is shared. evaluates (Gate→Control): many-to-many. One gate evaluates several controls; one control is reused across several gates. protects (Control→Obligation): many-to-many. One control may protect several obligations; one obligation may be protected by several controls. produces (Service→Record): one authoritative maintainer per record family; other services hold adjacent or derived views only ( KF-3004 §7.1). 5 · Behavioural Architecture Sections 3–4 are structural — what exists and how it relates. This section is behavioural — how the architecture acts over time. 5.1 The Event Model The architecture does not move because a document is passed along; it moves because an event is raised. An event is what happened ; the transition it triggers is the governed move it causes ( KF-2001 ). Events divide into two kinds, and keeping them distinct is what locates automation safely: Trigger events (engineering events) — occurrences that oblige the system to consider a transition: new evidence, a scheduled review, a policy change, a challenge, an AI recommendation, an application outcome, an authority decision. A trigger event may be raised by a human or an agent . Emitted events (architectural events) — notifications the architecture publishes when a transition completes: Object Created, Acceptance Granted, Version Created, Superseded, Retired, and the rest of the catalogue in §8. Trigger events cause transitions; transitions emit events. An emitted event may in turn be a trigger event for another service (a Version Created event triggers dependency re-checking). No event bypasses a gate. An AI recommendation is a trigger event, never an acceptance. 5.2 The Transition Model Every governed move follows one shape, whatever the stage: This is the KF-3005 standard transition pattern seen from the integration level. The decisive property: the evidence and events at the bottom are emitted by the act, not authored afterward (§9). An Indeterminate decision is never silently treated as Pass. 5.3 The Authority Model (integrated view) Transitions are not all equal. Some are engineering work an agent may perform under supervision; others are acts of authority that must resolve to an identifiable human. The architecture draws the line by transition, not by service: Transition class Example Who may perform Computation / structuring Structure, Operationalise agent or human, under a named role Evaluation / justification Evaluate, Justify human judgement, agent-assisted Acceptance / release Accept, Release identifiable human authority Stewardship / retirement Govern, Retire identifiable human authority Automation may propose any of these as a trigger event; it may not hold the authority for the acceptance, release, stewardship or retirement classes (KF-1103; KF-3000 §18; KF-3001 IC-16). The detailed authority, delegation and accountability model is KF-3008 ; this section shows only how authority gates the transition flow. 5.4 The Responsibility Model (integrated view) Authority is exercised through a chain that runs from a person to a lifecycle action: The chain is load-bearing in both directions: forward, it says who may act; backward, it makes every action attributable to a role, an authority and a person (invariant 2). Institutional authority (the right , held at SVC-06) and technical permission (the ability , assigned by SVC-16) are distinct and must not be conflated ( KF-3001 IC-13: authority is not permission). 6 · The Integrated Object Journey Worked example. KF-5001 instantiates this journey on a concrete Knowledge Brief, with the actual evidence, authority and records at each step. This is the heart of the document: one OKO walked through the whole architecture. For each step it shows current state, the services invoked, the records produced, the controls evaluated, the evidence emitted, the traceability updated, and the resulting state. The journey below is generic; it is the exact path the first vertical slice — a MacroLab Singapore Business Impact Assessment, provisionally A3 Consequential — is intended to instantiate and test. This chapter is the canonical walkthrough of the architecture. Every subsequent implementation, demonstration and conformance assessment should be understandable as an instantiation of this journey. A deployment is not a different architecture; it is this journey run on particular technology. A conformance assessment is not a separate procedure; it is this journey read backwards through its evidence. Notation per step: State → Services → Records → Controls → Evidence → Traceability → Next state. Capture. Candidate → SVC-01 Object Registry, SVC-15 Provenance → Identity Record, Intake Record, Provenance Seed → CTRL-ID-01 identity resolution, CTRL-ID-02 duplicate detection → evidence: the Identity and Intake records themselves → traceability: origin attached at birth → Candidate . Structure. Candidate → SVC-02 Representation → Structured Representation, Metadata, Relationship Map → CTRL-STA-01 state validity → evidence: the structured representation → traceability: representation linked to identity → Structured . Evaluate. Structured → SVC-04 Evaluation, SVC-03 Evidence → Evidence Records, Quality Assessment, Evaluation Verdict → CTRL-EVD-01 evidence presence, CTRL-EVA-01 evaluation completion → evidence: the verdict is the test result → traceability: claims linked to supporting and defeating evidence → Evaluated . Justify. Evaluated → SVC-05 Justification → Justification Record, Assumption Record, Rationale Record, Epistemic Status → CTRL-JUS-01 justification completeness, CTRL-EVD-03 counter-evidence visibility → evidence: the justification record → traceability: end-to-end claim-to-source chain assembled → Justified . Accept (transition, authority) . Justified → SVC-06 Authority and Acceptance → Acceptance Record, Scope-of-Reliance Record → GATE-ACC-01 orchestrating CTRL-AUT-01 authority mandate, CTRL-ACC-01 acceptance validity; assurance class A3 confirmed by the governance authority here → evidence: the acceptance record is the evidence of acceptance → traceability: reliance scope + authority + date bound to the version → Accepted . Operationalise / Release. Accepted → SVC-12 Operationalisation, SVC-10 Release → Actionable Form, Warrant Linkage, Release Record → GATE-REL-01 (state, acceptance, authority, dependency, provenance controls); depth per A3 → evidence: the release record → traceability: actionable form linked to its warrant → Operational . Govern. Operational → SVC-07 Stewardship and Review → Stewardship Assignment, Review Schedule, Review Record → CTRL-STW-01 stewardship validity, CTRL-REV-01 review currency → evidence: review records emitted on schedule → traceability: continuing standing recorded over time → Governed . Apply. Governed → SVC-13 Application and Outcome → Application Record, Explanation Record, Outcome Record, Feedback → GATE-APP-01 eligibility, CTRL-EXP-01 explainability, CTRL-OUT-01 outcome capture → evidence: application and outcome records → traceability: each material use tied to the version and form used → in use → outcomes . Evolve. Outcome/new-evidence trigger → SVC-09 Version and Lineage (re-enters at Evaluate/Justify, re-accepts) → Version Record, Change Record, Lineage Record → GATE-EVO-01 (re-evaluation, re-justification, dependency disposition, renewed acceptance) → evidence: the version and change records → traceability: new version linked to predecessor; warrant re-earned, not inherited → Next Version . Retire / Supersede. Trigger → SVC-14 Retirement and Preservation (+ SVC-09 supersession) → Retirement Record, Historical Object Record, Supersession Link → GATE-RET-01 (reason, authority, dependency disposition, preservation) → evidence: the retirement record → traceability: lineage preserved, history append-only → Historical . Two things are visible only at this integrated scale. First, every record named above was emitted by doing the step , not by a separate filing activity — the journey is the evidence trail. Second, the six invariants held at every step : one identity throughout, every transition attributed and justified and inspectable, provenance present from Capture, lineage preserved through Evolve and Retire. The A3 class raised the depth at Evaluate, Justify, Accept and Apply; it never changed the path . 7 · Integration Patterns The journey recurs as a small set of reusable patterns. Later implementations instantiate these rather than reinventing flow. Each pattern is a named composition of §4 relationships and the §5.2 transition shape. Capture Pattern — admit candidate; assign identity; record origin. (SVC-01, SVC-15; GATE-REG-01.) Establishes the invariant floor before any judgement. Review Pattern — evaluate and justify; assemble the claim-to-source chain. (SVC-03/04/05; GATE-EVA-01, GATE-JUS-01.) Depth graded by class. Acceptance Pattern — an authority certifies a scope of reliance. (SVC-06; GATE-ACC-01.) The point where justification becomes authorised reliance and class is confirmed. Revision Pattern — controlled change producing a new version that re-earns warrant and authority. (SVC-09; GATE-EVO-01.) Never overwrites; always links. Supersession Pattern — a successor replaces a predecessor for a defined scope, lineage preserved. (SVC-09/10; SUPERSEDES.) Retirement Pattern — end active use while preserving history. (SVC-14; GATE-RET-01.) Monitoring Pattern — scheduled and event-driven review that keeps standing current and raises Evolve/Retire triggers. (SVC-07, SVC-11; GATE-REV-01.) A pattern is conformant when it preserves the invariants, attributes its transitions, and emits its evidence natively — regardless of the technology that runs it. 8 · Architectural Event Catalogue The canonical vocabulary of emitted events (§5.1). These are the notifications the architecture publishes as transitions complete; they are the machine’s observable behaviour and the seam along which services collaborate. Event Emitted on Typical downstream trigger Object Created Capture registration provenance seeding; structuring Evidence Added new evidence attached re-evaluation; Evolve proposal Review Requested schedule or challenge fires governance review Review Completed review recorded Evolve, Retire, or standing renewed Acceptance Granted authority accepts release eligibility; operationalisation Acceptance Withdrawn authority withdraws suspension; dependency re-check Version Created controlled change dependency impact; re-acceptance Released release authorised application eligibility Superseded successor replaces lineage link; dependent revalidation Retired active use ends preservation; dependent notification Each emitted event carries, at minimum: the object and version identity, the transition, the responsible actor or authority, and recorded time ( KF-3004 Common Record Properties). An event is therefore already a unit of evidence (§9). The authoritative event records are maintained by SVC-08 (Lifecycle and Transition) and the originating services; this catalogue is the shared vocabulary, not a new store. 9 · Evidence Generation Model The principle, stated once at the integration level: Architectural behaviour generates conformance evidence as a natural consequence of work, not through a separate administrative act. not The acceptance record is the evidence of acceptance; the transition record is the audit event; the evaluation verdict is the test result; the provenance link is the evidence of derivation; the supersession link is the evidence of lineage ( KF-3004 §5.2). A distinct evidence artefact is created only where the act’s own records cannot carry the required proof, and then against a recorded justification that they cannot ( KF-3001 IC-24). This is what keeps assurance affordable. Without it, a governed system generates a second knowledge-management problem — the management of evidence that the knowledge was managed. With it, the cost of assurance is folded into the cost of doing the work. 10 · Traceability Model Traceability is not a single artefact; it accumulates in three layers, each produced by ordinary architectural behaviour. Structural traceability — the relationships (§4): identity → version → representation; claim → evidence; form → warrant; successor → predecessor. Produced as records are created and linked. Behavioural traceability — the events (§8): the ordered history of what happened to the object and when. Produced as transitions emit events. Evidential traceability — the proof (§9): the records demonstrating that each material obligation was discharged. Produced as the acts emit their evidence. A conformance claim ( KF-3007 ) is reconstructed by reading the three layers together: the relationships say what is connected, the events say what happened in order, the evidence says on what basis. The depth to which each layer must be reconstructable is set by assurance class (§11): an A0 correction need not be traceable through every principle and control; an A4 acceptance must be reconstructable end to end. 11 · Assurance Integration This chapter bridges to KF-2003 without redefining it. It shows how assurance flows through the architecture as a single graded quantity: The class enters the architecture at one place — the scope of reliance recorded at Acceptance and Release (SVC-06/10) — and from there parameterises gate depth ( KF-3005 §28), control strength (§32) and reconstruction depth ( KF-3007 ), all under KF-3001 IC-23. The path is invariant; the depth is graded. Two objects of different classes traverse the same journey (§6), pass the same gates and satisfy the same six invariants; the higher-class object satisfies each to greater depth. Class never lowers the invariant floor. 12 · Implementation Guidance Technology-neutral obligations an implementation (KF-4000) must honour when realising this model. When implementing Knowledge Foundry, ensure that: relationships remain explicit — the §4 relationship types are recoverable, not implied by convention; events remain attributable — every emitted event resolves to an actor or authority and a time; evidence remains event-native and reconstructable — the act emits its evidence; assurance reads it without re-authoring; invariants remain preserved under composition — no combination of services, however optimised, breaks single identity, attribution, justification, inspectability, provenance or lineage; coupling remains loose — services collaborate across named boundaries and never overwrite one another’s authoritative records. Which technologies deliver these is an implementation decision. That they are delivered is not. 13 · Relationship with the Conformance Framework KF-3006 and KF-3007 are complementary and must not be confused: KF-3006 defines how the architecture operates — the relationships, behaviours, events, evidence and traceability through which a governed OKO is produced. KF-3007 determines whether that operation conforms — applying the four proportionate tests (Constitutional, Operational, Integrity, Reconstructability) to the traceability this model shows the architecture producing. KF-3006 makes the machine run; KF-3007 inspects the run. The traceability layers of §10 are exactly the material KF-3007 Test 4 reconstructs, and the event-native evidence of §9 is exactly what its Test 3 grades. An architecture that integrates as described here is one that can be found conformant there — the two documents are built to meet. 14 · Emergence and Architectural Completeness 14.1 Governance Is an Emergent Property No single architectural element creates governed knowledge. Governance emerges from the coordinated behaviour of principles, lifecycle, capabilities, services, controls, evidence and traceability acting together on one object. The properties that distinguish an Operational Knowledge Object — trustworthiness, inspectability, accountability and institutional reliance — are therefore emergent properties of the integrated architecture , not characteristics of any individual component. This is the systems-engineering claim at the centre of the programme. Trust does not live inside an object, a service or a record; it is produced by the way they behave together. It follows that trust can be lost by a failure of integration even where every component is individually sound — a correctly built service that reaches past a boundary, an evidence record detached from the act that should have emitted it, a transition that skips its gate. Integrity is a property of the composition, which is why this document exists. 14.2 Architectural Completeness The purpose of architectural integration is not to maximise the number of architectural elements or relationships. Its purpose is to demonstrate that every normative obligation established by the Canon can be realised, governed, evidenced and reconstructed through the integrated behaviour of the architecture — and no more than that. This closes the loop opened by the earlier concern about a “completeness proof”. Completeness is not the property that every element maps to another element; it is the property that every obligation is discharged by the whole. An architecture is complete when the spine of §Figure 1 runs unbroken from principle to conformance for every obligation the Canon imposes, at the depth each object’s assurance class requires. Elements and relationships are justified only insofar as they serve that run; any that do not are complexity for its own sake, and the Integration Admission Test exists to keep them out. 15 · Summary The Knowledge Foundry architecture functions as an integrated system because: principles constrain how elements may be composed; the lifecycle governs progression through stages; services realise capabilities under single accountability; transitions invoke services and gates evaluate controls; controls protect obligations and invariants; events emit evidence as a by-product of work; evidence accumulates as three-layer traceability; traceability supports proportionate conformance; conformance preserves the trust the whole system exists to protect. Read alone, each domain document describes one organ. Read through this model, they are one body: an event enters, a governed transition follows, an OKO advances one justified state, and the evidence that it did so is left behind without anyone stopping to write it down. Relationship to Subsequent Documents KF-3007 · Architectural Conformance Framework applies the four tests to the traceability this model produces. KF-3008 · Architectural Authority Framework holds the detailed authority, delegation and permission model this document views integrately in §5.3–§5.4. KF-3009 · Architectural Crosswalks and Traceability holds the exhaustive element-to-element mappings this document summarises. KF-4000 · Knowledge Operating System instantiates these relationships, behaviours and patterns in a particular deployment. Closing Statement KF-3006 is where the Reference Architecture stops being a set of specifications and becomes a system. It adds no new element and no new obligation; it shows that the elements already defined compose into a single governed behaviour — capability through service, transition through gate, control through evidence, evidence through traceability, traceability through conformance — and that this behaviour preserves, at every step and every assurance class, the invariants that make the object trustworthy. It is the systems view that the series needed before it could be inspected, and the map the first vertical slice will follow.

d: How the Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture is demonstrated to conform to its own architectural commitments
x: Up to KF-3006 the programme has been designing the architecture. KF-3007 is where the architecture becomes demonstrable — where it can show, from its own operation, that it is working as intended. It answers the question that distinguishes Knowledge Foundry from a document store, a personal knowledge tool or an AI answer engine: not does the system hold knowledge , but how can an institution demonstrate — rather than merely assert — that its knowledge architecture is functioning as intended? A conformant architecture is not one that is believed to be correct, nor one that merely claims to satisfy its design intent. It is one whose architectural commitments can be demonstrated from observable evidence. The architecture has, in effect, begun to distinguish truth from proof : the purpose of this framework is not to establish trust by declaration, but to make trust continuously demonstrable. Purpose The Architectural Conformance Framework defines how the Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture is evaluated against its own architectural commitments. It establishes the principles, criteria, evidence requirements and assessment methods through which architectural conformance may be demonstrated, monitored and reconstructed over time. The verb is deliberate. Conformance here is not checked , audited or inspected as an external act imposed on a finished system. It is demonstrated — shown to hold from evidence the architecture already produced by operating. The whole framework rests on one sentence: Architectural conformance is demonstrated when every material architectural claim can be reconstructed from observable evidence through explicit traceability. That sentence links, without adding a new conceptual layer, everything the programme has built: Canonical Principles become architectural obligations; obligations are discharged through the lifecycle, services and controls; discharge emits evidence; materiality sets its depth; traceability makes it reconstructable; and reconstruction is what “demonstrated” means. The rest of this document is that sentence, unfolded. Figure 1 · The Conformance Chain The framework assesses along one logical chain — and the chain matters, because the assessment never evaluates an obligation directly. It evaluates whether the claim that an obligation has been discharged is supported by evidence. Each chapter that follows populates one link of this chain: the obligation (§5), the claim (§9), the evidence (§10), the assessment (§7), the finding (§13). The Conformance Claim is the bridge the framework turns on: obligations are architectural facts, but conformance is always a statement about a claim , supported or not by what the architecture recorded while it worked. Scope and the Conformance Admission Test KF-3007 is technology-neutral. It defines how conformance is demonstrated , not the tools that store or compute the evidence (KF-4000), and not the obligations themselves (those are defined in their home documents). A statement belongs in KF-3007 only if: it concerns how architectural conformance is demonstrated, evidenced, judged or reconstructed; it can be stated without naming a specific technology, product or deployment; and it references obligations defined elsewhere in the programme without redefining them. A statement that creates a new obligation belongs in the document that owns that obligation; a statement that names a technology belongs in KF-4000. 1 · Introduction Worked example. KF-5001 §4 demonstrates these tests, and a reconstructed Conformance Claim, on a single governed object. 1.1 Purpose To make the architecture demonstrable: to define the obligations against which an implementation is assessed, the dimensions and tests through which assessment proceeds, the evidence on which it draws, and the findings it yields — all proportionate to the reliance placed on the knowledge governed. 1.2 Scope In scope: the philosophy and principles of conformance; the definition of architectural conformance and of an architectural obligation; the conformance dimensions; the four-test assessment model; the conformance criteria; the Conformance Claim; the evidence model; the assessment process; findings and exceptions; architectural review; and continuous conformance. Out of scope: the definition of any obligation (its home document); organisational compliance, HR or process audit; technology, tooling and deployment (KF-4000); and the judgement calls of a particular assessment, which this framework structures but does not pre-decide. 1.3 Relationship to Other Documents KF-1000 · Canon — the principles from which every architectural obligation ultimately derives; conformance preserves architectural intent, and intent originates here. KF-2001 · Lifecycle — the gates, transitions and invariants whose preservation is the substance of behavioural and lifecycle conformance. KF-2003 · Materiality and Assurance — the assurance classes that grade how deep evidence, assessment and review must go (§11). KF-3006 · Architectural Integration Model — describes how the architecture operates ; KF-3007 determines whether that operation conforms . The traceability layers of KF-3006 §10 are exactly what this framework reconstructs. KF-3001 –3005, 3008, 3009 — the domains whose obligations are assessed and whose records supply the evidence. KF-3006 makes the machine run; KF-3007 inspects the run. The two are built to meet. 2 · Philosophy of Conformance Seven convictions set the tone of everything that follows. Architecture is judged by behaviour, not by documentation. A conformant architecture is one that behaves as intended on real objects, not one that merely describes itself well. Assessment reads behaviour, not intentions. Conformance is evidence-based. A claim of conformance stands only on observable evidence. Absent evidence, an obligation is not assessable , which is a finding in itself — never a silent pass. Conformance is proportional. The depth of assurance demanded matches the reliance placed on the object ( KF-2003 ). Exploratory work is not held to the standard of a board decision, and a board decision is not held to less. Proportionality applies to the depth of evidence, review and assessment — not to the architectural obligations themselves. The Canon and the lifecycle invariants remain universal; only the level of demonstration varies. Low assurance never means “no provenance”; it means less depth above an unchanged invariant floor. Conformance is reconstructable. It is not enough that the system behaved correctly; a reviewer must be able to reconstruct that it did, after the fact, from the record. Assessment minimises administrative burden. Because evidence is event-native ( KF-3001 IC-24), assessment reads the records the architecture already produced. Conformance does not commission a parallel paperwork exercise; that would be a second knowledge-management problem. Conformance emerges from normal operation. A well-integrated architecture is continuously demonstrating conformance simply by working. Assessment formalises and inspects that stream; it does not create it. Assessment strengthens the architecture. Findings are not merely reports on implementation quality; they are architectural feedback that informs future revisions of the Reference Architecture itself. The architecture is a learning system, not a static specification — and its conformance framework is one of the instruments through which it learns. 3 · What Is Architectural Conformance? Architectural conformance is the observable correspondence between the intended behaviour of the Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture and the observable behaviour of an implemented system. The operative word is correspondence , not compliance . Compliance suggests obedience to an external rulebook; correspondence asserts that what the architecture intends and what the system does are the same, and that the sameness can be shown. An implementation is free to differ from the reference architecture in structure, technology and arrangement ( KF-3000 Part VIII); it is not free to differ in behaviour where that behaviour discharges an obligation. Conformance is the demonstrable claim that, behaviourally, it does not. 4 · Conformance Principles Every assessment conducted under this framework shall: preserve architectural intent — assess against the obligations the architecture actually imposes, not against a reviewer’s preference; remain technology-neutral — judge behaviour and evidence, never the choice of tools; rely on observable evidence — ground every finding in a record that exists, not in inference or reputation; distinguish objective finding from judgement — separate what the evidence shows from what the assessor concludes from it , and record both; remain reconstructable — leave its own trail, so that an assessment can itself be reviewed; respect assurance class — demand exactly the depth KF-2003 fixes for the object, no more and no less; preserve traceability — never break, in the act of assessing, the traceability it depends on. 5 · Architectural Obligations The Canon establishes principles. The architecture translates them into obligations . The framework assesses whether those obligations are satisfied. The obligation is therefore the unit of conformance — the thing an assessment is of . 5.1 Where obligations come from Obligations are not invented here; they are gathered from where they already live: Canonical Principles (via the handoff of KF-1301), lifecycle gates and the six invariants ( KF-2001 ), engineering practices ( KF-2002 ), the architectural principles, invariants and interaction constraints ( KF-3001 AP / INV / IC), the six Governance Primitives (KF-1104), and the proportionality rules of KF-2003 . The authoritative enumeration and its upstream tracing are held by KF-3009 (Crosswalks); this framework defines how any obligation is specified and assessed. 5.2 Obligation specification Each architectural obligation is specified through five fields: Purpose — the architectural intent it protects. Applicable elements — the capabilities, services, gates, controls or records it binds. Evidence expected — the records whose presence demonstrates discharge (event-native wherever possible). Assessment method — how correspondence is shown: record inspection, cross-service reconciliation, control testing, reconstruction, or independent review. Possible exceptions — the bounded, attributable deviations that may be accepted without breaching an invariant (§14). Illustrative obligation. OBL — Justified Transition. Purpose: no state advances without recorded warrant (Principle VIII; invariant 3). Applicable elements: every transition; SVC-08; GATE-JUS-01 and each gate. Evidence expected: the transition record and its justification reference, emitted by the act. Assessment method: reconstruct any transition and confirm a justification is recoverable. Exceptions: none — this is invariant-protecting and ungraded. Illustrative obligation. OBL — Sufficient Acceptance Authority. Purpose: reliance is authorised by an identifiable human authority (Principle III). Applicable elements: Accept and Release transitions; SVC-06; GATE-ACC-01. Evidence expected: the acceptance record naming authority, scope and date. Assessment method: confirm the accepting authority held a valid mandate for the object’s assurance class. Exceptions: a time-limited governance exception at one class below, recorded and visible (§14). 6 · Conformance Dimensions Conformance is not one score. Reducing it to a single pass/fail hides where an architecture is strong and where it is thin. Assessment evaluates eight dimensions, each answering a different question: Dimension Asks Structural Do the required elements and relationships exist and remain distinct? Behavioural Do transitions, gates and controls behave as intended on real objects? Lifecycle Is the staged progression, with its gates and returns, honoured? Governance Are authority, stewardship, acceptance and review exercised as required? Evidence Is the required evidence present, event-native and proportionate? Traceability Can the structural, behavioural and evidential trails be reconstructed? Authority Does every consequential act resolve to an identifiable human authority? Information integrity Are records protected, single-owned and append-only where required? A dimension may be strong while another is weak; the assessment reports the profile, not an average. Each dimension is evaluated through the four tests of §7, to the depth §11 requires. 7 · Architectural Completeness and the Assessment Model 7.1 Architectural completeness precedes conformance Architectural conformance assumes architectural completeness. Before behaviour can be assessed, the architecture itself must demonstrate that every normative obligation established by the Canon possesses an identifiable realisation path, governance mechanism and evidential outcome. Completeness therefore evaluates the integrity of the architecture ; conformance evaluates the integrity of its implementation . The two answer different questions: Completeness — is the architecture internally coherent? Does every obligation have somewhere to be discharged, governed and evidenced? Conformance — does reality correspond to the architecture? Does the implemented system actually discharge them? An incomplete architecture cannot be conformant, because there would be obligations with nowhere to be shown satisfied. Completeness is established once per architectural revision and re-checked whenever a domain document changes (§15); conformance is demonstrated continuously and per object (§16). 7.2 The four tests The dimensions of §6 are what is assessed. The four tests below are how — the coverage logic through which any dimension is judged. They replace an open-ended list of disconnected questions with four graded tests, applied in order. Constitutional coverage — every Canonical Principle produces at least one enforceable obligation; every obligation has at least one permissible realisation path; nothing below the line contradicts the Canon. Ungraded. Operational coverage — every capability has an identified realisation mechanism; every transition has trigger, mechanism, authority and recorded outcome; every gate evaluates explicit exit criteria. Existence ungraded; depth graded. Integrity coverage — every material control addresses an explicit risk, obligation, policy or invariant; every material obligation generates proportionate, event-native evidence; the six invariants hold at full strength. Graded. Reconstructability — material status and conformance claims can be reconstructed to the depth their reliance requires; a reviewer can establish what happened, why, by whom and on what evidence. Graded. Coverage, not correspondence: an obligation is conformant when covered by one or more mechanisms, never on condition that it maps one-to-one to a dedicated element. Single-owner accountability (one accountable service per capability, one authoritative maintainer per record family) is retained and is a different thing from realisation, which may be shared. 8 · Assessment Criteria The four tests are applied through a practical checklist — the criteria against which evidence is read. The architecture defines these criteria; the framework applies them, which is why they are assessment criteria rather than a separate conformance standard. They are the review questions the programme has used throughout, now seated inside the tests and graded by materiality rather than posed as an absolute proof: Does every Canonical Principle produce one or more architectural obligations? (Test 1) Does every obligation possess at least one realisation pathway? (Test 1) Does every capability possess one or more realisation mechanisms? (Test 2) Does every lifecycle transition have trigger, authority, criteria and recorded outcome? (Test 2) Does every gate evaluate explicit, inspectable exit criteria? (Test 2) Does every material control protect an explicit obligation, risk, policy or invariant? (Test 3) Does every material obligation generate proportionate, event-native evidence? (Test 3) Do the six lifecycle invariants hold for every object, at full strength? (Test 3) Can every accepted object be reconstructed to the depth its class requires? (Test 4) Can every material conformance claim be supported from evidence through traceability? (Test 4) A criterion answered “no” is not automatically a Non-Conformance; it is a finding (§13) whose kind depends on materiality and on whether an invariant is breached. 9 · The Conformance Claim The framework introduces one formal concept, and only one. A Conformance Claim is an explicit assertion that a defined architectural obligation has been satisfied for a defined object, transition or scope. Examples: “this lifecycle transition preserved provenance” ; “this acceptance possessed sufficient authority” ; “this object satisfied its Consequential-class evidence obligations” ; “this traceability chain is complete.” A claim is specific: it names the obligation, the subject and, where graded, the assurance class it is claimed against. The claim is the logical hinge of the whole framework. The chain below elaborates Figure 1, making the traceability step explicit: A claim that cannot be supported from observable evidence through explicit traceability is not thereby false — but it is not demonstrated , and an undemonstrated claim carries no conformance weight, however plausible. This is the operational meaning of the framework’s central sentence: demonstration is the reconstruction of a claim from evidence through traceability, to the depth its materiality requires. 10 · The Evidence Model 10.1 What counts as evidence Evidence is the observable record that an obligation was discharged. The framework draws on the records the architecture already maintains ( KF-3004 ): event records — the emitted architectural events ( KF-3006 §8); decision records — gate decisions and their composed control results; approval / acceptance records — authority, scope of reliance and refusals; traceability and provenance records — origin, derivation, custody; version and lineage history — versions, changes, supersession; lifecycle transition records — every governed move; relationship graphs — the structural links among objects, versions and claims. 10.2 Evidence is event-native Wherever possible, evidence is emitted by the governed act, not authored separately ( KF-3001 IC-24; KF-3004 §5.2): the acceptance record is the evidence of acceptance, the transition record is the event record of the act, the evaluation verdict is the test result. A distinct evidence artefact is created only where the act’s own records cannot carry the required proof. This is what makes assessment affordable and continuous rather than periodic and burdensome. 10.3 Independence of evidence A conformance judgement may not rest solely on the self-assertion of the service or actor being assessed ( KF-3001 IC-18). Each material judgement cites at least one independently generated source — record inspection, cross-service reconciliation, control testing or external review — and the assurance function reads records without altering them (IC-17). The Conformance and Audit Service (SVC-18) is the architectural means by which evidence is gathered and kept current; it is read-only over everything it assesses. 11 · Materiality and Assurance This framework does not redefine materiality; it consumes it. Assurance flows as one graded quantity, entering at the scope of reliance recorded at acceptance and release: An A0 Exploratory object demonstrates conformance shallowly and rarely; an A4 Critical object demonstrates it comprehensively, independently and often. The invariants are never graded: identity, attribution, justification, inspectability, provenance and lineage are demonstrated at full strength at every class. Only the depth above that floor scales. Assurance class therefore parameterises every dimension (§6), every test (§7) and every review cadence (§15) at once, from a single recorded value. 12 · The Assessment Process An assessment is technology-neutral and proceeds in seven steps: The process is itself governed: an assessment records its own scope, evidence, findings and reasoning, so that the assessment can be reconstructed (Conformance Principle: assessment remains reconstructable). 13 · Findings 13.1 The four kinds of finding An individual finding is one of four kinds — mirroring mature systems-engineering and quality practice without importing its terminology wholesale: Observation — something noted as interesting or contextual, not itself a problem. Recommendation — an improvement opportunity; conformance is not at risk, but could be strengthened. Exception — an intentional, attributable, bounded deviation, accepted as risk with no invariant breached (§14). Non-Conformance — an architectural obligation is not satisfied; where an invariant is breached, the Non-Conformance is architectural, not merely operational. 13.2 The overall assessment outcome Findings roll up into one assessment outcome, deliberately not “pass / fail”: Conformant — obligations in scope are satisfied and demonstrated. Conformant with observations — satisfied; observations or recommendations recorded. Partially Conformant — some obligations satisfied; specific, bounded gaps recorded with remediation. Non-Conformant — one or more material obligations unsatisfied, or an invariant breached. Not Assessable — evidence is insufficient to demonstrate the claim. This is a real outcome, never silently converted to Conformant, and never to Non-Conformant either: it obliges either evidence or escalation. Consistent with KF-3005 , a Not-Assessable / Indeterminate condition is never treated as Pass, and an exception never converts an invariant breach into conformance. 13.3 Confidence in Findings Conformance and confidence in the finding are not the same thing, and the framework keeps them distinct. Two objects may both be found Conformant while warranting very different confidence: one with complete, event-native evidence, unbroken traceability and strong provenance; another with sparse evidence, partially reconstructed history and thin traceability. Both may satisfy their obligations; our confidence that they do differs. Every material finding therefore carries a confidence qualifier reflecting the completeness, independence and directness of the evidence it rests on — for example high (complete, event-native, independently corroborated), moderate (adequate but partly reconstructed) or low (sparse, or reliant on the assessed party’s own assertion). Confidence never changes the finding, but it travels with it: a Conformant-at-low-confidence result is a signal to strengthen evidence, not a defect in the object. Confidence interacts with assurance class. A Consequential or Critical object found conformant only at low confidence is itself worth a recommendation (§13.1), because at high reliance the demonstrability of conformance matters as much as conformance — an obligation discharged but poorly evidenced has not been fully demonstrated. Confidence is thus how the framework surfaces the gap between being conformant and being able to show it . 14 · Exceptions Architecture is never perfect, and a framework that cannot record imperfection drives it into hiding. Exceptions make deviation visible and governed rather than silent. The framework recognises: accepted deviations — a difference from the reference architecture that satisfies the obligation by another means (a conforming variation); temporary waivers — a time-limited governance exception permitting operation one class below the norm, accepted as risk by a named authority; known limitations — an acknowledged gap not yet remediated, recorded with its consequence; compensating controls — an alternative control that discharges the obligation where the standard mechanism cannot; future remediation — the recorded plan and owner for closing a gap. Every exception is attributable, bounded and visible until closed, formally accepted as risk, or rendered irrelevant by retirement ( KF-3001 IC-19). No exception may waive an invariant: an invariant breach is a Non-Conformance, not an exception. 15 · Architectural Review This chapter institutionalises architectural governance and is the home of the “completeness” discipline — recast, as elsewhere, from an absolute proof into a periodic, materiality-graded review. Review occurs at defined moments: Continuous review — the event-native checks of §16, running as the architecture operates. Vertical-slice review — assessment of a real object taken end to end (the first being the MacroLab Singapore assessment); the primary means by which this framework and KF-2003 are themselves validated before being frozen. Major-release review — before a release enters consequential reliance. Periodic architecture review — at a cadence set by the highest assurance class in scope. Reference-architecture revision — when a domain document changes, to confirm coverage still holds. Independent review — conducted without sole reliance on the assessed parties (IC-18), for A4 and regulated overlays.
