KF-3009 does not redefine terms; it locates them. 14 · Architectural Evolution The architecture is designed to change without losing coherence. Two distinct governance modes keep evolution disciplined — and the distinction between adding architecture and changing it is itself load-bearing. 14.1 Controlled Extension (new concepts) Adding to the architecture. The numbering space is reserved rather than filled ad hoc: KF-3010+ — reserved for future architectural domains, admitted only if they pass the KF-3000 Architectural Admission Test and own a concept no existing document owns. Deeper treatments — a dedicated temporal or dependency model, say — would extend, not revise, the existing domains, and would be traced here. Discipline — no new document may duplicate a concept owned in §4; a proposed addition that would must instead amend the owning document. This is the Navigational Principle applied to growth. 14.2 Controlled Revision (existing concepts) Changing what already exists. Revision follows the inheritance rule the Canon fixes: a lower level may change how it satisfies a higher one, but may not silently revise the higher one. Amend at the home — a concept is revised only in its owning document (§4); every secondary reference then inherits the change. Constitutional amendments — a change to a Canonical Principle is made against the Landscape’s evidence and propagated downward ( KF-1000 ); it is never overridden quietly in a lower document. Re-trace after revision — when any home document changes, the crosswalks here and the conformance completeness check ( KF-3007 §7.1) are re-run to confirm coverage still holds. The series is considered conceptually complete at KF-3008 ; anything beyond elaborates, operationalises or validates that core. Extension adds a new home; revision changes an existing one; neither duplicates a concept already owned. 15 · Summary The Knowledge Foundry Reference Architecture is intentionally modular. Architectural understanding therefore depends not only on the individual documents but on the relationships that bind them together. This document provides those relationships — the map, the ownership boundaries, the crosswalks, the relationship catalogue and the master traceability — ensuring that the architecture may continue to evolve while remaining coherent, navigable and traceable. The series answers six questions in order: what is the architecture ( KF-3000 ), what are its domains ( KF-3001 –3005), how do they operate together ( KF-3006 ), how is its integrity demonstrated ( KF-3007 ), who may legitimately make it consequential ( KF-3008 ), and how does the whole fit together ( KF-3009 ). Ending with synthesis rather than another specialised framework is the point: the last document is the one that makes all the others easier to understand and maintain. Together these documents establish a complete architectural lineage from constitutional principle to institutional reliance. KF-3009 closes the Reference Architecture by making that lineage explicit, navigable and maintainable. Closing Statement KF-3009 is the atlas to the constitution. It creates no law and owns no concept save the relationships among the rest. Its success is measured not by what it adds but by what it makes navigable: an architect, an implementer, a reviewer or a governance officer should be able to enter the architecture anywhere, find where every concept lives, follow any obligation from principle to conformance, and trust that the whole remains one coherent, traceable system. With it, the Reference Architecture is not merely a set of documents — it is a map of a single governed knowledge system, and a means of keeping it coherent as it evolves.

d: Worked instantiations of the architecture — illustrative, not normative
x: Purpose The KF-5000 series shows the Knowledge Foundry architecture at work on concrete Operational Knowledge Objects . Its documents teach and demonstrate; they do not legislate. Like the KF-0000 navigation series, KF-5000 introduces no new architectural concept — every element it shows is defined in its home document (Canon, Lifecycle, Materiality, and the KF-3000 series) and is only instantiated here. The series exists because an architecture is easier to trust once it has been seen to run. A reader who has followed one governed object from capture to retirement understands the whole shape of the system before studying any single part in depth. The distinction the series preserves KF-5001 · Canonical Vertical Slice is illustrative : a domain-neutral object (a four-day-week Knowledge Brief) constructed to make every architectural stage visible. It proves the parts fit together and that the architecture is subject-independent. It does not validate the architecture — a constructed object cannot surprise its designer. KF-5002+ · Case Studies are evaluative : real domain instantiations — beginning with MacroLab’s Singapore Business Impact Assessment — in which the architecture meets uncontrolled reality. These are where the architecture is stress-tested, and where the Draft for Experiment documents ( KF-2003 , KF-3007 , KF-0002 ) are eventually validated before baselining. The order is deliberate: understand the architecture on the canonical slice; then evaluate it on real cases. MacroLab is thereby positioned as a case study of Knowledge Foundry, not as its defining example. Contents ID Title Kind KF-5001 Canonical Vertical Slice — the four-day-week Knowledge Brief Illustrative exemplar — Teaching Learning Domain — any subject as a governed knowledge domain Illustrative sketch KF-5002+ Case Studies (MacroLab Singapore Business Impact Assessment, and others) Evaluative case studies An illustrative teaching-and-learning domain Illustrative, not validated — a sketch of what the discipline looks like applied to a taught subject. Any course can be treated as a governed knowledge domain rather than a folder of slides recreated each term. Take any subject — Corporate Finance is used here only as an illustration; the shape is the same for public health, contract law or machine learning. The subject becomes an Operational Knowledge Object domain: the canonical concepts and the explanations that carry them; the evidence behind each claim; worked examples and the assessment tied to stated learning outcomes; and the research and revisions that keep it current. Each element has provenance, an accountable owner, and a governed way of changing. What changes for the institution: every cohort improves the same asset instead of rebuilding it, so departmental knowledge accumulates rather than resetting; teaching and research feed one another; a claim relied on in a lecture can be traced to its source and its justification; and what the department knows survives the turnover of who happens to teach it. The aim is that students reason from a trusted, inspectable domain — and that AI used in the course is grounded in approved, governed material rather than whatever it happens to generate. This is a sketch of intent, not a validated result. Like every exemplar here, it illustrates the architecture; it does not prove it. Validation comes only from a real course governed this way — the kind of first case the programme is built to invite. Relationship to the rest of the programme KF-5000 sits beside KF-4000 (Implementation): where KF-4000 defines how the architecture is built in a deployment, KF-5000 shows how it behaves on individual objects. Both are downstream of the architecture and neither may revise it. For where every concept is defined, see KF-3009 (Crosswalks) and KF-0002 (Controlled Vocabulary).

d: One governed knowledge object, walked from capture to retirement — the "Hello, World!" of Knowledge Foundry
x: Programming has a tradition: before the language reference, a tiny complete program — “Hello, World!” — proves the language, compiler and runtime work together, and lets a newcomer see the whole shape of a thing before learning its parts. This document is that program for Knowledge Foundry. It takes one Operational Knowledge Object and follows it from the moment it enters the system to the moment it leaves, showing at every step which services act on it, which records it leaves behind, which gates and controls it must pass, who holds the authority to make it consequential, and how its conformance can later be reconstructed. The reader never has to swap objects out of mind. This document teaches Knowledge Foundry, not the four-day week. The subject is incidental. A reader should finish understanding how governed knowledge works — not holding a view on working hours. Like KF-3009 , KF-5001 introduces no new architectural concept; it only instantiates concepts defined in their home documents, cited as it goes. The example is a Knowledge Brief — a governed statement that answers one consequential question — because a brief is the simplest object that still exercises the whole architecture: several kinds of evidence, genuine counter-evidence, an authority that must accept reliance, and a life that continues after acceptance. 1 · The Object Knowledge Brief KB-4DW-01 — “Should our organisation move to a four-day working week?” Attribute Value Identity KB-4DW-01 (assigned once, immutable for life) Type Knowledge Brief — one consequential question, one governed answer Intended reliance informs the Executive Committee’s decision on whether to run a trial Assurance class A3 Consequential ( KF-2003 ) — it will materially influence a significant organisational decision Overlays internal · confidential Steward the People Operations lead Accepting authority the Executive Committee That single classification — A3 — will quietly govern how deep every later step must go. Hold it in mind; §6 returns to it. 2 · The Guided Journey The object advances one lifecycle stage at a time ( KF-2001 ). At each stage below: what happens to the brief · the services that act ( KF-3003 ) · the records it emits ( KF-3004 ) · the gate and controls it passes ( KF-3005 ) · the conformance dimension it exercises ( KF-3007 §6). Every record named is emitted by the act itself — nobody stops to fill in a separate form ( KF-3006 §9). Capture — state: Candidate The question is posed and candidate material is admitted: the Iceland public-sector trials, the UK 2022 pilot, two single-firm case studies, several peer-reviewed studies, and our own retention and output data. Capture is deliberately permissive — nothing is trusted yet — but one thing cannot be deferred: origin . Each source is recorded with where it came from. Services: Object Registry (SVC-01), Provenance (SVC-15). Records: Identity Record (KB-4DW-01), Intake Record, Provenance Seed. Gate: GATE-REG-01; controls: identity resolution and duplicate detection (CTRL-ID-01/02). Dimension: Structural. Authority: Creation (the Steward) — light, because nothing is yet relied upon. Structure — state: Structured The raw material is given form: the question, the candidate claims, the sources and their relationships are made inspectable. The object can now be reasoned about. Service: Representation (SVC-02). Records: Structured Representation, Metadata, Relationship Map. Gate: GATE-STR-01. Dimension: Structural. Evaluate — state: Evaluated Each piece of evidence is assessed for quality — and they are not equal. The Iceland and UK pilots are large and externally evaluated; the single-firm cases are vivid but weak; our internal data is primary but short-horizon. The counter-evidence is admitted here, not buried : reverted pilots, volunteer-firm self-selection, coverage costs in customer-facing roles. Services: Evaluation (SVC-04), Evidence (SVC-03). Records: Evidence Records, Quality Assessment, Evaluation Verdict, Counter-evidence Records. Gate: GATE-EVA-01; controls: evidence presence, evaluation completion, counter-evidence visibility (CTRL-EVD-01/03, CTRL-EVA-01). Dimension: Evidence. Justify — state: Justified The reasoned case is assembled. Claims are linked to their supporting and defeating evidence; assumptions are written down ( “our role mix resembles the pilot firms; productivity means output-per-week; the window is ≥ 6 months” ); an epistemic status is set: Warranted for a bounded trial among knowledge-worker teams under the stated assumptions — not yet warranted for permanent, organisation-wide adoption. Counter-evidence and the sector-dependence claim remain attached. Service: Justification (SVC-05). Records: Justification Record, Assumption Record, Rationale Record, Epistemic Status Record. Gate: GATE-JUS-01; control: justification completeness (CTRL-JUS-01). Dimension: Evidence. Because the object is A3 , this stage also draws an independent reviewer (§6) — an A1 note would not have. Accept — transition; state: Accepted Now the decisive act, and the one the whole architecture is built around: justification is not acceptance. The brief is well-warranted, but warrant is not reliance. The Executive Committee — not the author, not the reviewer — decides that the organisation will rely on it, and fixes the scope of that reliance: a six-month trial for knowledge-worker teams, not permanent adoption. Service: Authority and Acceptance (SVC-06). Records: Acceptance Record, Scope-of-Reliance Record. Gate: GATE-ACC-01; controls: authority mandate and acceptance validity (CTRL-AUT-01, CTRL-ACC-01). Dimension: Authority. The acceptance record — naming the authority, the scope and the date — is the evidence that acceptance occurred (§4). Operationalise — state: Operational The accepted brief is turned into something the organisation can act on: a recommendation to run a six-month four-day-week trial for knowledge-worker teams, measured on output-per-week and retention , linked back to the warrant that justifies it. Services: Operationalisation (SVC-12), Release (SVC-10). Records: Actionable Form, Warrant Linkage, Release Record. Gate: GATE-REL-01. Dimension: Governance. Govern — state: Governed The object is given an owner and a review schedule so its legitimacy is maintained , not assumed. Currency conditions are set: a new major study or the trial’s own results will trigger review. Service: Stewardship and Review (SVC-07). Records: Stewardship Assignment, Review Schedule. Gate: GATE-REV-01. Dimension: Governance. Apply — state: in use → outcomes The recommendation informs the actual trial decision. Its use is recorded, and the trial’s results — output held steady, retention rose, two client-facing teams struggled — return as outcomes. Service: Application and Outcome (SVC-13). Records: Application Record, Explanation Record, Outcome Record, Feedback. Gate: GATE-APP-01. Dimension: Behavioural. Evolve — state: Next Version The trial’s outcomes are new evidence. The brief re-enters at Evaluate, its claims are re-justified against real internal data, and — because a new version does not inherit warrant — it passes through Acceptance again . Version 2 recommends extending the trial for knowledge-worker teams and excluding client-facing teams pending a different approach. Service: Version and Lineage (SVC-09). Records: Version Record, Change Record, Lineage Record. Gate: GATE-EVO-01. Dimension: Lifecycle. The predecessor is not overwritten; v1 and v2 are linked. Supersede / Retire — state: Historical A year on, the brief is folded into a broader Flexible Working Framework that governs four-day weeks, hybrid and compressed hours together. KB-4DW-01 is superseded — its successor linked, its history preserved append-only. Had the idea been abandoned instead, it would have been retired with the reason recorded. Either way, nothing is erased: the organisation can still reconstruct, years later, what it once decided and why. Service: Retirement and Preservation (SVC-14), with Version and Lineage (SVC-09). Records: Supersession Link (or Retirement Record), Historical Object Record. Gate: GATE-RET-01. Dimension: Traceability. What only the whole journey shows. Every record above was emitted by doing the step , not by a separate filing exercise — the journey is the evidence trail. And the six lifecycle invariants held at every step: one identity throughout, every transition attributed and justified and inspectable, provenance present from Capture, lineage preserved through Evolve and Supersession. 3 · The Same Story as a State Machine Every arrow is a governed transition: recorded, attributed, justified. There are no silent moves — that is the single difference between this and a document that merely changes status. 4 · Conformance, Demonstrated Long after the decision, someone asks: was this brief properly governed? KF-3007 answers it against the object, through four tests: Constitutional coverage — every act traces to a Canonical Principle: the object was governed not as knowledge but as an OKO (I), engineered as a lifecycle (II), accepted by collective authority (III), justified before reliance (VIII). Operational coverage — every transition has a trigger, an authority, criteria and a recorded outcome; every gate evaluated explicit exit conditions. Integrity coverage — the six invariants held; counter-evidence stayed attached; evidence was proportionate to A3 . Reconstructability — the material claims can be rebuilt from the record. A worked Conformance Claim. Claim: “The acceptance of KB-4DW-01 held sufficient authority for A3 reliance.” Supported by: the Acceptance Record (authority = Executive Committee; scope = six-month trial; date), the Authority Mandate Record confirming the Committee’s remit for A3 decisions, and the independent-review record required at A3. Assessment: Constitutional + Operational + Integrity + Reconstructability all satisfied. Finding: Conformant , at high confidence — the evidence is complete, event-native and independently corroborated ( KF-3007 §13.3). Had the independent review been missing, the same reconstruction would have returned Not Assessable for that claim — never a silent pass. 5 · Authority, Demonstrated The acceptance was made by the Executive Committee , and the architecture can resolve that authority all the way down ( KF-3008 §5.1): Because the object is A3 , three authority conditions applied that a lower class would not have required: the accepting authority was confirmed , an independent review stood between justification and acceptance, and separation held — the People Operations lead who evaluated and justified the brief was not the body that accepted it ( KF-3008 §11). Authority here is not seniority: the Committee’s right to accept rests on its mandate for consequential decisions, not on rank. 6 · Materiality, Demonstrated Everything above was shaped by one value set at the very start: A3 Consequential. Materiality never changed the path — an A0 note and an A4 board paper cross the same gates — but it set the depth at each one ( KF-2003 ; KF-3001 IC-23): At this stage Because it is A3 Had it been A1 (Working) Justify independent review; counter-evidence recorded; explicit assumptions a named owner’s own reasoning would suffice Accept confirmed authority; defined scope of reliance no acceptance required at all Govern active monitoring; scheduled review review on change only Reconstruct claims reconstructable end-to-end shallow, on request The six invariants held identically at both classes. Only the depth above that floor scaled. This is the whole of materiality in one object: same architecture, same guarantees, proportionate effort. 7 · The Point — Generality Nothing in the journey depended on the four-day week. Swap the subject and every stage, service, record, gate, authority and conformance test is unchanged: Domain Example Operational Knowledge Object Personal knowledge a literature review on spaced repetition Organisation the four-day-week brief (this slice) Research a systematic-review conclusion Healthcare a clinical guidance note Education a curriculum standard Engineering a design decision record Economics (MacroLab) a Singapore Business Impact Assessment Knowledge Foundry does not govern management, medicine, engineering or economics. It governs Operational Knowledge Objects. The subject matter changes; the architecture does not. That is what the slice exists to prove — and why the architecture, not the example, is the thing to remember. 8 · Using This Exemplar Every architecture document can point to the same running object rather than inventing its own: To see… Read KF-5001 … Alongside the lifecycle on a real object §2 KF-2001 the elements collaborating §2–§3 KF-3006 §6 how conformance is demonstrated §4 KF-3007 who may make it consequential §5 KF-3008 how reliance sets the depth §6 KF-2003 that the architecture is domain-neutral §7 the Canon’s central claim Status and Honest Limits This is a canonical illustration , and it illustrates — it does not validate. A constructed object confirms the architecture on an object built to succeed; it cannot surprise us, and surprise is what an experiment is for. The documents still marked Draft for Experiment ( KF-2003 , KF-3007 , KF-0002 ) therefore remain provisional until one real, uncontrolled object has been run and allowed to break something. KF-5001 makes the architecture legible; it does not close that experiment. That is the honest boundary of a “Hello, World!” — it proves the parts fit together, not that they survive the world.

t: KF-L001-B01 · Knowledge as the Object of Knowledge Systems
d: Representation, Evidence and Justification
x: Purpose To examine the foundational concepts that underpin knowledge systems and to determine what exactly is engineered, governed, represented and evolved across the diverse traditions examined in the Literature Landscape. Rather than attempting to resolve centuries of philosophical debate concerning the nature of knowledge itself, this chapter investigates the practical concepts that repeatedly appear across Knowledge Engineering, Knowledge Management, Information Science, Governance and Artificial Intelligence. Its purpose is to establish a coherent conceptual vocabulary for the remainder of the Literature Landscape and to provide a common foundation for the subsequent Literature Synthesis. Executive Summary Every scholarly tradition examined in the preceding chapters refers to knowledge. Knowledge Engineering represents knowledge (B02). Knowledge Management cultivates it (B03). Governance disciplines regulate its change (B04). Foundation models increasingly manipulate it parametrically (B05). Yet surprisingly few traditions explicitly agree on what constitutes the object that these systems manipulate. This chapter does not seek a universal definition of knowledge. It examines instead the concepts that consistently recur across the literature: information, representation, claims, evidence, justification, accepted knowledge, and the knowledge systems that operate upon them. The chapter advances one interpretive claim, developed cumulatively and marked throughout as provisional. Knowledge systems rarely manipulate knowledge directly. They operate upon representations, evidence relationships and processes of justification through which knowledge is established, maintained and revised — and upon the acceptance by which a community certifies a representation as knowledge at all. This restates, at the level of foundational vocabulary, a line already load-bearing across the Landscape: Every knowledge system governs representations, not knowledge itself. Consistent with the Literature Landscape methodology, whether this interpretation adequately reconciles the preceding chapters is reserved for C01. Orientation for the Standalone Reader The preceding chapters examined knowledge through four complementary dimensions. B02 investigated the engineering of knowledge systems and read that history as a progressive expansion of the object of engineering. B03 examined knowledge as enduring collective capability across eight adjacent traditions. B04 examined the governance of knowledge change and named six recurring Governance Primitives. B05 evaluated whether foundation models fundamentally alter those conclusions, and found that they relocate capabilities across the symbolic–parametric boundary rather than abolishing them. This chapter steps back from those perspectives. Rather than examining a particular scholarly tradition, it investigates the foundational concepts that all of those traditions appear to share. A note on placement. Within the agreed chapter order (B02 → B03 → B04 → B05 → B01 → C01) this chapter is written last among the evidence chapters and therefore assumes the reader has already met the traditions. It functions less as an introductory primer than as a conceptual consolidation: the point at which the vocabulary used loosely across four chapters is made precise, immediately before the Synthesis. A reader encountering B01 first will still find the concepts self-contained, but the cross-references reward prior reading. 1. Introduction Knowledge is among the most frequently used — and least consistently defined — concepts in the scholarly literature. Philosophers debate its justification. Information scientists distinguish it from information. Knowledge engineers represent it computationally. Organisations attempt to manage it. Artificial intelligence increasingly models it parametrically. Each tradition adopts definitions appropriate to its own purposes. Each definition is locally coherent and globally incompatible with the others. This chapter treats that incompatibility as data rather than as a defect to be corrected. Operational knowledge systems cannot wait for epistemology to converge; they are built and governed regardless. The interesting question is therefore not what knowledge ultimately is , but what these systems actually operate upon when they claim to handle knowledge. The objective is accordingly modest and deliberately so. This chapter does not resolve philosophical disputes concerning the essence of knowledge. It investigates the concepts that recur across the knowledge sciences and examines how they relate to one another within knowledge systems. 2. Central Research Question The chapter is organised around one guiding question. What is the object manipulated by knowledge systems? Supporting questions include: What distinguishes information from knowledge? What is a representation? What constitutes a knowledge claim? What is evidence? What is justification? When does information become accepted knowledge? What exactly do knowledge systems engineer, govern and evolve? The question is posed operationally, not metaphysically. It asks what a working system holds, transforms and hands on — not what knowledge is in the last analysis. 3. Analytical Lens Unlike previous chapters, which analysed scholarly traditions, this chapter analyses foundational concepts. The Landscape’s recurring tradition-lens — Scale → Capability → Time (introduced in B03) — is designed to compare disciplines. It is the wrong instrument for comparing concepts, which have no scale of operation and no institutional time horizon of their own. This chapter therefore adopts a concept-oriented lens of six recurring analytical questions. Dimension Guiding Question Definition How is the concept defined? Purpose Why is the concept necessary? Relationship How does it relate to neighbouring concepts? Limitations What does the concept fail to explain? Role in Knowledge Systems How is the concept operationalised? Implications What follows for subsequent chapters? The two lenses are complementary rather than competing. The six-question lens characterises each concept; §6 then shows how the concepts, once characterised, populate the Capability and Time axes of the tradition-lens and map onto B04’s six Governance Primitives. B01 supplies the vocabulary; the axis-lens spends it. Figure B01·1 — the recurring KF-L001 review method, applied uniformly across every evidence chapter of the Landscape. 4. Corpus of Investigation Unlike previous chapters, whose corpora consisted of intellectual traditions, this chapter examines the principal conceptual building blocks that recur throughout the knowledge sciences. Each concept below is examined through the six-question lens of §3. The treatment is compact by design: the aim is a shared vocabulary precise enough to be reused, not a monograph on each term. 4.1 Knowledge Central Question: What does the literature mean by “knowledge”? Representative literature: Plato; Gettier (1963); Polanyi (1966); Goldman (1979). Definition. The classical account defines knowledge as justified true belief — a belief that is true and held for adequate reasons (Plato, Theaetetus ; Meno , where true belief is “tethered” by an account, aitias logismos ). Gettier (1963) demonstrated with brief counterexamples that justified true belief can still fail to be knowledge, when the justification is true only by accident. Six decades of proposed repairs (causal, reliabilist, no-false-lemmas, defeasibility) have refined but not closed the definition. Purpose. The concept exists to mark a status stronger than mere opinion: a claim one is entitled to act upon and to transmit to others as settled. Relationship. Knowledge sits atop the other concepts in this chapter. It presupposes a representation to be believed, evidence in its favour, and justification linking the two. Polanyi (1966) adds an orthogonal distinction: much knowledge is tacit — “we know more than we can tell” — and therefore resists representation altogether. Limitations. No operational definition commands consensus. Worse for engineering, the two most-cited features of knowledge — truth and tacitness — are precisely the two a machine cannot directly inspect. A system cannot verify that a belief is true (only that it is justified and accepted), and it cannot store what is tacit (only what has been made explicit). Role in Knowledge Systems. Because truth and tacitness are inaccessible, systems substitute a tractable operational knowledge object: they hold representations, track the evidence and justification attached to them, and record the community’s acceptance. “Knowledge,” in an operational system, is the name given to a representation that has cleared those three tests. Implications. If knowledge itself is inaccessible to the system, then the object of engineering, management and governance cannot be knowledge as such. This is the chapter’s central move, established here and defended across §§4.2–4.8. (The tacit/explicit distinction is used here only to motivate the representational limit; its social and managerial development belongs to B03 and is not duplicated.) 4.2 Information Central Question: How is information distinguished from knowledge? Representative literature: Shannon (1948); Buckland (1991); Floridi (2011); with Ackoff (1989) and Dretske (1981) in support. Definition. There is no single definition, but three influential ones frame the field. Shannon (1948) defines information syntactically, as the reduction of uncertainty, and pointedly excludes meaning. Buckland (1991) distinguishes information-as-process, information-as-knowledge and information-as-thing — the last being the tangible object (a document, a record) that systems actually store. Floridi (2011) offers a semantic definition: information is well-formed, meaningful and (on the strong reading) truthful data. Purpose. The concept isolates the transmissible, storable, measurable substrate beneath knowledge. Shannon’s version is what makes storage and communication engineerable at all. Relationship. The folk model — the DIKW hierarchy (data → information → knowledge → wisdom; Ackoff, 1989) — treats information as knowledge’s raw material. That hierarchy is widely taught and widely criticised (Rowley, 2007; Frické, 2009) for implying a clean, one-directional refinement that the concepts do not support. Dretske (1981) supplies a cleaner bridge: knowledge is belief caused by the information that makes it true. Limitations. Shannon’s measure ignores meaning; Floridi’s truth-condition is contested; the DIKW ladder mistakes a vocabulary for a mechanism. None of the three, alone, explains how information acquires the warrant that distinguishes it from knowledge. Role in Knowledge Systems. Systems overwhelmingly operate on Buckland’s information-as-thing. What they physically hold are informational artefacts. The transition from such an artefact to “knowledge” is not a change of substance but the attachment of evidence, justification and acceptance — the work of §§4.5–4.7. Implications. If the difference between information and knowledge is warrant rather than substance, then a knowledge system is an information system plus the machinery that governs warrant. This reframes the object of engineering as warranted information , not a separate substance called knowledge. 4.3 Representation Central Question: How is knowledge represented? Representative literature: Davis, Shrobe Szolovits (1993); Peirce; Newell Simon (1976). Definition. A representation is a surrogate — a stand-in that lets a system reason about something without operating on the thing itself. The canonical statement (Davis, Shrobe Szolovits, 1993) analyses any knowledge representation through five roles simultaneously: a surrogate for the world; a set of ontological commitments about what exists; a fragmentary theory of intelligent reasoning; a medium of efficient computation; and a medium of human expression. Purpose. Representation makes knowledge manipulable. Only once something is represented can it be stored, indexed, inferred over, transmitted or governed. Relationship. Semiotics locates the general structure: Peirce’s triad of sign, object and interpretant insists that a sign is never its object and always requires interpretation. The Physical Symbol System Hypothesis (Newell Simon, 1976) is the strong engineering wager that symbol manipulation suffices for intelligence. B05’s parametric representations sit at the far end of the same axis — distributed and sub-symbolic, but still surrogates. Limitations. Every representation is partial and committed: its ontological commitments admit some distinctions and foreclose others (Davis et al., 1993). It cannot capture the tacit remainder (§4.1), and it can be faithful or unfaithful without announcing which. Role in Knowledge Systems. The representation is the thing the system actually holds and changes. Engineering (B02) is the design of representations; governance (B04) is the disciplined change of representations over time. Implications. Because a representation is a surrogate and never its object, no system operates on knowledge unmediated. This is the concept that most directly grounds the chapter’s guiding line: systems govern representations, not knowledge. 4.4 Claims Central Question: What constitutes a knowledge claim? Representative literature: Toulmin (1958); Popper (1959); argumentation theory and knowledge representation. Definition. A claim is a representation asserted as true — a proposition put forward for acceptance and therefore capable of being supported or defeated. In representational terms it is an assertion or axiom; in argumentation it is the conclusion a structure of reasons is built to bear. Purpose. The claim is the unit that carries a truth-value and a burden of proof. Only something asserted can be evidenced, justified, accepted, contested or revised. Relationship. Toulmin (1958) decomposes the surrounding structure — claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal — showing that a claim never stands alone but is embedded in the reasons that license it. Popper (1959) adds the demarcation condition: a claim earns scientific standing only if it is falsifiable, i.e. exposes itself to defeating evidence. Limitations. A claim’s truth is not settled by its being asserted, nor even by its being justified (Gettier again). The claim isolates the bearer of warrant without supplying the warrant. Role in Knowledge Systems. The claim is the atomic governable unit. Provenance attaches to claims; validation targets claims; versioning tracks claims as they are asserted, qualified, retracted and superseded. B04’s Governance Primitives all take claims as their operands. Implications. If the claim is the unit that is asserted and defended, then evidence and justification (next) are best understood not as free-standing objects but as relations to a claim. 4.5 Evidence Central Question: What justifies accepting a claim? Representative literature: Sackett et al. (1996); Achinstein (2001); Wang Strong (1996). Definition. Evidence is that which raises or lowers the credibility of a claim. It is inherently relational: nothing is evidence simpliciter , only evidence for or against some claim. Achinstein (2001) distinguishes potential, veridical and subjective evidence; a Bayesian gloss treats evidence as whatever changes the probability of a hypothesis. Purpose. Evidence converts an asserted claim into a credible one. It is the currency in which credibility is bought. Relationship. Evidence-based practice (Sackett et al., 1996) institutionalises the concept as graded — some evidence counts for more — and thereby introduces quality as a first-class property. Information-quality research (Wang Strong, 1996) supplies the dimensions (accuracy, completeness, timeliness, and others) along which evidential inputs are themselves assessed. Limitations. Evidence underdetermines claims: the same evidence can support rival claims, and its weight depends on background assumptions that are rarely explicit. Evidence establishes credibility, not truth. Role in Knowledge Systems. Evidence is stored and governed as links — the traceable relations between a claim and its supporting or defeating grounds. This is exactly B04’s Evidence/Justification primitive, and its integrity is what Provenance/Traceability and Validation/Quality exist to protect. Implications. If evidence is a relation and not a possession, the system’s real asset is the graph of claims and their evidential links — not a heap of facts. 4.6 Justification Central Question: Why should a claim be believed? Representative literature: Goldman (1979; 1999); with foundationalism/coherentism and internalism/externalism as framing debates. Definition. Justification is the structure of reasons connecting evidence to a claim such that accepting the claim is warranted. Where evidence is the material, justification is the argument that assembles it. Reliabilism (Goldman, 1979) locates justification in the reliability of the process that produced the belief; internalist accounts locate it in reasons accessible to the believer; foundationalist and coherentist accounts disagree over whether justification terminates in basic beliefs or in mutual support. Purpose. Justification is what makes belief rational and defensible rather than merely caused. It is the concept that answers challenges. Relationship. Justification is the hinge of the classical definition of knowledge and the site of the Gettier problem — showing that even true, justified belief can fall short. Social epistemology (Goldman, 1999) extends justification beyond the individual to testimony, expertise and institutional processes, which is where operational systems in fact live. Limitations. Justification guarantees neither truth nor acceptance. It can be locally impeccable and globally mistaken; and a well-justified claim may still be rejected by the community that matters. Role in Knowledge Systems. This is the pivotal operational point of the chapter. A system cannot engineer truth — truth is not inspectable. It can engineer justification: it can record why a claim is held, by what process, on what evidence, and expose that structure to audit. Justification is the richest thing a knowledge system can actually govern. Implications. If justification is what systems can govern and truth is not, then the honest description of a “knowledge” system is a justification-management system. The candidate concern of governed knowledge evolution — the controlled transition of a system from one justified state to another — takes justification, so defined, as its object. (The chapter states this dependency; it does not adjudicate any methodology’s contribution, which is reserved for C01.) 4.7 Accepted Knowledge Central Question: When does a community recognise knowledge as accepted? Representative literature: Kuhn (1962); Wenger (1998); Lave Wenger (1991); Argyris Schön (1978). Definition. Accepted knowledge is a claim that a community with the authority to do so has certified and adopted as settled for its purposes. Acceptance is a social status, not a property of the claim in isolation. Purpose. Acceptance closes the loop between the individual’s justified belief and the collective’s usable stock. It is what turns “a well-justified claim” into “what we know.” Relationship. Kuhn (1962) shows acceptance operating at the scale of paradigms and scientific communities; Communities of Practice (Lave Wenger, 1991; Wenger, 1998) at the scale of situated groups; organisational learning (Argyris Schön, 1978) as the single- and double-loop revision by which accepted knowledge is corrected. Acceptance is therefore the concept that most clearly requires B03’s social dimension and B04’s notion of authority. Limitations. Communities can accept the false and reject the true; acceptance tracks warrant and power, not truth. It is also revisable — today’s accepted knowledge is tomorrow’s superseded claim. Role in Knowledge Systems. Acceptance is operationalised as authorisation and release: the recorded act by which a claim moves to “approved,” “published” or “current,” under some authority. This is precisely B04’s Authority and Versioning/Release primitives. Implications. If acceptance is authorised release, then the object of a knowledge system includes not just claims and their justification but their acceptance-state — who certified what, when, and under what authority. 4.8 Knowledge Systems Central Question: What exactly do knowledge systems manipulate? Representative literature: Knowledge Engineering (B02); Knowledge Management (B03); AI (B05); Information Systems. This concept is not a further building block but the convergence point the previous seven build toward; it is analysed here to state what the chapter has been assembling. Definition. A knowledge system is any system that holds representations and governs their evidence, justification and acceptance so as to make warranted claims available, revisable and trustworthy over time. Purpose. Such systems exist to let a community act on, transmit and revise what it takes itself to know, without each member re-deriving it. Relationship. The traditions surveyed across the Landscape are, on this reading, specialisations by which part of the vocabulary they foreground: engineering foregrounds representation (B02); management foregrounds conversion and acceptance (B03); governance foregrounds the disciplined change of claims and their justification (B04); AI foregrounds a new representational substrate (B05). Limitations. No tradition foregrounds all of the vocabulary at once. Each holds part of the object steady while working on another part — a division of labour that B04 named for change-governance specifically and that this chapter generalises to the whole vocabulary. Role in Knowledge Systems. Trivially, this is the role. The substantive point is negative and is the chapter’s thesis: at no layer does the system reach past its representations to touch knowledge itself. Implications. The seven preceding concepts jointly specify the object. A knowledge system manipulates representations of claims, the evidence and justification attached to them, and their acceptance-state under some authority. It does not manipulate knowledge. That is the finding carried to §8 and to C01. 5. Comparative Analysis Each concept has been analysed through the six-question lens of §3. Read across, three patterns recur. Conceptual dependency. The concepts form a dependency chain rather than a set of alternatives. Knowledge presupposes justification; justification assembles evidence; evidence attaches to claims; claims are asserted representations; representations stand in for information about reality. Remove any link and the ones above it lose their footing. The recurring retreat from truth. At every concept where truth might have been the operative property — knowledge (4.1), information (4.2, Floridi’s truth-condition), claims (4.4), justification (4.6), acceptance (4.7) — the operationalisable property turns out to be something adjacent that a system can actually inspect: warrant, credibility, justification-structure, authorised acceptance. Truth is the property the literature reaches for and the property systems cannot hold. Disciplinary foregrounding. Traditions differ less in their vocabulary than in which term they treat as primary and which they take for granted (§4.8). The comparative concept map summarises the relationships and, for each concept, the Governance Primitive (B04) and the operational knowledge object through which systems actually handle it. Concept Neighbouring concepts Inaccessible Property Operational Knowledge Object Governance Primitive (B04) Information reality, representation meaning / truth (contested) information-as-thing (Buckland) — (substrate) Representation information, claim fidelity to its object the surrogate itself Provenance/Traceability Claim representation, evidence truth of the assertion the asserted, versionable unit Versioning/Release Evidence claim, justification the truth it would establish evidential links Evidence/Justification; Validation/Quality Justification evidence, knowledge truth of the conclusion the recorded reason-structure Evidence/Justification; Reversibility/Audit Accepted knowledge justification, knowledge truth of what is accepted authorised acceptance-state Authority; Versioning/Release Knowledge all of the above knowledge itself (truth + tacit remainder) representation that cleared the tests (all six, collectively) The right-hand columns are the chapter’s contribution to the Landscape vocabulary: they show every foundational concept resolving, under engineering pressure, into something a system can store and govern — and none of them resolving into knowledge. 6. Cross-Concept Patterns The chapter investigates whether a common conceptual progression emerges across otherwise diverse traditions. A provisional operational sequence is: Figure B01·2 — the operational sequence: a loop, not a ladder. The stages a claim passes through inside a working system, with feedback edges from acceptance back to representation. Three qualifications are essential, and each keeps the sequence within the Landscape’s restrained posture. It is operational, not metaphysical. The sequence is not a theory of how knowledge really arises. It is a description of the stages a claim passes through inside working systems — evaluated for descriptive fit, not asserted as truth. It is a loop, not a ladder. Justification and acceptance feed back: a defeated claim revises the representation; a superseded acceptance-state triggers re-justification. Reading the sequence as one-directional would repeat the DIKW error criticised in §4.2. The concern with governed change lives precisely in the return edges, where an accepted state is transitioned to a new justified state. What persists through every iteration of the loop is not knowledge itself, but the governed transition from one accepted representation to another. It maps onto the Landscape lenses. The lower stages (evidence → justification → acceptance) populate the Capability and Time axes of B03’s Scale→Capability→Time lens and correspond one-to-one with B04’s six Governance Primitives. The sequence is thus not a new framework but the spine on which the existing lenses hang. One further pattern, connecting to B05. Foundation models enter this sequence at representation : they supply a new, parametric surrogate. They do not add or remove a stage. The claims, evidence, justification and acceptance downstream of the representation remain obligatory. This is the vocabulary-level statement of B05’s finding — The substrate changes; the epistemic obligations do not. 6.1 Limitations of This Review This chapter does not attempt to resolve longstanding philosophical debates concerning the nature of knowledge. Its conclusions are bounded by: a selective corpus , chosen for recurrence across the knowledge sciences rather than for completeness within philosophy; an emphasis on operational rather than metaphysical questions , which deliberately brackets truth; an interdisciplinary scope that trades depth in any single tradition for comparability across several; an interpretive synthesis whose central claim is offered as a reading, not a proof. Its purpose is to establish a shared conceptual vocabulary rather than a universal epistemology. 7. Existing Contributions Across the literature, several concepts may be regarded as mature foundations of knowledge systems — settled enough to be relied upon before any synthesis is attempted. These include: the distinction between information and knowledge, framed as a difference of warrant rather than substance (Shannon, 1948; Buckland, 1991; Floridi, 2011); symbolic representation and its five roles (Davis, Shrobe Szolovits, 1993); the tacit/explicit distinction marking the limit of representation (Polanyi, 1966); evidence as a graded, relational property (Sackett et al., 1996; Achinstein, 2001); justification as the governable structure of reasons (Goldman, 1979); acceptance as a social, authorised status (Kuhn, 1962; Wenger, 1998); the structure of a claim and its defences (Toulmin, 1958; Popper, 1959). This inventory establishes the conceptual foundations already available. It is genuinely mature: none of it is any methodology’s to claim, and the Synthesis inherits it as given. 8. Candidate Integrative Insight Only after examining the literature does the chapter advance its candidate observation. It is offered as an interpretation of the assembled concepts, not as a demonstrated result, and its adjudication is reserved for C01. Proposition B01 · The Object of Knowledge Systems Knowledge systems do not manipulate knowledge directly. They manipulate representations of claims, the evidence and justification attached to them, and their acceptance-state under some authority — the machinery through which knowledge is established, maintained and revised. The insight is negative in an important sense. It does not tell us what knowledge is; it tells us what the object of engineering, management and governance is not . Every layer surveyed in the Landscape — symbolic and parametric, individual and social, static and evolving — operates on the operational knowledge object, never on knowledge unmediated. To fix the vocabulary in a single figure, the object resolves through the following anchor sequence, which C01 adopts as the spine of the Synthesis: Figure B01·3 — the anchor sequence, adopted by C01 as the spine of the Synthesis. The Conceptual Object is the abstract object this chapter defines; the Operational Knowledge Object is the concrete artefact a knowledge system actually manipulates — the versioned representation together with its attached evidence, justification and acceptance-state. The distinction is dormant here and becomes load-bearing in C01; it also fixes the term that replaces the looser “proxy” used earlier in the drafting. If this reading holds, it dissolves a recurring confusion in the field. Debates about whether a system “really contains knowledge” are, on this account, mis-posed: no system does, and none needs to. What a system can contain, warrant, govern and revise is the vocabulary of §4. Whether that reframing does real work — or merely relabels a familiar intuition — is exactly the kind of question the Synthesis exists to test. 9. Burden of Proof Consistent with the Literature Landscape methodology, this chapter defines evidence, not theory. It establishes what any methodology claiming to engineer knowledge systems would need to explain, structured around the three standard questions. Established (what is mature). The conceptual foundations of §7 are settled and inherited as given: the warrant-based distinction between information and knowledge; representation and its five roles; the tacit/explicit limit; evidence as graded and relational; justification as a governable reason-structure; acceptance as an authorised social status; and the structure of a claim and its defences. Unresolved (what remains open). No tradition foregrounds the whole vocabulary at once, nor operationalises the concepts together rather than one at a time. A methodology claiming to engineer knowledge systems would need to demonstrate: what it treats as the operational knowledge object, given that knowledge itself is inaccessible to the system; how claims are related to evidence, and how that relation is stored and traced; how justification is represented, recorded and audited; how acceptance is authorised, released and revised; how representations evolve without loss of warrant; how symbolic and parametric representations interoperate within one governed object (per B05); how these concepts are operationalised together rather than one at a time (per §4.8’s division of labour); how tacit knowledge is accommodated despite being only partially representable (per Polanyi, §4.1). Implication (what the synthesis must explain). Whether existing traditions already discharge these requirements — individually or collectively — is not judged here. The requirements are stated as the standard against which the Synthesis will assess any candidate methodology. 10. Relationship to Previous and Subsequent Chapters B02 examined knowledge from an engineering perspective; B01 specifies the conceptual object upon which engineering, governance and computation operate. B03 examined knowledge as collective capability; B01 supplies the acceptance and justification vocabulary its social account presupposes. B04 examined the governance of knowledge change; B01 shows that its six primitives are the operational counterparts of this chapter’s concepts. B05 examined whether foundation models alter previous assumptions; B01 locates their contribution at a single stage (representation) and confirms the obligations downstream are unchanged. B01 therefore establishes the conceptual vocabulary that underpins all four perspectives. Together, the five evidence chapters provide the material for the Literature Synthesis (C01), where the overall gap — deferred throughout the Landscape — is finally stated and tested. 11. Guiding Principle The organising principle of this chapter is intentionally simple. Knowledge systems rarely manipulate knowledge itself. They manipulate representations, claims, evidence, justification and acceptance — through which knowledge is constructed, communicated, governed and revised. Every knowledge system governs representations, not knowledge itself. Understanding these conceptual building blocks provides the foundation for integrating the engineering, social, governance and computational perspectives developed throughout the Literature Landscape — and for the Synthesis that follows. The enduring challenge of knowledge systems is therefore not the storage of knowledge, but the disciplined governance of representations through which knowledge is recognised. With the object now clarified, the Landscape can synthesise the engineering, capability, governance and computational traditions into a single conceptual framework. That synthesis is C01.
