t: KF-L001-B05 · Foundation Models and the Knowledge Sciences
d: Testing the Assumptions of Knowledge Systems
x: Purpose This chapter critically examines whether foundation models fundamentally alter the assumptions underlying knowledge engineering, collective knowledge capability and knowledge governance as surveyed in B02, B03 and B04. It is not a survey of AI technologies. It is an interrogation of the assumptions about knowledge systems that recent advances in artificial intelligence are alleged to have overturned. Applying the common analytical methodology used throughout the Literature Landscape, the chapter evaluates which assumptions remain valid, which require modification, which become more or less important, and which genuinely new capabilities have emerged. Its purpose is not to determine whether AI changes everything, but to determine precisely what it changes — and, equally importantly, what it does not. Executive Summary Foundation models have transformed artificial intelligence from a set of narrowly specialised systems into broadly capable computational partners. Knowledge can now be generated rather than only retrieved; reasoning can be approximated in natural language; and complex workflows can increasingly be delegated to semi-autonomous systems. These developments have prompted a strong claim: that earlier approaches to knowledge engineering, knowledge management and governance are now obsolete. This chapter evaluates that claim and finds it overstated. Examined assumption by assumption, foundation models do not eliminate the engineering, stewardship and governance capabilities matured by the traditions surveyed earlier in the Landscape. They relocate those capabilities across a new boundary — between symbolic representations, which are explicit and inspectable, and parametric representations, which are distributed and opaque. Read through the analytical spine of the Landscape, the finding is continuous rather than revolutionary. B03 argued that every knowledge system governs representations, not knowledge itself; foundation models introduce a genuinely new representation, not a new knowledge. B04’s six Governance Primitives — evidence/justification, authority, provenance/traceability, validation/quality, versioning/release, reversibility/audit — remain necessary under foundation models, but several of them (provenance and reversibility above all) become markedly harder to instantiate in a parametric substrate. Consistent with the Literature Landscape methodology, whether this relocation constitutes a genuinely new paradigm, or an evolutionary extension of the traditions already surveyed, is reserved for C01; this chapter does not argue for any candidate methodology. Orientation for the Standalone Reader The three preceding evidence chapters examined knowledge from complementary perspectives. B02 — The Evolution of Knowledge Engineering — traced how the object of engineering progressively expanded across successive generations, and identified a candidate gap around the cross-layer governance of knowledge change. B03 — Knowledge Beyond Engineering — examined how knowledge becomes enduring collective capability across eight adjacent traditions, and introduced the Landscape’s recurring analytical lens: Scale → Capability → Time. B04 — Governing Knowledge Change — examined how knowledge change becomes legitimate, and distilled six Governance Primitives together with the notion of a division of governance labour across traditions. This chapter asks a different kind of question. Rather than surveying a further tradition, it tests whether the emergence of foundation models overturns the conclusions the previous chapters reached. The unit of analysis is therefore not a tradition but an assumption — a deliberate structural pivot explained in Section 4. 1. Introduction Foundation models are among the most consequential developments in the history of artificial intelligence. Trained at scale on broad data and adaptable to many downstream tasks, they exhibit broad linguistic competence, in-context and few-shot learning, and behaviours often described as emergent reasoning (Bommasani et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2020). These capabilities have prompted claims that traditional approaches to representing, organising and governing knowledge are no longer necessary. If a model can answer a question directly, why curate an ontology? If it can generate an explanation, why maintain a document repository? If it can act through tools, why engineer a workflow? At the same time, persistent concerns — hallucination, opacity, provenance loss, model drift, and the difficulty of correction — suggest that many longstanding problems remain unresolved and, in some respects, are aggravated (Ji et al., 2023; Bender et al., 2021). The purpose of this chapter is therefore to separate genuine discontinuities from evolutionary extensions of the traditions already surveyed. It approaches the question with the restraint applied throughout the Landscape: strong claims of novelty are treated as hypotheses to be tested against the literature, not as premises. 2. Central Research Question The chapter is organised around a single guiding question. What fundamentally changes under foundation models? Supporting questions: Which long-held assumptions remain valid? Which require revision? Which become more important? Which become less important? Which genuinely new capabilities emerge? Which new governance challenges appear? Does AI change the nature of knowledge itself — or only its representation? The final question is stated deliberately in its sharpened form. Section 6 returns to it directly, and the answer the chapter defends is anticipated by B03: knowledge systems govern representations, not knowledge; foundation models supply a new representation, not a new epistemology. 3. Analytical Lens Each assumption is examined through six recurring questions. This is a chapter-specific lens, purpose-built for stress-testing assumptions; it does not displace the Landscape-wide Scale → Capability → Time device from B03. Section 6 reconnects the two explicitly, and Assumption Six is analysed using B04’s six Governance Primitives so that B05 remains commensurable with the chapters around it. Dimension Guiding Question Traditional Assumption What assumption previously held? AI Development What has changed? Continuing Validity What remains true despite the change? New Capability What genuinely new capability emerged? Remaining Limitations What problems remain unresolved — or worsen? Relevance to Governed Knowledge Evolution What should be inherited, adapted or reconsidered? The “Relevance to Governed Knowledge Evolution” row records burden-of-proof implications only. It states what any AI-native knowledge methodology would have to account for; it does not claim that any particular methodology accounts for it. That argument is reserved for C01. Figure B05·1 — the recurring KF-L001 review method, applied uniformly across every evidence chapter of the Landscape. 4. Corpus of Investigation The corpus consists not of technologies but of eight assumptions about knowledge systems that foundation models are said to challenge. On the pivot from traditions to assumptions. B02–B04 each surveyed eight traditions. B05 surveys eight assumptions. The change is deliberate. The prior chapters asked what a mature field knows; this chapter asks what a field’s inherited commitments can still be relied upon to be true. Because foundation models cut across every tradition at once, an assumption-based corpus keeps the analysis integrative rather than fragmenting it into eight parallel technology reviews. The representative literature under each assumption is illustrative of where the assumption is contested, not an exhaustive survey. 4.1 Assumption One — Knowledge must be explicitly represented Representative literature: symbolic AI and knowledge representation (Brachman Levesque, 2004); foundation models (Bommasani et al., 2021); studies of emergent internal structure and probing (Tenney et al., 2019). Central question: Can implicit parametric representations replace explicit symbolic knowledge? Traditional assumption. From expert systems onward, usable knowledge had to be made explicit — encoded in rules, frames, ontologies or graphs — so that it could be inspected, reused and reasoned over. AI development. Foundation models store knowledge implicitly, distributed across billions of parameters. No sentence, triple or rule is written down, yet the model can produce fluent, often accurate, knowledge-bearing outputs across domains. Continuing validity. Explicit representation remains indispensable wherever knowledge must be inspected, audited, contested or guaranteed. Parametric knowledge cannot be pointed at; a regulator, auditor or downstream system still requires an explicit artefact. B03’s principle holds without amendment: the system governs a representation, and a parametric weight matrix is simply a new — and unusually opaque — kind of representation. New capability. Broad coverage without hand-authoring. A single model exhibits competence across domains that would each have required a dedicated, laboriously engineered knowledge base. Remaining limitations. Implicit knowledge is not addressable, not selectively editable, and not reliably separable from error. Probing shows structure exists internally, but that structure is not an interface. Explicit and implicit representation are therefore complementary, not substitutes. Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. Any AI-native methodology must operate across both explicit and implicit representations simultaneously and maintain a defensible mapping between them. Representation becomes plural, not obsolete. 4.2 Assumption Two — Retrieval is the primary mechanism for accessing knowledge Representative literature: information retrieval (Manning et al., 2008); dense retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020); retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020); enterprise search practice. Central question: Does generation fundamentally replace retrieval? Traditional assumption. To access knowledge, a system locates and returns the relevant existing artefact. Access is finding. AI development. Generation offers a second mode: the system composes an answer rather than returning a document. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) then re-couples the two — grounding generation in retrieved evidence at inference time. Continuing validity. Retrieval does not merely survive; it is promoted. The most reliable AI knowledge architectures are retrieval-augmented precisely because generation alone lacks grounding and provenance. Retrieval supplies the evidentiary substrate that generation cannot. New capability. Synthesis across sources, and answers to questions for which no single artefact exists. Generation interpolates where retrieval can only return. Remaining limitations. Ungrounded generation fabricates; grounded generation inherits the quality and coverage limits of its retrieval layer. Generation shifts, but does not remove, the burden of having good sources — and it introduces a new failure mode in which fluent output masks an absent or misused source. Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. The dichotomy of “retrieval vs generation” is false. The methodological requirement is to govern the coupling — to ensure generated claims remain traceable to retrieved, authorised evidence. This is the provenance primitive from B04 restated under generation. 4.3 Assumption Three — Reasoning requires explicit symbolic structures Representative literature: chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022b); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023); tool use (Schick et al., 2023). Central question: What kind of reasoning emerges from foundation models? Traditional assumption. Reasoning is the manipulation of explicit symbols under formal rules — deductive, sound, and inspectable. AI development. Foundation models exhibit approximate, language-mediated reasoning: chain-of-thought decomposition, tool invocation, and interleaved reasoning-and-acting produce answers that look like multi-step inference without an explicit symbolic engine. Continuing validity. Where soundness, verifiability or guarantees are required, explicit symbolic and formal methods remain necessary. Parametric reasoning is plausible, not provable; it is a heuristic approximation, and its steps are rationalisations that may not correspond to the computation that produced the answer. New capability. Flexible, general-purpose reasoning over natural-language problems without task-specific symbolic engineering — a breadth classical methods never achieved. Remaining limitations. No soundness guarantee; sensitivity to prompt phrasing; confidently wrong chains. The reasoning is probabilistic and non-deterministic, which sits uneasily with any domain requiring reproducibility. This motivates neuro-symbolic hybrids (Assumption Eight). Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. Reasoning becomes a spectrum from probabilistic to formal. A methodology must place work on that spectrum deliberately, and must not treat plausible generation as though it carried the guarantees of deduction. 4.4 Assumption Four — Knowledge systems are largely static Representative literature: catastrophic forgetting and continual learning (French, 1999; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017); model editing (Meng et al., 2022; Mitchell et al., 2022). Central question: Can parametric knowledge evolve deliberately? Traditional assumption. A knowledge base changes when a human deliberately edits an identifiable artefact; between edits it is stable and its state is known. AI development. Parametric knowledge changes through retraining, fine-tuning and targeted model-editing techniques (e.g. locating and rewriting factual associations). Change is now possible inside the model, not only in the documents around it. Continuing validity. Deliberate, addressable, reversible change remains the goal — and remains far easier over explicit artefacts than over weights. B04’s entire apparatus of versioning, release and reversibility presupposes that one can name a state and return to it; parametric substrates make that presupposition hard to satisfy. New capability. Direct intervention on internal knowledge, and continual adaptation without full re-authoring. Remaining limitations. Edits interact unpredictably, may not generalise, and can regress unrelated capabilities; catastrophic forgetting persists. Crucially, parametric knowledge is difficult to version and roll back with confidence — the state before an edit is not cleanly recoverable. Change became possible before change became governable. Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. This is the sharpest point of contact with B02’s candidate gap and B04’s primitives. The controlled transition of a knowledge system from one justified state to another — B02’s framing of the gap — is precisely what parametric substrates make difficult. Any AI-native methodology must deliver versioning and reversibility over representations that natively resist both. 4.5 Assumption Five — Humans remain the primary knowledge workers Representative literature: human–AI interaction (Amershi et al., 2019); hybrid intelligence (Dellermann et al., 2019); generative and LLM agents (Park et al., 2023). Central question: How does AI redistribute cognitive labour? Traditional assumption. Humans create, curate, judge and are accountable for knowledge; machines assist. AI development. Foundation models and agentic systems now perform substantial portions of drafting, synthesis, retrieval and multi-step task execution, shifting the human toward specification, review and adjudication. Continuing validity. Accountability, judgement under ambiguity, and the authority to authorise a knowledge state remain human. B04’s authority primitive does not transfer to a model: a system may generate a claim, but legitimation of that claim as organisational knowledge is an act of authority that remains with people and institutions. New capability. Delegation of cognitive labour at scale, and continuous rather than episodic knowledge production. Remaining limitations. Automation bias, deskilling, diffusion of responsibility, and the difficulty of holding a probabilistic system accountable. Redistribution of labour is not redistribution of accountability. Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. Cognitive labour is redistributed; governance authority is not. A methodology must define the human–AI division of labour while keeping the division of governance labour (B04) anchored to identifiable human authority. 4.6 Assumption Six — Governance applies primarily to symbolic knowledge Representative literature: Model Cards (Mitchell et al., 2019); Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2021); NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST, 2023); ISO/IEC 42001 (2023); model risk governance (e.g. SR 11-7). Central question: Can existing governance mechanisms govern parametric knowledge? This assumption is analysed directly against B04’s six Governance Primitives, so that B05’s most governance-heavy section speaks the Landscape’s shared vocabulary. Evidence / Justification. Partially transferable. RAG and citation restore some evidentiary grounding, but a parametric answer’s true justification (its training-data support) is not recoverable. Weakened. Authority. Transferable in principle. Authority remains human and institutional; what changes is the object being authorised (see Assumption Five). Preserved. Provenance / Traceability. Severely strained. Training-data provenance is generally lost, and outputs cannot be traced to the specific inputs that produced them. This is the primitive most damaged by the parametric shift. Most weakened. Validation / Quality. Transferable but harder. Evaluation shifts from artefact inspection to behavioural/statistical testing; correctness becomes distributional rather than checkable per item. Adapted. Versioning / Release. Partially transferable. Model versions can be released, but fine-grained knowledge-item versioning within a model is not yet tractable (see Assumption Four). Partially weakened. Reversibility / Audit. Severely strained. Rolling back a specific piece of learned knowledge, or auditing why a specific output occurred, is largely unsolved. Most weakened. Continuing validity. Governance is more necessary under foundation models, not less — the classic error this chapter corrects. Model cards, datasheets, the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 exist precisely because the primitives do not transfer for free. Remaining limitations. Two primitives — provenance and reversibility — presently lack robust parametric instantiations. Governance frameworks for AI are emerging but immature, and largely procedural rather than technical. Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. The burden is explicit: an AI-native methodology must instantiate all six primitives across both symbolic and parametric knowledge, with particular attention to the two that the substrate most resists. B04’s guiding principle carries over intact — knowledge systems remain trustworthy only because their changes are governed — and becomes harder, not obsolete. 4.7 Assumption Seven — Organisational memory resides primarily in documents Representative literature: organisational memory (Walsh Ungson, 1991); knowledge graphs (Hogan et al., 2021); vector databases and dense indexes (Johnson et al., 2019). Central question: Where does organisational knowledge now reside? Traditional assumption. The institution’s memory lives in documents and records, curated and preserved as explicit artefacts. AI development. Memory is now distributed across documents, knowledge graphs, vector indexes and model parameters. Some organisational knowledge is effectively encoded into fine-tuned or adapted models. Continuing validity. Durable, authentic, preservable records remain the backbone of organisational memory — the archival and LIS concerns from B03 do not lapse. A model is a poor system of record: it cannot attest to what it once “knew,” and cannot be preserved as evidence of a decision. New capability. Memory that is queryable by meaning (embeddings) and partially internalised into behaviour (parameters), not only by document lookup. Remaining limitations. Parametric memory is unstable across model updates, cannot be authenticated, and risks silent loss when a model is replaced. Memory that lives only in weights is memory the organisation cannot guarantee it still has. Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. Organisational memory becomes multi-substrate. A methodology must preserve authentic records as the anchor while accommodating graph, vector and parametric memory — and must prevent model turnover from silently erasing institutional knowledge. 4.8 Assumption Eight — Knowledge Engineering becomes less important Representative literature: neuro-symbolic AI (d’Avila Garcez Lamb, 2023); GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024); knowledge graphs (Hogan et al., 2021); enterprise knowledge systems. Central question: Does AI reduce or increase the need for knowledge engineering? Traditional assumption. If models can generate knowledge, the laborious engineering of ontologies, graphs and pipelines becomes unnecessary. The folk syllogism is simple: more AI, less engineering. It is this assumption, more than any other, that underwrites the claim that foundation models render previous knowledge traditions obsolete — and it is the assumption the evidence contradicts most directly. AI development. In practice the opposite emerges. Reliable AI systems are overwhelmingly hybrid. Knowledge graphs are used to ground and constrain generation, so that a model answers from a curated structure rather than from its own unaudited parameters (GraphRAG). Neuro-symbolic approaches pair parametric flexibility with symbolic guarantees where correctness must be assured. And around the generative core sits an increasingly elaborate engineered apparatus: retrieval indexes and chunking strategies, grounding graphs and schemas, evaluation harnesses and test sets, guardrails and validators, orchestration layers, and agent scaffolding that decomposes tasks and checks intermediate results. The generative model is the cheap component. The reliable system around it is engineered, and engineered heavily. Continuing validity. Knowledge engineering does not disappear; it moves. The task shifts from authoring knowledge artefacts by hand toward designing and orchestrating the system in which a generative core can be trusted. The skill that once produced an ontology now produces the grounding graph, the retrieval design, the evaluation regime and the governance wrapper. This is not less engineering; it is engineering relocated up a level of abstraction. New capability. Less hand-authoring of content; far more architectural engineering — the deliberate composition of symbolic and parametric components into a system whose behaviour is more reliable than either part alone. Remaining limitations. The hardest problems — grounding, provenance, evaluation, controlled change — are engineering problems, and foundation models make them more prominent, not fewer. Removing the model’s need for a hand-built knowledge base did not remove the system’s need for engineering; it merely moved the difficulty from content to architecture, where it is less visible and often underestimated. The counter-narrative, stated plainly. The popular chain runs in one direction: Figure B05·2 — the popular (and unsupported) inference. The evidence supports a different chain: Figure B05·3 — the chain the evidence actually supports. Each link is load-bearing. The engineering changes because the object is now a hybrid system rather than a symbolic artefact. It requires more architecture because reliability is a property of the composition, not of the model. It requires more governance because a probabilistic, opaque, continually changing core must be constrained by exactly the primitives B04 identified. And it requires more orchestration because the work is no longer to state knowledge once but to coordinate retrieval, generation, validation and human authority at run time, on every request. The naïve expectation — that capability at the centre would dissolve the need for structure around it — inverts what practice shows. Bridge to B02. This is where B05 returns to B02 most directly, and deliberately so. B02 read the history of Knowledge Engineering as a progressive expansion of the object of engineering — from rules, to knowledge bases, to ontologies, to knowledge graphs, to the socio-technical systems that surround them. If the object has expanded once more — from knowledge artefacts to Hybrid Symbolic–Parametric Knowledge Systems that are simultaneously symbolic and parametric — then foundation models are not the end of knowledge engineering but its latest enlargement. That reading is available, and Assumption Eight makes it visible. What Assumption Eight does not do is settle it. Consistent with the Literature Landscape methodology, whether this enlargement constitutes a genuinely new stage in B02’s trajectory, or a redistribution of work within the existing one, is reserved for C01. B05 records the shift and its direction; it does not pronounce on its status. The restraint is intentional: the observation that engineering increases under foundation models is well-supported by the literature, whereas any claim that this marks a new epoch is an interpretation that must survive C01, not a premise B05 is entitled to assert. Relevance to governed knowledge evolution. The burden this places on any AI-native methodology is architectural, not merely representational. It is not enough to represent knowledge, symbolic or parametric; the methodology must engineer the coupling, grounding, evaluation and governance that make a generative core trustworthy — and it must do so as a first-class concern rather than a wrapper bolted on afterward. If B02’s throughline is right that the object of engineering keeps expanding, then the demand foundation models place on knowledge engineering is the largest expansion yet: from artefact, to system, to governed hybrid system. 5. Comparative Analysis The following matrix summarises how each assumption fares under foundation models. The Effect column uses a common scale: Holds (unchanged), Holds+ (more important than before), Revised (true but modified), Strained (partially undermined), Superseded (no longer primary). # Assumption AI development Effect One-line reason 1 Knowledge must be explicitly represented Implicit parametric storage Revised Explicit still required for inspection/audit; representation becomes plural 2 Retrieval is primary Generation + RAG Holds+ Grounding elevates retrieval rather than replacing it 3 Reasoning needs symbolic structures CoT / ReAct / tools Revised Approximate reasoning emerges; formal reasoning still needed for guarantees 4 Knowledge systems are static Fine-tuning / model editing Strained Change became possible before it became governable 5 Humans are primary knowledge workers Agents / hybrid intelligence Revised Labour redistributes; accountability and authority do not 6 Governance is for symbolic knowledge AI governance frameworks Holds+ Governance more necessary; provenance reversibility most strained 7 Memory resides in documents Graphs / vectors / parameters Revised Memory becomes multi-substrate; records remain the anchor 8 Knowledge Engineering matters less Neuro-symbolic / GraphRAG Superseded (the claim) Engineering moves to orchestration; need increases No assumption is straightforwardly abolished. The dominant effects are Revised and Holds+ — the signature of redistribution rather than replacement. 6. Cross-Cutting Patterns Reading down the matrix, a small number of tensions recur: explicit vs implicit representation; symbolic vs parametric knowledge; retrieval vs generation; deterministic vs probabilistic reasoning; human vs AI cognition; governance across hybrid systems. In every case the pattern is the same: the capability is not eliminated but relocated across a new boundary . This is where B05 rejoins the Landscape’s shared lens. Through Scale → Capability → Time (B03). Foundation models act most visibly on the Capability axis (what a system can do expands dramatically) and most problematically on the Time axis (governing change, provenance and reversibility over parametric substrates is unsolved). On the Scale axis they lower the cost of broad coverage while raising the cost of guarantees. The lens thus locates AI’s contribution precisely: large capability gains, unresolved temporal governance. The sharpened question — does AI change the nature of knowledge itself? The chapter’s answer is no, and B03 supplies the reason: every knowledge system governs representations, not knowledge itself. Foundation models introduce a new representation — distributed, parametric, opaque — and thereby change the mechanics of engineering, retrieval, reasoning and governance profoundly. They do not change the underlying relations that make something count as knowledge (that it be justified, authorised, preserved, situated). Claims that AI changes “the nature of knowledge” mistake a change of representation for a change of kind. The substrate changes; the epistemic obligations do not. This proposition is offered as a recurring one for the Landscape — a companion to B03’s every knowledge system governs representations, not knowledge itself — and is the chapter’s most compact answer to the sharpened question. Later chapters (B01 on the object of knowledge, C01 on synthesis) may refer back to it directly: whatever new substrate a knowledge system adopts, the obligations to justify, authorise, preserve and govern its representations are unchanged. The synthesis names this directly: the human, symbolic, parametric and hybrid modes catalogued in this chapter are what C01 formalises as Computational Modality — the cross-cutting axis along which the operations of a knowledge system are redistributed, never removed. 6.1 Limitations of This Review The review is constrained by the rapid pace of AI development, unstable terminology, limited longitudinal evidence, an emphasis on scholarly over commercial literature, and a deliberately selective corpus. Several cited capabilities are recent enough that their durability is not yet established — and the literature itself contests some of them (for instance, whether “emergent abilities” are real discontinuities or artefacts of measurement; Schaeffer et al., 2023). The chapter should be read as an interpretive synthesis of a moving field, not a settled account. 7. Existing Contributions Setting interpretation aside, several AI capabilities can already be regarded as established contributions to knowledge systems: general-purpose parametric representations as broadly adaptable substrates; retrieval-augmented generation as a grounding architecture; agentic workflows and tool use; model editing as targeted parametric change; hybrid symbolic–parametric systems (neuro-symbolic, GraphRAG); an emerging AI-governance apparatus (model cards, datasheets, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001); multimodal reasoning. This inventory records what has demonstrably emerged, prior to any claim about its broader significance. 8. Candidate Integrative Insight Advanced only after the evidence above, and marked as interpretation reserved for confirmation in C01. Foundation models do not invalidate the mature capabilities developed by the traditions surveyed in B02–B04. They relocate those capabilities across the symbolic–parametric boundary: Knowledge becomes simultaneously symbolic and parametric (Assumptions 1, 7). Retrieval and reasoning are re-coupled to generation, not replaced by it (Assumptions 2, 3). Governance becomes more important, and unevenly transferable: authority and validation adapt, while provenance and reversibility are the primitives the parametric substrate most resists (Assumptions 4, 6). Engineering shifts from constructing artefacts toward orchestrating hybrid systems (Assumption 8). The literature therefore suggests that foundation models do not replace previous knowledge traditions. Rather, they increase the interdependence between them. Engineering (B02), organisational capability (B03) and governance (B04) become more tightly coupled, because Hybrid Symbolic–Parametric Knowledge Systems require all three simultaneously: a generative core must be engineered into a system, embedded in organisational practice, and governed across its continual change, or it cannot be relied upon at all. Where the previous chapters could examine their traditions largely in parallel, foundation models force them into a single, mutually dependent stack. The candidate insight can be stated in one line: foundation models change where knowledge capabilities reside, not whether they are needed. Consistent with the Literature Landscape methodology, whether this relocation amounts to a genuinely new paradigm, or an evolutionary continuation of the traditions already surveyed, is reserved for C01. 9. Burden of Proof Consistent with the Literature Landscape methodology, this chapter defines evidence, not theory. It establishes what any methodology claiming to support AI-native knowledge systems would have to demonstrate, structured around the three standard questions. Established (what is mature). The AI period has demonstrably delivered new capabilities: parametric representation, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic tool use, model editing, hybrid symbolic–parametric systems, an emerging AI-governance apparatus, and multimodal reasoning (Section 7). Unresolved (what remains open). No assumption is abolished; capabilities are relocated across the symbolic–parametric boundary, and two Governance Primitives resist that relocation. Such a methodology would need to show how it: governs symbolic and parametric knowledge together; validates AI-generated knowledge against authorised evidence; maintains provenance across hybrid systems, including where training-data provenance is lost; supports deliberate, continual revision of parametric knowledge; coordinates human and AI judgement while keeping authority human; governs autonomous agents’ contributions to the knowledge state; preserves organisational memory despite continual model evolution; explains how evidence quality is evaluated when generation exceeds direct retrieval. Implication (what the synthesis must explain). Mapped onto B04’s primitives, requirements 3 and 4/7 fall hardest on provenance and reversibility/versioning — the sharpest test any candidate methodology will face — and the newly added requirement 8 falls on validation/quality: once a system routinely answers beyond what any single retrieved source states, evaluating the quality of the evidence behind a generated claim becomes a distinct problem from evaluating retrieval, and one that C01 will need to address directly. 10. Relationship to Previous and Subsequent Chapters B02 examined the engineering of knowledge systems and the expanding object of engineering. B05 supplies the AI-era data point for that trajectory (Assumption 8) without adjudicating whether it is a new stage. B03 examined how knowledge becomes collective capability, and gave the Scale → Capability → Time lens B05 reuses in Section 6. B04 examined how knowledge change becomes legitimate, and gave the six Governance Primitives B05 applies in Section 4.6. B01 (object) and C01 (synthesis) remain. The overall gap, and the question of whether AI redistribution constitutes a new paradigm, are deferred to C01. Rather than replacing the earlier traditions, AI is evaluated here as a potential reconfiguration of their established principles. 11. Guiding Principle The organising principle is intentionally simple. Foundation models change where knowledge resides. They do not remove the need to engineer, steward or govern it. They require those activities to operate simultaneously across symbolic, organisational and parametric forms of knowledge — and they make two of B04’s Governance Primitives, provenance and reversibility, materially harder to honour. Or, in the single line this chapter proposes to carry forward: The substrate changes; the epistemic obligations do not. Having examined how AI changes knowledge systems, the Landscape can now ask the deeper question that underlies every preceding chapter: what exactly is the object that these systems manipulate? That is the subject of B01. Editorial Note (v0.4) Change from v0.3: one sentence added at the end of §6, immediately after the discussion of B05’s recurring line, naming the chapter’s human/symbolic/parametric/hybrid finding as what C01 formalises as the Computational Modality axis. The addition extends an existing forward-reference to B01/C01 rather than introducing a new one, so the evidence-then-defer discipline is preserved: B05 still records its finding and defers adjudication to the Synthesis. No other content changed. References remain inline pending the v1.0 reference/DOI pass applied to the finalised chapters.

d: What Integrated Understanding of Knowledge Systems Emerges from the Literature?
x: Purpose To synthesise the findings of the Literature Landscape into a coherent understanding of knowledge systems. Rather than reviewing additional literature, this chapter integrates the findings developed across B01–B05. Its purpose is to identify recurring principles, complementary contributions, unresolved tensions, genuine research gaps, and the requirements any integrated methodology must satisfy. Only after those requirements are established does the chapter consider whether a candidate methodology — Knowledge Foundry — might respond to them. It does not evaluate whether that candidate succeeds; that is the work of the chapters beyond the Landscape. Executive Summary The Literature Landscape investigated knowledge systems from five complementary perspectives: engineering, collective capability, governance, artificial intelligence, and foundational concepts. Individually, each tradition provides mature explanations for important aspects of knowledge systems. Collectively, they reveal a single structure. A knowledge system is one governed object, operated on along three dimensions, and enacted across computational modalities. The object is the concept complex established in B01: representation → claim → evidence → justification → acceptance. The three dimensions are operations on that object: it is engineered (B02), collectivised (B03) and governed through legitimate change (B04). The computational modality — human, symbolic, parametric or hybrid — is a cross-cutting axis (B05) that varies who performs each operation and where representations reside, without adding a further operation. No reviewed tradition treats these together. Each holds part of the structure steady while working on another part. The deficiency of the literature is therefore not of components but of coordination — and that observation establishes the requirements against which any candidate methodology, including Knowledge Foundry, must subsequently be evaluated. Orientation for the Standalone Reader This is the synthesis chapter. It reviews no new literature. It reads the findings of the five evidence chapters (B01–B05) and asks whether they support a single integrated understanding. The chapter proceeds in one direction only, and the direction matters: Figure C01·1 — the one-directional synthesis pipeline. Knowledge Foundry enters only at Candidate. Everything up to Requirements is a claim about the literature. Only at Candidate does Knowledge Foundry enter, and it enters as one possible response, not as a demonstrated solution. The methodology and its evaluation lie beyond the Landscape. Preserving that order is what keeps the synthesis honest. 1. Introduction The preceding chapters deliberately separated evidence from interpretation. Each investigated one question and closed with only a provisional integrative insight, explicitly deferred to this chapter. The purpose of C01 is to determine whether those individual insights collectively support a broader interpretation — and, if they do, to convert that interpretation into a set of requirements precise enough to be tested. 2. Central Research Question What integrated understanding of knowledge systems emerges from the Literature Landscape? Supporting questions: Which findings recur across otherwise separate traditions? Which complement one another? Which tensions remain genuinely unresolved? Which assumptions survive the whole review? Which gap persists once the mature contributions are set aside? 3. The Evidence Base The five findings, stated as findings rather than as literature. Each is the portable line its chapter earned. Chapter Question it answered Finding B01 · Concepts What is the object? Systems manipulate representations, claims, evidence, justification and acceptance — never knowledge directly (Proposition B01). B02 · Engineering What do we construct? The object of engineering expands over time — from rules to ontologies to graphs to parametric substrates. B03 · Capability How does knowledge endure? Knowledge is collective and socially authorised; every knowledge system governs representations, not knowledge itself. B04 · Governance How does knowledge change legitimately? Legitimate change requires governance, which decomposes into six recurring primitives. B05 · Computation Do foundation models change the conclusions? Computational modality redistributes the operations across the symbolic–parametric boundary; the substrate changes, the epistemic obligations do not. B01 is set first deliberately. It is categorically unlike the others: it does not describe an activity but defines the object on which every activity operates. That difference is the hinge of the integration that follows. 4. Cross-Chapter Integration This is the intellectual heart of the Landscape. The integrating move is to stop reading B02–B05 as four subjects and to read them as structure around a single object. B01 is not a fifth perspective. It is the ontology underlying every other chapter — the object that engineering constructs, that capability collectivises, that governance changes, and that computation enacts. Once B01 is recognised as substrate, the remaining chapters resolve into three operational dimensions and one cross-cutting axis: Figure C01·2 — the integrated reference model: one governed object, three operational dimensions, one cross-cutting modality axis. Two clarifications make this precise. Why three dimensions, not four. Engineering, capability and governance are operations — things done to the object. Computation is not a fourth operation. B05 never argued that artificial intelligence introduced a new knowledge dimension; it demonstrated that engineering, capability and governance persist, and that what AI changes is the modality in which they are performed. Treating computation as a peer dimension would be a category error. Why “modality,” not “computation.” What varies across B05’s evidence is not computation as such but the mode of computation — human judgement, symbolic manipulation, parametric inference, or hybrids of these. Naming the axis Computational Modality states B05’s actual conclusion: the object and its three operations are constant; the modality in which they are enacted is what redistributes. A note on the object. The diagram distinguishes two senses of “object” that the rest of the thesis keeps apart. The Conceptual Object is the abstract object B01 defines — representation → claim → evidence → justification → acceptance — and answers what the object is . The Operational Knowledge Object is the concrete artefact a knowledge system actually manipulates — the versioned representation together with its attached evidence, justification and acceptance-state — and answers what systems actually operate upon . The operational knowledge object is a concrete instance of the conceptual object. The distinction is dormant in the Landscape and becomes load-bearing once the methodology is specified; it also fixes the term that replaces the looser “proxy” used earlier in the drafting. The disciplines have become a geometry. That geometry is what the rest of the chapter reasons over. 5. Persistent Patterns Six propositions recur across the evidence base with enough force to be treated as settled findings of the Landscape. They are numbered here as Landscape Propositions (L-P1–L-P6) so that the remaining thesis can cite them directly rather than re-deriving them chapter by chapter. L-P1. Knowledge systems manipulate representations, not knowledge. (Proposition B01; B03.) L-P2. The object of engineering expands over time. (B02.) L-P3. Knowledge is collective and socially authorised. (B03.) L-P4. Legitimate change requires governance, which decomposes into six primitives — evidence/justification, authority, provenance, validation, versioning, reversibility. (B04.) L-P5. Computational modality redistributes the operations without removing epistemic obligation. (B05.) L-P6. The persistent challenge is the governed transition between accepted states, not storage. (B01 §11; B04.) The register is a structural device, not merely a summary. A later chapter that writes “by L-P4” invokes the whole governance result in two characters, and the thesis reads as one research programme rather than five separate reviews. 5.1 Interpretive Maxims The Landscape carries one further class of statement, and it is worth naming explicitly, because the thesis now trades in three: a Proposition (L-Pn) is a claim derived from the literature; a Requirement (Rn, §8) is something a candidate methodology must satisfy; an interpretive maxim is a memorable way of thinking about a proposition — not itself a finding, but an operational reading of one. Keeping maxims separate from propositions protects the logical structure: a maxim earns its place by clarifying a proposition, never by adding evidence. The Landscape names one. Inspectable Objects Principle (interpretive maxim) Knowledge systems hold inspectable objects, never truth. An operational interpretation of Proposition L-P1: knowledge systems can inspect, compare, version and govern representations, but truth itself always remains external to the system. 6. Persistent Tensions The literature leaves genuine tensions unresolved. This section does not paper over them; it sorts them. Some are dissolved by adopting a stance and pass out of scope. The remainder are genuinely open, and each becomes a requirement in §8. The open tensions are not defects in the literature — they are the coordinates of the integrated gap. Tension Status Disposition Truth vs justification Dissolved by stance B01’s operational bracket: systems govern justification and acceptance, not truth. Out of scope; underpins R2. Noted, not solved. Tacit vs explicit Genuinely open Polanyi’s representational limit → R9. Symbolic vs parametric Genuinely open The modality boundary → R7. Human vs AI judgement Genuinely open Modality coordination → R8. Engineering vs emergence Genuinely open Constructed vs learned representations → spans R1 + R7. Governance vs autonomy Genuinely open — sharpest Governed change vs autonomous enactment → R6 + R8. The hardest requirement, and the clearest candidate territory. 7. The Integrated Gap This is where the thesis appears. Note the exact claim, and note what it is not. The literature does not lack engineering. It does not lack governance. It does not lack artificial intelligence or knowledge management. Each is mature in isolation. The deficiency is of a different kind. Proposition C01 · The Integrated Gap The literature explains how knowledge systems are engineered, socialised, governed and computationally enacted — but it does not explain how these operations are coordinated over the lifecycle of a single governed knowledge object. This is the strongest claim the evidence supports, and no stronger. It incorporates B01 (the governed object), B02 (engineered), B03 (socialised), B04 (governed) and B05 (computationally enacted) without importing any Knowledge Foundry terminology. It is falsifiable: it would be refuted by any reviewed framework that coordinates all three operations on one object across time, under varying modality. The Landscape found none. Proposition C01 stands in deliberate parallel to Proposition B01. B01 established what the object is ; C01 establishes what the literature, taken whole, fails to do with it . Together they are the two load-bearing propositions of the Landscape. 8. Requirements for an Integrated Methodology The requirements are derived from the evidence — not proposed to suit any methodology. They are stated before Knowledge Foundry is named, and they preserve a full audit trail: each requirement is traceable to the chapters, patterns and tensions that generate it. A condensed formulation is possible for later publication; the thesis retains all ten, because traceability matters more than elegance under examination. ID Requirement Derived from B04 primitive Modality R1 Engineer and construct representations B02; L-P2 (pre-governance) all R2 Manage evidence and justification B01; B04; L-P1 Evidence/Justification all R3 Authorise acceptance and release B03; B04; L-P3 Authority; Versioning/Release all R4 Preserve provenance and traceability B04 Provenance/Traceability all R5 Validate the quality of inputs and claims B04; B01 Validation/Quality all R6 Govern change as controlled transition between accepted states B04; B01 (loop); L-P6 Versioning/Release; Reversibility/Audit all R7 Integrate symbolic and parametric representations B05; symbolic–parametric tension (cross-cutting) symbolic + parametric R8 Coordinate human and AI judgement B05; human-vs-AI, governance-vs-autonomy tensions Authority; Reversibility/Audit human + machine R9 Accommodate tacit knowledge despite partial representability B01 (Polanyi); B03 — mainly non-symbolic R10 Maintain collective memory over time B03; B01 (loop) Versioning/Release all R1–R6 correspond one-to-one to engineering plus the six governance primitives: they are what a single dimension already demands. R7–R10 arise only when the dimensions are considered together under varying modality. R7–R10 are therefore the register’s operational statement of Proposition C01 — the requirements no isolated tradition was obliged to meet. 9. Knowledge Foundry as Candidate Methodology Only now, and only as a candidate, does Knowledge Foundry enter. Not “the solution.” A candidate response to R1–R10. The distinction is enforced in the wording. The mapping below records, for each requirement, what Knowledge Foundry claims to address and at what locus. It does not record that it succeeds. Mechanism is specified in the methodology chapters; success is tested in the evaluation chapters. Both lie beyond the Landscape, and stating either here would argue for Knowledge Foundry before it has been specified. Requirement Knowledge Foundry’s claim (candidacy only) Mechanism Evaluation R1–R5 Claims to adopt the mature foundations — engineering and the five governance primitives — rather than reinvent them specified later deferred R6 Claims its distinctive contribution here: change as a controlled transition from one justified state to another specified later deferred R7 Claims cross-modality coverage of symbolic and parametric representations specified later deferred R8 Claims a coordination model for human and machine judgement specified later deferred R9 Claims to accommodate the tacit remainder specified later deferred R10 Claims continuity of collective memory across transitions specified later deferred Two guardrails are explicit. First, Knowledge Foundry is not positioned as a successor stage to the reviewed traditions; it claims to be a cross-layer governance of change over them. Second, whether it satisfies R1–R10 is an open empirical question — the reason the remaining thesis exists. 10. Relationship to Subsequent Chapters The Literature Landscape ends here. Its hand-off artifact is the requirements register (R1–R10). The remaining thesis is structured as the attempt first to specify a methodology against that register, and then to test whether the specification satisfies it. Every later claim traces back through R1–R10 to the evidence chapters, and through the Landscape Propositions to the literature. The pipeline is therefore complete and one-directional: Figure C01·3 — the complete programme pipeline; every later claim traces back through R1–R10 to the evidence. Guiding Principle The Literature Landscape does not demonstrate that Knowledge Foundry is necessary. It demonstrates that any methodology capable of integrating the engineering, social, governance and computational dimensions of knowledge systems must satisfy a common set of requirements. Knowledge Foundry is introduced only as one candidate response to those requirements. References C01 introduces no new sources. All citations are to B01–B05 and to the works reviewed therein; the DOI pass for those works is held at their respective chapters, deferred to v1.0 per house convention. Appendix — Editorial Notes (flagged decisions, remove at v1.0) Fork decisions applied in this draft (all as agreed): A — B01 rendered as substrate/ontology, set first in §3 and beneath the object in the §4 diagram; not a fifth peer. B / G — Computation reframed as a cross-cutting axis, not a peer dimension; the three true dimensions are Engineering, Capability, Governance. The axis is renamed Computational Modality (Human · Symbolic · Parametric · Hybrid), per Decision G, to match B05’s actual conclusion. C — Patterns promoted to numbered Landscape Propositions L-P1–L-P6, set apart and citable. D / H — The gap is boxed as Proposition C01, in parallel with Proposition B01, using the sharpened wording of Decision H (coordination over the lifecycle of a single governed object). E — All ten requirements retained for traceability; a condensed six-requirement version is reserved for later publication and not built here. F — KF mapping kept thin, and phrased throughout as “claims to” rather than “satisfies,” with mechanism and evaluation explicitly deferred. Two cross-cutting items, now resolved (this pass): Operational-truth line — promoted as an interpretive maxim, not a proposition. Per your refinement, it is set apart in §5.1 as the Inspectable Objects Principle and explicitly typed as an operational interpretation of L-P1. This also introduces the thesis’s three statement classes: Proposition (L-Pn), Requirement (Rn), interpretive maxim. Terminology standardised. “Proxy” is retired across the Landscape in favour of Operational Knowledge Object (the concrete artefact a system manipulates), kept distinct from the Conceptual Object (B01’s abstract object; §4). C01 and B01 are updated this pass. B02–B05 are not in the current working set — when next opened, run the same find-and-replace (“proxy” → “operational knowledge object”) for full Landscape consistency. The acronym OKO is deliberately not introduced yet; it can be adopted later if the methodology chapters make it useful.

t: KF-0002 · Controlled Vocabulary and Architectural Distinctions
d: The authoritative terms of the Knowledge Foundry programme, the distinctions they must preserve, and their user-facing projection
x: Purpose This document is the single authoritative home for Knowledge Foundry terminology. It exists so that a term means the same thing in the Canon, the methodology, the architecture, the implementation, the interface and the training material — and so that distinctions the programme depends on are not quietly collapsed by casual synonymy. It does not re-cut the architecture’s concepts; those are defined in their home documents. It collects them, records the distinctions that must never be treated as synonyms, and defines the small user-facing vocabulary that ordinary users meet in place of the full ontology. Where a definition here and a definition in a home document appear to differ, the home document governs the concept and this document is corrected. Namespace note. This document is numbered KF-0002 on the assumption that the KF-0000 series is reserved for programme-wide constitutional and navigational artefacts (glossary, programme map, document register). It is deliberately not numbered KF-1001, which is already occupied by the Canon’s opening chapter (“The Nature of Governed Knowledge Systems”). If the KF-0000 series is designated otherwise, this document is renumbered without changing its content. The document has four sections: authoritative definitions , required distinctions , permitted user-facing language , and mapping rules . Section 1 · Authoritative Definitions Terms are grouped by the layer that owns them. Each definition is a compact restatement of the governing document; the citation is the authority. Constitutional ( KF-1000 ) Governed knowledge system — a socio-technical system that holds operational knowledge objects and governs their transition from one justified state to another across modalities (KF-1001). Operational Knowledge Object (OKO) — the unit of design: a versioned representation together with its attached evidence, justification and acceptance-state (KF-1101). The system governs the object, never “knowledge itself”. Canonical Principle — an enduring obligation true of any governed knowledge system, admitted only if it survives the two-question test ( KF-1000 Part III). Governance Primitive — one of the six operations by which warrant is conferred: evidence, authority, provenance, validation, versioning, reversibility (KF-1104). Constitutional invariant — one of the five properties whose loss would make a system cease to be a governed knowledge system: inspectability, justification, provenance, governed evolution, human accountability (KF-1050). Lifecycle and method (KF-2000) Lifecycle stage — a distinct engineering responsibility with an entry condition and an exit gate ( KF-2001 ). Transition — a governed move between states; always attributable and justified ( KF-2001 ). Event — an occurrence that triggers a transition; may be raised by a human or an agent, but the transition it triggers remains governed ( KF-2001 ). Gate — a justification checkpoint; the point at which an object may advance only if the obligations of its stage are discharged ( KF-2001 ; KF-3005 ). Lifecycle invariant — one of the six continuously checkable properties of an object at every instant: single identity, attributable transitions, justified transitions, inspectable transitions, provenance always present, lineage preserved ( KF-2001 ). Materiality — the degree to which an object, claim, decision or transition may affect consequential action, reliance, obligation, exposure, representation or preservation ( KF-2003 ). Assurance class — the ordinal grade (A0 Exploratory · A1 Working · A2 Routine · A3 Consequential · A4 Critical) that sets the depth of assurance required; attaches to the release / scope of reliance ( KF-2003 ). Governance overlay — an orthogonal attribute (regulated, confidential, public, client-facing, legally-privileged) adding obligations without changing class ( KF-2003 ). Architecture ( KF-3000 series) Capability — an enduring ability the architecture must possess, independent of workflow, role, service, technology or modality ( KF-3002 ). Service — a logical mechanism with defined responsibility that realises capabilities and maintains records ( KF-3003 ). Component — the technical element that implements part of a service (KF-4000). Practice — the disciplined human or socio-technical method by which work is performed ( KF-2002 ). Control — a reusable mechanism that establishes whether one required condition holds; protects an obligation, risk, policy or invariant ( KF-3005 ). Information / Record object — a structured unit of governed information with one authoritative maintaining service ( KF-3004 ). Evidence record — the durable record that a material obligation or decision was discharged; wherever possible emitted by the governed act itself ( KF-3004 §5.2). Conformance claim — an assertion that an object is governed, accepted, current or reliable, reconstructable to the depth its reliance requires ( KF-3007 ). Release — a version authorised for a defined scope of operational reliance; the anchor to which assurance class attaches ( KF-3000 §2). Navigation ( KF-3009 , KF-0001 ) Relationship — a semantic connection between architectural elements; the canonical relationship types are fixed in KF-3009 §10. Dependency — a relationship in which one element requires another for correct operation. Every dependency is a relationship; not every relationship is a dependency. Traceability — the ability to reconstruct lineage across one or more relationships using observable evidence ( KF-3009 ; KF-3006 §10). Traceability is what makes a relationship demonstrable rather than merely asserted. Section 2 · Required Distinctions These pairs carry the programme’s intellectual weight. They must not be treated as synonyms in any document, interface or procedure. Collapsing any one of them re-introduces the ambiguity the discipline exists to resolve. Distinction The difference that must be preserved Evidence vs. justification Evidence is what supports a claim; justification is the reasoned case — including counter-evidence, assumptions and rationale — for why it may be believed. Justification vs. acceptance Justification establishes why an object may be believed; acceptance establishes that an identified authority will rely on it. Neither substitutes for the other. Principle vs. invariant A principle governs progression (what a transition must earn); an invariant governs conformance (what must remain true at every instant). Capability vs. service A capability is what must be possible; a service is one mechanism by which it is delivered. A capability need not reduce to a single service. Object vs. representation The object is the enduring governed identity; a representation is one form of its content. One object may have several representations. Identity vs. version Identity is immutable and singular; a version is one immutable state of the object’s content under that identity. Provenance vs. lineage Provenance is origin and derivation of content; lineage is the historical relationship between objects and versions (branch, supersede, consolidate). Transition vs. event An event is what happened ; a transition is the governed move it triggers. An event never bypasses a gate. Control vs. gate A control tests one condition; a gate orchestrates several controls into one decision ( KF-3005 §29). Evidence record vs. conformance claim An evidence record is the durable proof an obligation was discharged; a conformance claim is an assertion reconstructable from such records. Assurance class vs. maturity profile A class grades how much rigour a particular object is governed to ( KF-2003 ); a maturity profile describes how much architecture an implementation has stood up ( KF-3000 §20). Relationship vs. dependency vs. traceability A relationship is any semantic connection between elements; a dependency is a relationship of required operation ; traceability is the reconstruction of lineage across relationships from observable evidence ( KF-3009 ). Section 3 · Permitted User-Facing Language Ordinary users experience governance; they do not study its ontology. Interfaces and operating procedures may use the following five-state vocabulary in place of the internal lifecycle states. These terms are controlled projections of the architecture — simplifications sanctioned here — not replacements for the formal vocabulary, which continues to govern beneath them. User-facing term What the user understands Draft Being worked on; not yet approved to rely on Under Review Being checked; approval not yet complete Approved Approved to rely on, within a stated scope Needs Updating Something has changed; its currency is in question Superseded Replaced by a newer object or version No other user-facing state names are sanctioned without amendment to this document. Assurance class may be surfaced to users in plain terms (e.g. “for significant decisions”) but the class codes A0–A4 are architectural, not user-facing. Section 4 · Mapping Rules The user-facing terms map to internal architecture as follows. The mapping is the contract: an interface showing a user term asserts that the corresponding internal condition holds. User-facing term Internal meaning Draft Object exists but is not accepted for operational reliance (pre-Acceptance lifecycle states) Under Review One or more required evaluation or justification activities are incomplete (Evaluate / Justify stages, or a returned object) Approved Accepted for a defined scope of reliance (Acceptance recorded; a valid Release within scope) Needs Updating A currency or validity condition has been breached or questioned (a Continuing-Review or dependency event has fired) Superseded A successor object or version has replaced the object for defined use (Supersession Link recorded; lineage preserved) Rules of use. 1. A user term may be shown only when its internal condition is satisfied; the interface does not assert states the architecture has not reached. 2. The mapping is many-to-one downward: several internal states may present as one user term (e.g. Evaluate and Justify both present as Under Review ). It is never one-to-many: a single internal condition does not present as two contradictory user terms. 3. The internal state remains the source of truth for every governed decision. User terms are for comprehension, not for authority. Status and Maintenance This document is Draft for Experiment . The five-state projection and the required distinctions are to be tested against the first vertical slice: does the five-state vocabulary suffice for a real user of a Consequential object, and do the distinctions hold up when one object is taken end to end? It moves to Approved after that evidence. The glossary is maintained as a controlled vocabulary in its own right — changes are governed, attributable and versioned, exactly as the architecture requires of any governed record.
